author: Alkarim Billawala / alkarim.billawala.ca
weeks: Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders

questions.stem: A curriculum committee is reviewing a proposed diagnostic category defined entirely by a pattern of behaviour that the patient's community finds objectionable. The patient reports no distress about the behaviour and continues to work and maintain relationships without difficulty. Applying the principles that made DSM-III a paradigm shift, which of the following is the strongest single reason to exclude this category?
options: It was not derived from a Neo-Freudian understanding of the symptoms
It does not cause subjective distress and/or significant impairment in function
It can only be reported by the patient, not observed by the examiner
Its inter-rater reliability has not yet been compared with that of DSM-II
questions.explain: Why: DSM-III's first rule is that for something to be considered a disorder it MUST cause subjective distress and/or significant impairment in function — exactly what this proposal lacks, and exactly the flaw PW03 attributes to DSM-II, whose "diseases" often represented behavioural deviances without clear dysfunction or distress. Not the others: DSM-III deliberately abandoned expert interpretation of symptom meaning, so Neo-Freudian derivation is a reason against, not for; DSM-III accepts signs and symptoms either reported by the patient or observed by the examiner, so patient report alone is not disqualifying; and while reliability is DSM-III's third rule, the decisive defect here is the absence of distress or impairment, not an untested reliability figure.

guide.s: subjective distress and/or significant impairment in function

questions.stem: A resident preparing grand rounds on the 1930s reviews the era's somatic treatments for institutionalized patients with intractable symptoms, all of which were rationalized by anecdotal reports of patients seeming briefly more lucid after fevers or seizures. Which statement best reflects what appropriately conducted research eventually showed?
options: Insulin-induced coma was the only modality with durable benefit, particularly in psychosis
Fever-inducing treatments outperformed the others but carried unacceptable mortality
Electroconvulsive therapy was the only survivor, and although developed for psychosis it was found most helpful for mood symptoms
Psychosurgery was effective but was discredited solely because untrained operators performed it
questions.explain: Why: PW03 is explicit — research supporting all of these except ECT was consistently negative when done appropriately, and "even ECT, which was developed to treat psychosis, was found most helpful for mood symptoms." That indication drift is the quotable fact on the slide. Not the others: insulin coma and fever therapy are among the modalities whose research was negative, not survivors; and lobotomy's problem was not merely who performed it — outcomes were usually worse, risks unacceptable and consent not rigourous, with untrained operators an additional failure rather than the reason it failed.

questions.stem: A medical historian is asked why the dominant psychoanalytic explanation for unexplained neurological symptoms could not be extended to soldiers returning from the Western Front with paralysis, tremor and mutism despite no physical injury. Which explanation does PW03 give?
options: Charcot's Salpetriere work had already been discredited by the outbreak of the war
The construct held that hysteria is a feminine disease of weak women with repressed sexual fantasies, which could not accommodate male soldiers
Military physicians had no access to the psychoanalytic literature during wartime
The soldiers' symptoms were shown on post-mortem examination to have an anatomical basis
questions.explain: Why: The module states that the idea that these symptoms were connected to repressed sexual fantasies "is quickly thrown out (hysteria is a feminine disease, present in weak women with repressed sexual fantasies)" — the gendered construction of the diagnosis, not new data, is what broke it, the module's clearest illustration of social assumptions shaping diagnosis. Not the others: Charcot's work is presented as the origin of Freud's observations, not as discredited; access to literature is never raised, and psychoanalysis became more prominent through the wars; and no anatomical basis was found — the symptoms were attributed to the experience of war "shocking" the nervous system, with Menninger and colleagues treating them by talk therapy and hypnosis.

questions.stem: In the early 1970s a group of psychiatrists in St. Louis produced symptom-based checklists that could be tested statistically for stability and validity, and pharmaceutical companies simultaneously pressed for a way to identify homogenous enough groups of patients for their new psychotropics. Which finding from the social scientists studying psychiatric practice most directly created the problem both of those efforts were solving?
options: Diagnosis was being made on behaviour considered deviant rather than on symptoms causing suffering
Neo-Freudian psychiatrists regarded repressed ideas as more important than diagnosis
Inter-rater reliability in psychiatric diagnosis was as low as 30%
There was a fundamental difference between treating confirmable biological derangements and theoretical constructs
questions.explain: Why: All four were the social scientists' concerns, but the checklist programme and pharma's need for homogeneous trial populations are both solutions to unreliable diagnosis: the St. Louis work continued until inter-rater reliability and stability of diagnosis could be improved to high enough levels, and a drug trial needs patients who would receive the same label from any assessor. Reliability "as low as 30%" is the number PW03 attaches to that problem. Not the others: the deviance critique and the biology-versus-construct critique are answered by DSM-III's distress-or-impairment rule rather than by a checklist; and the Neo-Freudian devaluation of diagnosis is the attitude being displaced, not the measurable defect the checklists were built to fix.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old carpenter reports several weeks of neck pain with numbness that he demonstrates by rubbing the pad of his thumb and the radial side of his forearm. Power is full throughout and reflexes are symmetric. Using the dermatome test points that are the standard for this course, which single nerve root does his sensory symptom localize to?
options: C5
C6
C7
C8
questions.explain: Why: The course's circled test points are C5 lateral upper arm · C6 thumb · C7 middle finger · C8 little finger · T1 medial arm, and the C6 band runs along the lateral forearm into the thumb — exactly the territory described. Not the others: C5 is tested over the lateral upper arm in the deltoid region; C7 is the middle finger; C8 is the little finger and the medial border of the hand, and on this figure the medial forearm band is T1 rather than C8.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old woman has six weeks of shock-like pain radiating down the right arm. On examination she has weakness of elbow extension and of finger extension, a depressed right triceps reflex, and reduced pinprick over the middle finger. Tone is normal and the plantar response is flexor. Which single nerve root best explains all of her findings?
options: C5
C6
C7
C8
questions.explain: Why: The primer's power list pairs elbow extension, finger extension (C7), the triceps reflex is C7, and the C7 dermatome test point is the middle finger — one root accounts for the motor, reflex and sensory findings together, which is the intersection method PW02 teaches. Normal tone with a flexor plantar confirms an LMN root lesion rather than a cord lesion. Not the others: C5 is shoulder abduction with the biceps and brachioradialis reflexes and the lateral upper arm; C6 is elbow flexion and supination with the thumb; C8 is finger flexion and thumb flexion at the IP joint with the little finger, and has no reflex listed.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man developed sudden low back pain lifting a crate, followed by pain shooting down the back of the right leg. He has difficulty doing single-leg toe raises on the right, the right calf is visibly thinner, the right ankle reflex is absent, and pinprick is reduced along the lateral border of the right foot. Tone is normal and the plantar response is flexor bilaterally. Which root is affected, and what is this pattern of findings called?
options: L4 root, lower motor neuron signs
L5 root, lower motor neuron signs
S1 root, lower motor neuron signs
S1 root, upper motor neuron signs
questions.explain: Why: This is the primer's own worked example of S1 radiculopathy — gastrocnemius atrophy, weakness of ankle plantarflexion, hip extension, a reduced or absent ankle reflex, a flexor plantar response and decreased sensation over the lateral foot. Normal tone, atrophy, myotomal weakness, a diminished reflex and a flexor plantar together are what the primer calls lower motor neuron signs. Not the others: L4 would give knee extension weakness, a depressed knee reflex and medial malleolus sensory loss; L5 would give dorsiflexion, big toe extension and inversion weakness with dorsum-of-foot sensory loss and no reflex change; and UMN signs would require increased tone, brisk reflexes with clonus and an extensor plantar.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is referred with several months of progressive bilateral leg weakness and increasing difficulty walking. He also has longstanding neck and low back pain. Both legs have increased tone with a sudden catch on quick passive movement, brisk knee and ankle reflexes with sustained ankle clonus, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: MRI of the lumbar spine, since bilateral leg weakness implies multiple lumbosacral roots
MRI of the cervical spine, since the signs are upper motor neuron and a cervical cord lesion can cause leg weakness
Reassurance and physiotherapy, since asymptomatic degenerative disc is present in two-thirds of people
MRI of the cervical spine, since compression of the cervical nerve roots is the usual cause of bilateral leg weakness
questions.explain: Why: Increased tone, hyperreflexia with clonus and extensor plantars are upper motor neuron signs, which direct attention away from the lumbar spine and onto the cord in the cervical or thoracic region: a cervical cord lesion can cause leg weakness because it interrupts the UMN limb of the two-neuron pathway to the leg. This is the primer's worked error case — missing the UMN signs, imaging the lumbar spine and missing a compressive cervical myelopathy. Not the others: a lumbar root lesion produces LMN signs, so lumbar imaging risks false reassurance; the two-thirds asymptomatic-disc figure is an argument for localizing before imaging, not for withholding it in progressive myelopathy; and cervical nerve roots cannot cause leg weakness at all — the right region for the wrong reason.

guide.s: a cervical cord lesion can cause leg weakness

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman presents with two days of severe low back pain after a fall. She has not passed urine since yesterday and has a distended bladder; she cannot feel the toilet paper when she wipes. Ankle reflexes are absent bilaterally, plantar responses are flexor, and there is patchy numbness over both posterior thighs and the perineum. Which single examination finding, together with her bladder history, most specifically establishes the emergency diagnosis, and what herniation pattern produces it?
options: An extensor plantar response; a central herniation compressing the spinal cord
Saddle (perineal) anaesthesia; a central herniation compressing multiple lumbosacral nerve roots
Absent ankle reflexes; a lateral herniation compressing a single nerve root
A sensory level at T10; a central herniation compressing multiple lumbosacral nerve roots
questions.explain: Why: Cauda equina syndrome is low back pain + saddle (perineal) anaesthesia + bladder and/or bowel dysfunction, with or without limb findings, and the perineal loss in the S2–S4 concentric rings is the finding specific to it. A central lumbar herniation compresses the whole bundle of lumbosacral nerve roots, which is the pattern that produces it; a lateral herniation catches one root. Not the others: her plantars are flexor, and an extensor response would indicate a cord lesion, which lumbar disc disease almost never causes since the cord ends at L1; absent ankle reflexes alone are an S1 finding compatible with ordinary radiculopathy, and a lateral herniation would not explain bilateral perineal loss with retention; and a sensory level suggests a spinal cord lesion, not a lumbar herniation.

questions.stem: A student examining a patient with a suspected radiculopathy tests ankle eversion. Her textbook assigns eversion to L5-S1 via the superficial peroneal nerve. Which root should she record for this course, and why?
options: S1, because the peroneal nerve is predominantly S1
L4, to match the tibialis posterior
L5, because the course handout labels both inversion and eversion L5 and is the standard for assessments
L5-S1, because anatomy textbooks are more inclusive and therefore more accurate
questions.explain: Why: PW02 states that its dermatomes and myotomes are what will be used throughout the course including assessments, and on its lower-limb figure inversion and eversion are both labelled L5. When a textbook disagrees with this handout, the handout wins. Not the others: S1 in this course is plantarflexion and hip extension; L4 is knee extension and hip adduction with the knee reflex; and the handout explicitly notes that anatomy textbooks are more inclusive but that predominant single-root supply is what allows precise localization, so the more inclusive list is not the course answer.

guide.s: inversion and eversion are both labelled L5

questions.stem: A resident reviews a lateral radiograph of the cervical spine taken after a minor fall. The vertebral bodies are bright white, while a vertically oriented dark stripe lies immediately anterior to them. Which statement best explains the dark stripe?
options: It is air in the airway — low density gives low attenuation, so little of the beam is absorbed and the film is black
It is bone — high density gives high attenuation, which darkens the film
It is fat — its high attenuation absorbs the beam and produces the dark band
It is a windowing artifact, since radiographs are displayed with the same window and level settings as CT
questions.explain: Why: attenuation is determined by density, and the module's rule is low density → low attenuation → film black. Air in the trachea and pharynx is the least dense material on the slide-2.4 scale, so the prevertebral airway is the dark stripe — this is exactly the module's own quiz 2, keyed Low. Not the others: bone is high density and appears white, so the option inverts the rule; fat is low density (−60 to −100 HU) and the option misstates its attenuation; windowing is a CT display operation, not something applied to plain films.

guide.s: High density → High attenuation → film = white

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman presents 90 minutes after sudden right-sided weakness and aphasia. The non-contrast CT head looks unremarkable on the routine setting, and the stroke team wants to re-examine it specifically for early loss of grey-white differentiation. Which window setting is designed for that question?
options: Window (center) = 100; Level (range) = 2000
questions.explain: Why: slide 2.19 labels W30 L30 the stroke window — the narrowest of the three, so contrast is highest and a difference of a few Hounsfield units between grey and white matter is amplified. Not the others: W80 L40 is the routine brain window, the setting that already looked normal; W200 L100 is the widest, tuned to hyperdense acute blood, not to subtle hypodensity; the centre-100/range-2000 setting is the bone window, which blurs parenchyma into uniform grey.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has three weeks of worsening headache. His non-contrast CT head shows a large hypodense wedge in the right frontal lobe with local mass effect. After intravenous contrast, a bright rim with a non-enhancing centre appears within that region. What does the enhancing rim signify?
options: Contrast has leaked out of the intravascular space because the integrity of the vessel wall is compromised
Tumour cells are actively transporting contrast across an intact endothelium
The rim is calcification, which is dense and therefore bright on CT
The rim is clotted blood, which is denser on the Hounsfield axis than liquid blood
questions.explain: Why: slide 2.20 states the mechanism outright — in tumour, infection and active inflammation the vessel wall integrity is compromised, so contrast leaks out of the intravascular space. Ring enhancement is that leak at the margin of a lesion. Not the others: enhancement is leakage, not active uptake; calcification would be visible on the non-contrast study and would not appear only after injection; clotted blood is indeed hyperdense but, again, would already be bright before contrast.

guide.s: contrast leaking out of the intravascular space

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman at 20 weeks gestation needs imaging of her intracranial arteries for a suspected small aneurysm found incidentally. She is neurologically stable and being investigated as an outpatient. Two years ago she had anaphylaxis after iodinated contrast. Which is the most appropriate study?
options: MR angiography using the time-of-flight technique, which needs no contrast agent
CT angiography with a reduced dose of iodinated contrast
Catheter cerebral angiography through a femoral arterial puncture
MR venography with gadolinium
questions.explain: Why: the module gives two of its four deciders here — previous allergic reaction to iodine-based contrast and avoiding radiation in pregnancy both point to MR, especially given the former can be done without the administration of a contrast agent. Time-of-flight images arteries with no contrast at all. Not the others: CTA still delivers radiation and iodinated contrast, the exact two problems; catheter angiography is the invasive option and also uses radiation and injected contrast, and is not an initial test; MRV images veins, and the question is arterial.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man wakes with left hemiparesis and is scanned within the hour. On MRI, a region of right frontoparietal cortex is markedly bright on one sequence and, on the paired map, distinctly dark in the same region. What does this pattern represent, and by what mechanism?
options: Restricted diffusion, most commonly acute ischemia, via cellular swelling with intracellular water accumulation
Vasogenic oedema, made conspicuous because the CSF signal has been suppressed
Microhaemorrhage, because blood products are paramagnetic and distort the local magnetic field
Blood-brain barrier breakdown, because gadolinium is bright on T1
questions.explain: Why: bright on DWI with a spatially matching dark region on ADC is the module's definition of restricted diffusion (low ADC), and its first-listed cause is acute ischemia or stroke, acting through cellular swelling — cytotoxic edema due to cell death, which restricts free water movement between intra- and extracellular spaces. Not the others: CSF suppression is FLAIR, not DWI/ADC; the paramagnetic susceptibility effect is GRE/SWI, where blood appears dark on a single sequence rather than as a DWI/ADC pair; gadolinium enhancement requires contrast to have been given and is a T1 finding.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman reports limb tingling and a past episode of painful blurred vision. On T2 imaging the radiologist suspects small bright lesions hugging the margins of the lateral ventricles but cannot separate them from the adjacent bright CSF. Which sequence resolves the problem, and why?
options: FLAIR, because it is T2-weighted but suppresses CSF signal while the lesions stay bright
T1 with gadolinium, because most pathologies are bright on T1
Gradient echo, because demyelinating plaques are diamagnetic and appear dark
The ADC map, because demyelinating plaques restrict diffusion
questions.explain: Why: FLAIR is T2-weighted with the CSF signal suppressed, and the module's stated indication is oedema and demyelination, especially lesions near CSF-filled spaces such as the ventricles — exactly the periventricular multiple sclerosis plaques shown on slide 2.29. Not the others: the module's blanket rule is that most pathologies are bright on T2 and dark on T1, so the T1 option reverses it; GRE is for haemorrhage and calcification, and the module never calls demyelination diamagnetic; restricted diffusion is listed for acute ischemia, densely cellular tumours and abscesses, not demyelination.

guide.s: especially those near CSF-filled spaces such as the ventricles

questions.stem: An anatomy tutor asks about the most caudal segment of the neural tube, which is formed only after the caudal neuropore has already closed, from a remnant lying just caudal to it. From which tissue does that segment arise?
options: Mesoderm of the remains of the primitive streak
Ectoderm overlying the notochord
Neural crest arising at the crest of the neural folds
Endoderm of the yolk sac
questions.explain: Why: slide 7 states the two sources explicitly — primary neurulation forms the primary neural tube from ectoderm, while secondary neurulation forms the secondary neural tube from the mesoderm of the remains of the primitive streak, which condenses into the medullary cord once the caudal neuropore has closed. Not the others: ectoderm over the notochord is the primary route; neural crest gives dorsal root ganglia and the PNS, not the tube itself; endoderm contributes nothing to the nervous system in this module.

guide.s: mesoderm of the remains of the primitive streak

questions.stem: A newborn is delivered with no cranial vault; dark, degenerated tissue lies on the base of the skull above intact orbits, and the face is otherwise normally formed. The pregnancy was unplanned and no periconceptional supplement had been taken. Which statement about the underlying embryology is correct?
options: The neural plate formed but, left exposed to amniotic fluid after the rostral neuropore failed to close at about 25 days, it deteriorated
Neural induction by the notochord never occurred, so no neural tissue was ever produced
The caudal neuropore failed to close at about 28 days
Secondary neurulation failed, so the primitive streak remnant never cavitated
questions.explain: Why: the narration is explicit that in anencephaly the neural plate of the rostral neuropore remains exposed to the amniotic fluid, the tissues begin to deteriorate, and the condition is incompatible with life — degeneration of tissue that did form, not absence of formation. The rostral neuropore should close at about 25 days. Not the others: failed induction is not the described mechanism; caudal neuropore failure at ~28 days gives myeloschisis, a spinal lesion; secondary neurulation builds only the most caudal cord and has nothing to do with the cranial vault.

guide.s: remains exposed to the amniotic fluid

questions.stem: During a review session a student is asked to name the one brain vesicle that gives rise to two distinct adult structures, and to state the cavity it contributes. Which option is correct?
options: Metencephalon — pons and cerebellum; cavity the fourth ventricle
Myelencephalon — medulla and cerebellum; cavity the fourth ventricle
Diencephalon — thalamus and midbrain; cavity the third ventricle
Telencephalon — cerebral hemispheres and cerebellum; cavity the lateral ventricles
questions.explain: Why: slide 14's table gives Metencephalon → Pons and Cerebellum → Fourth ventricle; it is the only vesicle with two derivatives, and the cerebellum grows from the dorsal edges of the metencephalon. Not the others: the myelencephalon gives the medulla alone, though it shares the fourth ventricle; the diencephalon keeps its own name in the adult and gives the third ventricle, while the midbrain comes from the mesencephalon; the telencephalon gives the cerebral hemispheres and lateral ventricles only.

questions.stem: A student in the brainstem lab is trying to predict where sensory and motor nuclei will lie in the floor of the fourth ventricle, having learned the spinal cord arrangement first. Which statement is correct?
options: Alar (sensory) columns lie lateral and basal (motor) columns medial, because the pontine flexure everted the alar plates; the vestibular nucleus is one such alar derivative
Sensory columns lie dorsal and motor ventral, exactly as in the spinal cord, since the flexures do not affect nuclear position
The cephalic flexure produces the eversion, and the sulcus limitans is lost at this level
Both alar and basal columns are carried medially, with the roof plate ending up between them
questions.explain: Why: slide 17 states that at the level of the fourth ventricle the pontine flexure causes the alar plates to evert, carrying them laterally, so sensory becomes lateral and motor medial; the narrator names the vestibular nucleus, the spinal nucleus of CN V and the solitary nucleus as alar derivatives forced laterally. Not the others: the dorsal/ventral arrangement is the spinal cord's and is exactly what eversion changes; the cephalic flexure is at the midbrain and is given no histogenetic consequence, and the sulcus limitans persists as the boundary at both levels; eversion moves the alar plates laterally, not medially, and the roof plate is stretched across the top of the ventricle.

guide.s: the pontine flexure causes the alar plates to evert

questions.stem: An infant born with an open, unskinned lesion over the lower back develops a rapidly enlarging head in the first weeks of life. Imaging shows the cerebellum and medulla displaced downward through the foramen magnum. Which single step explains the enlarging head?
options: Compression of the foramen of Magendie, so CSF produced in the ventricles cannot escape into the subarachnoid space
Overproduction of CSF by the choroid plexus attached to the stretched roof plate
Failure of the cerebral aqueduct to form from the mesencephalon
Obstruction of the foramina of Luschka by the rhombic lip
questions.explain: Why: slide 19 and the narration give the chain in order — open spinal NTD, downward displacement of cerebellum and medulla into the foramen magnum, compression of the foramen of Magendie against the medulla, CSF unable to reach the subarachnoid space, and build-up in the ventricles. Not the others: the module attributes the hydrocephalus to obstructed outflow, not to overproduction; aqueductal failure is never discussed in this deck; the source names only Magendie and not the lateral foramina of Luschka, and the rhombic lip is the cerebellar primordium, not an obstructing mass.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old with longstanding developmental delay presents with new seizures. MRI shows multiple rounded nodules of grey-matter signal lining the walls of both lateral ventricles, with an otherwise normally gyrated cortex. What is the diagnosis and the gene the module names?
options: Periventricular nodular heterotopia — FLNA
Subcortical band heterotopia (double cortex) — DCX
Periventricular nodular heterotopia — DCX
Subcortical band heterotopia — FLNA
questions.explain: Why: slide 21's caption describes periventricular nodular heterotopia as grey matter that fails to migrate and remains located along the lateral ventricles, and pairs it with FLNA; the position of the ectopic grey tells you how far migration got, and here it never left the ventricle. Not the others: subcortical band heterotopia is a smooth band of grey interposed in the white matter between cortex and ventricles, and is the DCX disorder; the two mixed pairings swap the genes.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old structural engineer is described by her friends as intensely orderly: she plans holidays to the minute, keeps colour-coded lists, and has done so since her teens. She enjoys working this way, her colleagues find her reliable, and she has close friendships and no complaints about her life. Which single feature most clearly makes this a personality trait rather than a personality disorder?
options: The pattern is exhibited across a wide range of contexts
The pattern was already present in adolescence
There is no distress and no impairment of functioning
The pattern does not deviate from her cultural expectations
questions.explain: Why: the module defines a personality trait as an enduring pattern of perceiving and relating to the environment across a wide range of contexts, and a personality disorder as present only when those traits cause distress or impair functioning. She has neither, so the orderliness is a trait. Not the others: being exhibited across contexts is part of the definition of a trait, so it cannot be what excludes a disorder; onset in adolescence is criterion D and would support, not exclude, a PD; and cultural deviation is only one element of criterion A, which still requires criterion C's distress or impairment.

guide.s: cause them distress or impair their functioning

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man is assessed in a correctional clinic after his third arrest for fraud. He lies fluently, has never held a job longer than two months, has been in repeated physical fights, and says of the people he defrauded that they "should have known better." He clearly meets four of the seven behavioural criteria. Which additional piece of information is required before antisocial personality disorder can be diagnosed?
options: A raised score on the Hare Psychopathy Checklist–Revised
Evidence of conduct disorder with onset before age 15
Documented onset of the pattern before age 10
At least five of the seven criteria rather than four
questions.explain: Why: antisocial PD is the one PD with two extra mandatory requirements — the person must be at least 18 (he is 19) and must have evidence of conduct disorder with onset before age 15. Not the others: the PCL-R measures psychopathy, which is not a DSM diagnosis and is not required for ASPD; there is no age-10 onset rule; and ASPD's threshold is the lowest of all the PDs at 3 of 7, so four criteria already suffice.

guide.s: evidence of conduct disorder with onset before age 15

questions.stem: A 41-year-old night-shift archivist is referred after a workplace wellness screen. He lives alone, has declined every social invitation for a decade, and says he "doesn't see what people get out of" friendships or dating. His manager's praise and a formal reprimand both left him unmoved. Affect is flat. He denies odd beliefs, and there are no hallucinations or delusions. Most likely diagnosis?
options: Avoidant personality disorder
Schizoid personality disorder
Schizotypal personality disorder
Persistent depressive disorder
questions.explain: Why: he neither desires nor enjoys close relationships, chooses solitary activities, appears indifferent to praise or criticism and has flattened affect — the schizoid pattern of detachment plus restricted emotional expression (4 of 7 needed). Not the others: the "wanting" test settles avoidant — avoidant patients want relationships but fear rejection, and there is no fear of criticism here; schizotypal requires odd beliefs, perceptual distortions or odd speech, all absent; and a depressive disorder would bring low mood and a change from baseline rather than a lifelong lack of interest.

guide.s: Neither desires nor enjoys close relationships

questions.stem: A 23-year-old has attended the same community choir for three years but still feels acutely uneasy at every rehearsal, convinced that two members exchange looks about her and may be "working against" her. She dresses in several mismatched layers, answers questions in long metaphorical detours, and says she can tell when a room has "bad energy." She has no fixed delusions and no hallucinations. Which diagnosis best fits?
options: Avoidant personality disorder
Social anxiety disorder
Schizotypal personality disorder
Paranoid personality disorder
questions.explain: Why: her social anxiety does not diminish with familiarity after three years and is driven by paranoid fears rather than negative self-judgement — the module's explicit schizotypal discriminator — and she also shows odd appearance, odd speech and magical thinking (5 of 9 needed). Not the others: avoidant social anxiety comes from fear of criticism and feelings of inadequacy, and typically eases as people become familiar; social anxiety disorder would not explain the odd beliefs, speech and appearance; paranoid PD covers the suspiciousness but not the magical thinking, eccentric appearance or odd speech.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old consultant repeatedly tells his physician that he should be seen by "the department head, not a resident," describes himself as the only person at his firm who truly understands strategy, and becomes irritated when a nurse does not recognize his name. He dismisses a colleague's recent bereavement as "an excuse for missing deadlines." Which personality disorder does this best illustrate?
options: Histrionic personality disorder
Narcissistic personality disorder
Antisocial personality disorder
Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder
questions.explain: Why: grandiose self-importance, a belief in being special and entitled to high-status care, a need for recognition, and a clear lack of empathy are the narcissistic core pattern (5 of 9 needed). Not the others: the module's discriminator is why they want attention — histrionic patients want attention itself, through emotionality, appearance or seductiveness, with shallow rapidly shifting emotions, none of which appear here; antisocial PD requires a pattern of violating others' rights with conduct disorder before 15; OCPD is about orderliness, perfectionism and control, not admiration.

guide.s: need for admiration, and lack of empathy

questions.stem: A 52-year-old previously easy-going roofer has, over the eight months since a severe fall with a closed head injury, become suspicious of his family, accuses his wife of hiding money, and bears grudges over trivial remarks. His wife and sister both describe a complete change from his lifelong personality. Which general criterion for a personality disorder most clearly excludes the diagnosis of paranoid personality disorder here?
options: Criterion A — the pattern involves fewer than two of the four domains
Criterion B — the pattern is not inflexible and pervasive
Criterion C — there is no clinically significant distress or impairment
Criterion F — the pattern is attributable to another medical condition
questions.explain: Why: criterion F requires that the pattern is not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or another medical condition, and head trauma is the module's own example. Criterion D also fails, since a PD must be stable and of long duration with onset by adolescence or early adulthood, not mid-adulthood. Not the others: his presentation does involve cognition and interpersonal functioning, so criterion A's two-of-four domains is met; the pattern is pervasive across home and family; and it clearly causes distress and impairment, so criterion C is met too — which is exactly why the exclusions are what settle the case.

guide.s: Not attributable to the physiological effects

questions.stem: A paediatrician is taking a developmental history on a distressed 15-year-old with an emotionally intense temperament. Which element of the history would the biosocial theory classify as a social contributor to borderline personality disorder, rather than a biological one?
options: Colic and inconsolable crying through the first year
A father with alcohol use disorder and long-standing anger problems
A mother who responds to distress by saying "you're being dramatic, stop it"
Temper tantrums with door-slamming from about age four
questions.explain: Why: dismissing a child's emotional experience is invalidation — the social half of the biosocial theory, which holds that BPD arises when an emotionally sensitive temperament meets an invalidating environment. Not the others: colic with inconsolable crying and early temper tantrums are markers of the emotionally intense temperament (bio), exactly as they are in Victoria's history; and a family history of alcohol use and anger problems is the module's marker of the inherited trait of impulsivity, also bio.

questions.stem: A medical student presenting on a psychiatric inpatient ward states that borderline personality disorder is "rare, almost exclusively female, and essentially untreatable." Which statement corrects her most completely, according to the module?
options: Prevalence is 2–6% in the general population and 20% among psychiatric inpatients, there is no sex difference in community samples, and about 75% improve with DBT
Prevalence is under 1%, women outnumber men three to one, and about 25% improve with DBT
Prevalence is 2–6%, women outnumber men three to one, and medication is the mainstay of treatment
Prevalence is 20% in the general population, there is no sex difference, and no treatment has been shown to help
questions.explain: Why: the module's epidemiology string is 2–6% general population, 6% primary care, 10% psychiatry outpatients, 20% psychiatric inpatients, with no sex difference in community samples and 75% improving with DBT. Not the others: prevalence is far above 1% and 20% is the inpatient, not the population, figure; the three-to-one female excess is the misconception being corrected; and psychotherapy, not medication, is the mainstay, since no medication specifically treats BPD.

guide.t: 1 · Why BPD gets so many modules

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman describes compulsive online shopping she cannot afford, weekly binge eating, and cutting her forearms roughly twice a month when overwhelmed. She has no other symptoms on screening. How many of the nine DSM criteria for borderline personality disorder do these three behaviours satisfy?
options: One
Two
Three
Four
questions.explain: Why: impulsive spending and binge eating are two potentially self-damaging areas, satisfying criterion 4 (impulsivity in at least two areas), and the cutting satisfies criterion 5 (recurrent suicidal behaviour or self-harm) — two criteria. Not the others: one would undercount, because spending and binge eating together do meet criterion 4's two-area requirement; three and four overcount by counting the self-harm twice, but criterion 4 explicitly excludes suicidal and self-harming behaviour. Since the threshold is 5 of 9, she must be screened for the remaining criteria.

guide.t: 5 · The nine DSM criteria for BPD
guide.s: Does NOT include suicidal or self-harming behaviour

questions.stem: During a heated argument with her partner, a 26-year-old with a long history of unstable relationships briefly hears someone call her name and feels as though she is watching the scene from the ceiling. The experiences last minutes and never occur when she is calm. Which is the best interpretation?
options: A primary psychotic disorder requiring antipsychotic treatment
Transient stress-related paranoid ideation or dissociative symptoms — a borderline criterion
A substance-induced psychotic episode
Malingering, since the symptoms resolve so quickly
questions.explain: Why: brief, stress-bound hallucinations ("micropsychosis") together with depersonalization — the sense of being a spectator in your own life, watching from the ceiling — are exactly criterion 7 of BPD. Not the others: a primary psychotic disorder would not be confined to moments of acute stress with a clear baseline; nothing in the history points to a substance; and the module's teaching is that these phenomena are genuine and expected in BPD, not feigned.

guide.t: 5 · The nine DSM criteria for BPD

questions.topic: BPD · Balance of bio and social
questions.stem: Two adults both meet criteria for borderline personality disorder. Patient A was a placid infant whose emotional reactivity would sit around two standard deviations above the mean, and she experienced severe childhood physical and sexual abuse. Patient B was a strikingly intense infant at the extreme tail of the reactivity distribution, raised by loving parents who simply could not understand her reactions and often told her she was overreacting. Which principle does this contrast illustrate?
options: Environmental factors are the dominant cause of BPD in both patients
Biological vulnerability alone is sufficient to cause BPD in Patient B
The greater the biological vulnerability, the less environmental invalidation is required
Trauma is a necessary condition for the development of BPD
questions.explain: Why: the module marks Person A and Person B on the emotional-reactivity curve to make exactly this point — BPD risk is the product of two dimensions, so less biological sensitivity requires trauma-level invalidation while extreme sensitivity can be tipped by subtle invalidation. Not the others: neither dimension dominates, which is the whole argument; temperament on its own is a risk factor, not a cause, since not everyone who is intense and impulsive develops BPD; and trauma is only the severe end of a spectrum of invalidation, not a requirement.

guide.t: 3 · The balance of bio and social
guide.s: the more biological vulnerability, the less environmental invalidation is needed

questions.stem: A family physician sees a 22-year-old newly diagnosed with borderline personality disorder and, wanting to "cover all bases" at the first visit, starts an SSRI, an antipsychotic and a mood stabiliser together. What is the main problem with this plan?
options: Antidepressants are contraindicated in borderline personality disorder
No medication specifically treats BPD, and this is the polypharmacy the module warns against
Mood stabilisers should have been started before the antidepressant
Medication should be withheld until a formal DBT programme has begun
questions.explain: Why: the module's verdict on medication is "maybe" — no specific medication treats BPD, antipsychotics and mood stabilisers are controversial and best prescribed by psychiatrists, and "dangerous, or at least unhelpful, polypharmacy is all too common in BPD and should be avoided." The priority is a psychotherapy referral. Not the others: antidepressants are not contraindicated — they are reasonable for significant comorbid depressive or anxiety symptoms; there is no prescribed sequence of agents; and nothing requires waiting for DBT to start before treating a comorbidity.

questions.stem: A patient with borderline personality disorder is offered a place in a programme that provides weekly individual therapy, a weekly skills group, and a weekly meeting of the therapists themselves. She asks what else a complete dialectical behaviour therapy programme would include. Which component is missing?
options: Family therapy sessions with her parents
Monthly medication review by a psychiatrist
Between-session skills coaching by telephone
Quarterly inpatient admissions for skills consolidation
questions.explain: Why: DBT's four required modes are individual therapy, skills group, between-session skills coaching by phone, and weekly therapist team meetings — phone coaching is the one missing here. Not the others: family therapy is the module's own named distractor and is not one of the four modes; medication review is not a DBT mode at all, and no medication specifically treats BPD; and planned admissions run directly against the teaching that hospitalisation can become an escape behaviour and a potent reinforcer.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old in your office is visibly escalating — louder and faster speech, bigger gestures, slapping the arms of the chair — after you explain that the therapy waiting list is several months long. Which of your possible replies is a mindreading validation?
options: "So you've now been waiting three months for this referral."
"You look like you're feeling humiliated and completely let down right now."
"Anyone in your position would find that frustrating."
"Wait lists are a normal part of our system, so of course there's a wait."
questions.explain: Why: a mindreading statement is an educated guess about what the patient thinks or feels, based on what they have said or how they look — naming humiliation and being let down does exactly that. Not the others: restating the facts is a reflective statement; "anyone would find that frustrating" is normalizing; and the last option is the module's explicit example of what is not normalizing, because it normalizes the system rather than the patient's reaction, and is invalidating.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old is brought to the emergency department after burning her forearm with a lighter following an argument at home. She says it "makes the feelings stop," is clear that she did not want to die, and is looking forward to a school trip next week. What is the best interpretation and next step?
options: She is minimising suicidal intent, so she should be certified and admitted
This is deliberate self-harm serving an affect-avoidance function; believe her, but still assess suicide risk, screen for other diagnoses and refer to therapy
This establishes borderline personality disorder, so a DBT referral is the only step needed
Since there is no suicidal intent, the wound can be dressed and she can be discharged without further assessment
questions.explain: Why: deliberate self-harm is tissue damage in the absence of suicidal intent, and when a patient says she cut or burned to relieve emotion rather than to die she is most likely telling the truth — but self-harm still carries a markedly raised suicide risk, so the assessment, a diagnostic screen and a therapy referral all still follow. Not the others: certifying a future-oriented patient who denies intent is the very error the module works through; self-harm alone never establishes BPD, especially in adolescents, where teen depression and neurodevelopmental disorders also present this way; and discharging without a risk assessment ignores the 37-fold raised one-year suicide rate.

guide.s: in the absence of suicidal intent

questions.stem: You are discharging a patient who self-harms and who has now attended the emergency department three times in two months. A well-meaning colleague suggests telling her warmly to "come straight back to us any time you're feeling upset." Why does the module reject this, and what is the better wording?
options: It is too vague; she should instead be told to return only if the wound becomes infected
It risks reinforcing crisis-driven attendance; encourage coping skills and crisis lines, with the hospital available for emergencies
It is correct as stated, since frequent contact is protective in self-harm
It should be replaced by an offer of weekly appointments for the duration of the crisis
questions.explain: Why: the module flags this option as sounding kind while actually driving multiple unnecessary, unhelpful visits; the correct framing keeps the hospital available for emergencies while encouraging distress-tolerance skills and crisis lines, which are themselves a source of validation. Not the others: restricting return to wound infection ignores genuine emergencies and her raised suicide risk; frequent warm contact soon after self-harm is precisely what reinforces it; and increasing appointment frequency during a crisis can reinforce crisis behaviour, so it should be held steady or increased only if she can stay away from self-harm and suicide threats.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy is brought in after a suicide attempt. His mother reports that in the weeks beforehand he watched repeated news coverage that described in detail how a local musician had died by suicide, and that he had begun quoting the coverage to friends. Which phenomenon best accounts for the influence of that coverage on his behaviour?
options: Werther effect
Papageno effect
Structural stigma
Diathesis–stress interaction
questions.explain: Why: detailed, sensationalized or romanticized media coverage of a suicide increases suicidal behaviour through social learning and identification — the Werther effect, named from Goethe's 1774 novel; it is the reason there is a media ban on reporting suicide. Not the others: the Papageno effect is the protective mirror image, where recovery-focused coverage reduces suicidal ideation; structural stigma is racism and barriers such as getting time off work, not a media-imitation effect; diathesis–stress describes predisposition plus stressor, not the specific imitative response to a portrayal.

guide.t: 3 · Stigma and the two media effects

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman describes episodes of abrupt intense fear that peak within a few minutes, with palpitations, sweating, chest pain and a fear of dying. She has had six such episodes over four months and for the past three months has stopped taking the subway because she is afraid of having another one. Which combination satisfies DSM-5 criteria for panic disorder as taught in this lecture?
options: ≥4 of 13 attack symptoms peaking within minutes, plus ≥1 month of worry about further attacks and/or maladaptive behaviour change
≥5 of 9 attack symptoms over the same 2-week period, plus functional impairment
≥4 of 13 attack symptoms peaking within minutes, plus ≥6 months of avoidance
Any number of unexpected attacks, provided at least one required an emergency department visit
questions.explain: Why: criterion A is recurrent unexpected attacks — an abrupt surge peaking within minutes with ≥4 of 13 symptoms — and criterion B requires that at least one attack be followed by ≥1 month of persistent worry about further attacks or their consequences, and/or significant maladaptive behaviour change. Not the others: 5 of 9 over 2 weeks is the major depressive episode rule, not panic; 6 months is not the panic duration threshold (that would be closer to the generalized anxiety frame); and an emergency department visit is an illustrative clinical detail, not a criterion.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man reports five of the nine DSM-5 depressive symptoms over the past month: insomnia, poor concentration, fatigue, weight loss and guilt. He denies low mood and says he still enjoys his hobbies as much as ever. Applying the criteria as the lecture taught them, what is the correct conclusion?
options: He does not meet criteria, because at least one of the five symptoms must be depressed mood or loss of interest/pleasure
He meets criteria, because any 5 of the 9 symptoms over 2 weeks is sufficient
He does not meet criteria, because the symptoms must be present for at least 6 months
He meets criteria, because weight loss and insomnia are the two cardinal symptoms
questions.explain: Why: the DSM-5 major depressive episode requires 5+ symptoms in the same 2-week period and that at least one of them be depressed mood or anhedonia — a gate the lecture slide omits but which the lecturer assumed aloud ('one person has to have low mood and loss of interest'). Not the others: 'any 5 of 9' is precisely the wrong flashcard the guide warns against building from the slide; the duration requirement is 2 weeks, not 6 months; and weight loss and insomnia are ordinary criteria with no gatekeeping status.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has had low motivation, disrupted sleep and social withdrawal for eight months. She has lost two jobs and no longer sees friends, but she endorses only three of the nine depressive criteria. Which limitation of the categorical diagnostic system does her case most directly illustrate?
options: Arbitrary diagnostic thresholds excluding clinically significant cases
Comorbidity — multiple simultaneous labels for one brain
Heterogeneity — the same label covering very different patients
Cultural bias in the application of diagnostic criteria
questions.explain: Why: she is clearly impaired but falls below the symptom cutoff — the dramatization of limitation 1, arbitrary thresholds ('4/9 sx is not MDE, but 5/9 is'), which the lecture treats as the same problem as subthreshold illness. Not the others: comorbidity is the patient carrying several labels at once; heterogeneity is two patients with the same label looking nothing alike; cultural bias concerns misreading culturally normative behaviour, which this stem does not raise.

questions.stem: A family physician is explaining the Adverse Childhood Experiences study to a resident. Using the figures presented in this lecture, which statement is correct?
options: About 64% of adults reported at least one ACE, about 12% reported four or more, and risk rises with the score in a dose–response fashion
About 25% of adults reported at least one ACE, and the relationship to later illness is threshold-based rather than graded
About 64% of adults reported four or more ACEs, with no measurable effect on physical health outcomes
ACE scores predict psychiatric but not physical health outcomes
questions.explain: Why: the Kaiser–CDC study found ~64% with ≥1 ACE and ~12% with ≥4, and the central finding is a dose–response relationship — the higher the score, the higher the risk of multiple poor outcomes. Not the others: 25% was a poll distractor, and the keyed poll answer was 'greater than 60%'; 64% refers to ≥1 ACE, not ≥4; and the study links ACE dose to physical outcomes too — ischemic heart disease, COPD, cancer and obesity on the slide, with diabetes added aloud.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman describes a childhood with a father who was unpredictably frightening and physically violent. She now reports a shifting sense of who she is, episodes in which she feels detached and unreal, rapidly swinging emotions, and repeated self-harm. Which attachment pattern and developmental cascade best fits her presentation?
options: Disorganized attachment — fragmented self-concept, dissociation and affect lability
Avoidant attachment — deactivation, alexithymia and compulsive self-sufficiency
Anxious attachment — hypervigilance to rejection and chronic worry
Secure attachment with an acute stress reaction
questions.explain: Why: maltreatment or a frightening caregiver maps to disorganized attachment, whose cascade is a fragmented self-concept, dissociation and affect lability, and whose named clinical phenotypes are borderline personality disorder, complex PTSD and self-harm — exactly this picture. Not the others: avoidant follows emotionally unavailable or rejecting care and presents as self-sufficiency and mistrust, classically with substance misuse or restricting eating disorders; anxious follows inconsistent or intrusive care and presents with reassurance-seeking, GAD, panic or somatic symptom disorder; secure attachment is the two-thirds majority and does not produce this cascade.

questions.stem: During an assessment a 52-year-old man says he feels 'fine, totally normal'. Throughout the interview he is tearful, his face is downcast, and his emotional expression barely changes. In documenting the mental status exam, how should these observations be recorded?
options: Mood 'fine' as reported; affect tearful and restricted, incongruent with stated mood
Mood tearful and restricted; affect 'fine' as reported
Mood and affect both 'fine', since the patient's own report governs both
Affect labile, since he reports one emotional state and displays another
questions.explain: Why: mood is the patient's subjective, stated emotional state, while affect is your observation of it; where the two diverge, the MSE records both and notes the incongruence. Not the others: the second option reverses the two definitions; the third collapses the observational half of the exam, losing exactly the discrepancy that is clinically interesting; 'labile' describes the stability axis — affect that swings within the interview — not a mismatch between report and observation.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman describes brief episodes in which she smells burning rubber that no one else can smell, each lasting under a minute and followed by a feeling of unfamiliar dread. She has no psychiatric history. Which cause should be considered first?
options: A neurological cause such as temporal lobe epilepsy
Schizophrenia
Alcohol withdrawal
Borderline personality disorder
questions.explain: Why: olfactory hallucinations point away from a primary psychiatric illness and toward a medical or neurological cause, classically temporal lobe epilepsy — the rule of thumb is auditory means primary psychiatric, everything else means look for a medical, neurological or withdrawal cause. Not the others: auditory hallucinations, not olfactory, are the modality most common in schizophrenia; tactile hallucinations (bugs crawling) are the withdrawal picture in alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal; borderline personality disorder is not associated with a specific hallucinatory modality in this lecture.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man is brought in by his daughter after six weeks of profound low mood, refusal to eat and near-mutism. He states with total conviction that his intestines have rotted away, that he has no body left, and that everyone around him is already dead. Which delusion type is this, and what does it most suggest?
options: Nihilistic delusion, suggesting severe (psychotic) depression
Referential delusion, suggesting schizophrenia
Persecutory delusion, suggesting a delusional disorder
Grandiose delusion, suggesting mania
questions.explain: Why: nihilistic delusions are the belief that one is dead, does not exist, or the world has ended — and the lecture pairs them explicitly with very severe depression, the same pairing that reappears with the psychotic-depression patient in Lecture 3. Not the others: referential delusions are unrelated events or broadcasts carrying special personal meaning; persecutory delusions are the belief one is being followed, spied on or harmed; grandiose delusions involve special powers, fame or a mission and fit mania, not a mute and starving patient.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman reports that for the past 10 days she has been sleeping only three hours a night. On further questioning she says she feels energetic all day, has started four new projects, and her friends say she is talking so fast they cannot interrupt her. Which feature best distinguishes this sleep pattern from the sleep disturbance of a depressive episode?
options: A decreased need for sleep with preserved energy, rather than insomnia with fatigue
Difficulty falling asleep rather than early morning waking
Hypersomnia rather than insomnia
Sleep disturbance lasting more than 2 weeks
questions.explain: Why: the S of GST PAID is a decreased need for sleep — less sleep but still full of energy — whereas the S of MSIGECAPS is insomnia or hypersomnia in a patient who is tired; the pressured, hard-to-interrupt speech confirms the manic side. Not the others: sleep-onset versus early-waking insomnia is not the discriminator taught here; hypersomnia is one of the depressive presentations, not a manic one; and duration does not separate the two, since the distinguishing feature is the preserved energy.

questions.stem: A clerk notices that she dreads every appointment with one particular patient, finds herself cutting his sentences short, and later realizes he speaks in the same dismissive tone as her former supervisor. She is usually patient and unhurried with patients. Which phenomenon does this describe?
options: Countertransference
Transference
Resistance
Therapeutic alliance
questions.explain: Why: the clinician is unconsciously reacting to the patient out of her own history, and the signal named in the lecture is the deviation from her own baseline — 'when you're reacting differently than usual, that's a clue about the dynamic'. Not the others: transference runs the other way, the patient importing feelings from past relationships onto the clinician; resistance is the patient blocking emotionally difficult material; the therapeutic alliance is the collaborative working relationship, not an unconscious reaction.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man with a 5-month depressive episode drinks six beers most evenings to get to sleep, which worsens his mood the next day and keeps him from attending his therapy appointments. He was made redundant 6 months ago; his mother had bipolar disorder. In which cell of the 4 P's grid does the nightly drinking belong?
options: Biological perpetuating
Biological predisposing
Social precipitating
Psychological protective
questions.explain: Why: perpetuating factors are those that maintain the problem once established — substance use is the slide's own example, and here the drinking demonstrably keeps the episode going. Not the others: the predisposing biological factor here is the family history of bipolar disorder; the precipitating event is the redundancy, which is a social precipitant; and nothing in the stem functions as a protective strength.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man with schizophrenia is convinced that his medication is unnecessary because he was never ill, and he denies that the voices he describes are symptoms. Nevertheless he attends every appointment, takes the medication because his sister asks him to, manages his finances and keeps his housing. How should insight and judgement be recorded?
options: Insight absent, judgement fair to good
Insight and judgement both absent, since they are a single MSE item
Insight good, judgement impaired
Insight cannot be assessed while a patient is delusional
questions.explain: Why: insight is whether the patient recognizes that they are ill; judgement is whether their decisions and behaviour are sound, and the lecture states explicitly that the two dissociate — 'you could have poor insight, but you'd still be behaving appropriately, so your judgement could be OK'. Not the others: the slide lists them on one row but they are scored separately; his insight is clearly absent, not good; and a fixed false belief does not make insight unassessable — the absence of insight is itself the finding.

guide.s: Insight and judgement can come apart

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is assessed for 3 months of low mood, anhedonia and a 9 kg weight loss. He sits very still, answers only after long pauses, and speaks quietly in short sentences. Which MSE finding is the most characteristic feature of his presentation?
options: Slowed speech with increased speech latency
Pressured speech that is difficult to interrupt
Unkempt grooming and poor hygiene
Tangential thought process
questions.explain: Why: depression characteristically slows speech, with a long pause before a verbal response — speech latency — which is the mirror image of mania's fast speech. Not the others: pressured speech that is hard to interrupt is a cardinal manic sign; poor grooming may or may not be present and, as the lecturer said of the same distractor, is not as good a feature for narrowing the picture to depression; tangential thought process means moving away and never answering, which is not described here.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with a first episode of psychosis is started on risperidone. Three months later he reports breast tenderness and galactorrhoea, and his serum prolactin is elevated. Blockade of which dopamine pathway best explains this adverse effect?
options: Mesolimbic pathway
Mesocortical pathway
Nigrostriatal pathway
Tuberoinfundibular pathway
questions.explain: Why: the lecture lists four dopamine pathways and assigns prolactin regulation to the tuberoinfundibular pathway; antipsychotics generally drop dopamine, so blocking this pathway disinhibits prolactin release. Not the others: mesolimbic is emotion and reward (the pathway whose excess dopamine produces psychosis); mesocortical is cognition and motivation; nigrostriatal is movement, and would give extrapyramidal signs rather than galactorrhoea.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with major depressive disorder is started on fluoxetine. Her preceptor asks where the cell bodies of the neurons releasing the transmitter this drug acts on are located. Which of the following is correct?
options: Locus coeruleus
Raphe nuclei
Substantia nigra
Hippocampus
questions.explain: Why: fluoxetine is an SSRI and acts on serotonin, whose nucleus of origin on the slide is the raphe nuclei; serotonin governs mood, anxiety, sleep, appetite and pain. Not the others: the locus coeruleus is the norepinephrine nucleus; the substantia nigra is the origin of the nigrostriatal dopamine pathway; the hippocampus is a projection target, not a monoamine nucleus.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with psychotic depression and nihilistic delusions has failed three adequate antidepressant trials and a course of psychotherapy. ECT is recommended. Her daughter asks how many treatments will be needed and how often they are given. Which answer matches what was taught?
options: Two to three treatments, given once weekly
Eight to twelve treatments, given three times per week, usually over a few weeks
Twenty to twenty-five treatments, given daily
A single treatment, repeated only if relapse occurs at six months
questions.explain: Why: the dosing schedule given aloud is 8 to 12 seizures, spread three times a week, usually for a few weeks. Not the others: two to three weekly treatments is far below the stated course; daily treatment for twenty to twenty-five sessions is neither the frequency nor the number taught; ECT is not a single-session therapy, and the schedule is a course, not a one-off.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with treatment-resistant depression is booked for a procedure that requires general anaesthesia and a muscle relaxant. A friend who had deep brain stimulation for the same indication tells him he was awake during his own electrode placement. Which statement best explains the difference?
options: Deep brain stimulation is done under local anaesthesia because its electrodes sit only in the scalp
A generalized seizure cannot be induced in an awake patient, whereas brain tissue itself has no pain receptors, so an electrode can be placed while the patient is awake
Muscle relaxants are contraindicated in deep brain stimulation because they interfere with the implanted pulse generator
Electroconvulsive therapy uses magnetic fields, which are painful, whereas deep brain stimulation uses electrical current, which is not
questions.explain: Why: this is exactly the discriminator given for the ECT poll — you cannot give a seizure to an awake person, while DBS patients need not be fully asleep because there are no pain receptors on the surface of the brain. Not the others: DBS electrodes are placed into the brain, not the scalp; nothing in the lecture links muscle relaxants to the pulse generator; ECT applies electrical current through scalp electrodes, and it is rTMS and magnetic seizure therapy that use magnetic fields.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman begins weekly therapy for a long-standing pattern of mistrust in relationships. The sessions are unstructured, explore her relationship with her mother in early childhood, and repeatedly examine feelings she notices arising toward the therapist herself. Which modality is most consistent with this approach?
options: Cognitive behaviour therapy
Psychodynamic psychotherapy
Acceptance and commitment therapy
Dialectical behaviour therapy
questions.explain: Why: unconscious conflicts and early relationships shaping current patterns, exploration of transference and repetition of past relational patterns, and a less structured format are the defining features of psychodynamic psychotherapy; the stated discriminator is that CBT would not go back into childhood. Not the others: CBT is practical, time-limited and works on automatic thoughts with homework and worksheets; ACT focuses on acceptance and value-aligned action; DBT teaches emotion regulation, distress tolerance, interpersonal effectiveness and mindfulness skills, and is named for borderline personality disorder.

questions.stem: A surgical resident is humiliated by her staff physician in the operating room and says nothing at the time. She drives home and snaps angrily at her partner over an unwashed dish. Which defence mechanism does this best illustrate?
options: Projection
Displacement
Sublimation
Regression
questions.explain: Why: displacement is redirecting emotions to a safer target — the slide's own example is yelling at family after being criticized by a boss. Not the others: projection would be attributing her own anger to someone else; sublimation would channel the impulse into a socially acceptable outlet such as competitive sport or a long run; regression would be reverting to earlier developmental behaviour, such as an adult tantrum.

questions.stem: A second-year medical student scores 88 per cent on an examination. When congratulated he replies, 'that doesn't count, the exam was easy and everyone did well.' Which cognitive distortion does this statement best illustrate?
options: Disqualifying the positive
Mental filter
Fortune telling
All or nothing thinking
questions.explain: Why: disqualifying the positive is discounting good things that have happened or that you have done, and the slide's own example thought is 'that doesn't count'. Not the others: a mental filter is attending only to certain evidence, such as noticing failures but not successes; fortune telling is a form of jumping to conclusions that predicts the future; all or nothing thinking is black and white reasoning such as 'if I'm not perfect I have failed'.

questions.topic: Skills · TIPP and the physiological sigh
questions.stem: A 22-year-old man in the emergency department is acutely emotionally dysregulated after an argument. He is hyperventilating with a heart rate of 120. You place a cold pack on the back of his neck and coach him through a very slow, prolonged exhale through pursed lips. Which mechanism best explains why both manoeuvres help?
options: Both increase sympathetic outflow, discharging the panic response

Both lower heart rate — cold through the bradycardic diving reflex, slow exhalation through reduced intrathoracic pressure and altered venous return — and the low heart rate signals safety upward to limbic structures so the prefrontal cortex comes back online
Both raise arterial carbon dioxide, which directly sedates the cerebral cortex
Both act at 5-HT2A receptors to disrupt default mode network activity
questions.explain: Why: the unifying mechanism given for TIPP is that every letter drives heart rate down, and a low heart rate is the signal to the limbic system that the danger is over; for the exhale specifically the chain is reduced intrathoracic pressure, altered venous return, lower heart rate and blood pressure, an ascending brainstem signal, then the prefrontal cortex coming back online. The diving reflex is the named basis for the cold-water or ice-pack instruction. Not the others: the purpose of TIPP is to tip body chemistry from sympathetic to parasympathetic, not to increase sympathetic drive; carbon dioxide sedation is not the mechanism taught; 5-HT2A agonism and default mode network disruption is the psychedelics mechanism.

questions.stem: A medical student interviews a 44-year-old man on an inpatient unit. The man says he feels "fine, maybe a 7 out of 10", but throughout the interview he is tearful, his face barely moves, and his emotional expression does not vary with the topic. In the write-up, which statement correctly assigns these findings?
options: "A 7 out of 10" is the affect; the restricted expression is the mood
"A 7 out of 10" is the mood; the restricted expression is the affect
Both findings belong under thought content
Both findings belong under attitude
questions.explain: Why: the CS2 guide defines mood as the subjective emotional state as reported by the patient, scored 0–10 with 0 = worst, and affect as the objective state as observed by the interviewer, described by quality, intensity, range, stability and congruence. Not the others: the first option simply reverses the pair; thought content covers themes, preoccupations, delusions and suicidal ideation, not emotional state; attitude covers cooperativeness and guardedness toward the interviewer. Note also the incongruence between the reported 7/10 and the observed presentation — congruence with mood is itself an affect descriptor.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman is brought to hospital with four days of believing that staff are poisoning her food. On examination she is disoriented to place and date, her level of alertness fluctuates through the interview, and she cannot sustain attention. Applying the guide's hierarchical diagnostic scheme, what should this combination of findings prompt you to do?
options: Move down the hierarchy and treat this as a primary depressive presentation
Move up the hierarchy and look for a physical or drug-induced cause
Diagnose a primary psychotic disorder, since delusions are present
Defer any diagnostic reasoning until a longitudinal history is available
questions.explain: Why: confusion is the hallmark of rung 1 — physical and drug-induced conditions — and those conditions may show all the features of everything lower on the ladder. The psychoses on rung 2 are explicitly "unlikely to feature the confusion" that characterizes physical disorders, so delusions plus confusion push you upward. Not the others: rung 3 (depression and anxiety) is defined by affective symptoms without confusion or impaired reality-testing; calling this a primary psychosis ignores the hallmark that distinguishes rung 1 from rung 2; and while the course of the sickness does rely on the history, rung 1 conditions are the ones most open to specific, sometimes life-saving treatment, so the work-up cannot wait.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man tells you that since losing his job life has felt so stressful that he has been thinking about death. Following the CS2 guide's suicide screening sequence, which question comes next?
options: "What are some reasons for staying alive?"
"Have you attempted suicide in the past? When?"
"Are you thinking about ways that you would end your life?"
"Have you prepared or acquired the means?"
questions.explain: Why: the ladder runs ideation → method → means → intent → past attempts, and only then classifies acute versus chronic and active versus passive before closing on protective factors. He has given you ideation, so method is next. Not the others: protective factors are the final step, not the second; past attempts come after intent; and asking about means skips the method step. The order is the point — this is the single most OSCE-relevant list in the guide.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is assessed for low mood. You classify his symptoms and signs, you establish that he was made redundant two months ago and is facing eviction, and bloodwork shows a markedly raised TSH. Using the guide's three components of sickness, which component does the eviction and job loss represent?
options: Disease
Illness
Predicament
Prognosis
questions.explain: Why: after Taylor 1979, a working diagnosis needs three things — classification of the symptoms and signs (illness), discernment of the context in which they are to be understood (predicament), and discovery, if possible, of the underlying pathophysiological processes (disease). Job loss and eviction are context. Not the others: the raised TSH is the disease component; the symptom classification is the illness component; prognosis is one of the three outputs of history and examination (diagnosis, prognosis, treatment), not a component of sickness.

questions.stem: A student has ten minutes of a fifteen-minute interview left. The patient has twice mentioned drinking "a fair bit" since her separation, and the student has not followed it up, planning to ask about alcohol at the very end. Which process principle is being broken?
options: Avoid repetition: do not ask for information already elicited
Do not wait until the end of the interview to raise potentially important or sensitive topics
Move from open to closed questions when open questions are unproductive
Ask the patient to explain technical or obscure words they use
questions.explain: Why: step 31 says explicitly not to leave potentially important or sensitive topics to the end — and step 26 adds that you should raise emotionally loaded topics yourself when the patient gives verbal or non-verbal clues to their relevance, which two mentions of drinking plainly are. Not the others: nothing has been asked twice, so repetition is not the issue; open-to-closed movement addresses incoherent or ambiguous answers, not deferred topics; and asking the patient to define jargon concerns the patient's vocabulary, not the interview's timing.

guide.s: Don't wait until the end of the interview

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man with a first episode of psychosis states that he is not unwell and that the voices are real people speaking to him. Nevertheless, he has continued attending work, has kept his rent paid, and agreed to come to the appointment when his sister asked. Which is the most accurate MSE statement?
options: Insight is impaired and judgment appears intact
Judgment is impaired and insight appears intact
Both insight and judgment are impaired, since they always move together
Neither can be commented on without formal cognitive testing
questions.explain: Why: insight is the ability to realize that one has a mental health concern and to appreciate its implications — he denies illness, so insight is impaired. Judgment refers to recent behaviours as they relate to safety, social functioning and treatment decisions, and his behaviour has been appropriate. Not the others: reversing the pair misapplies both definitions; the two can dissociate, which is precisely why they are graded separately as none/impaired, partial or intact; and cognitive testing (MMSE or MoCA) belongs to the cognition domain, not to insight and judgment.

questions.stem: A student's psychiatric case report contains a complete history and a complete mental status examination, correctly categorized, with a clear diagnostic impression. The preceptor marks Data collection as "meets expectations" rather than "outstanding". Which addition would most likely move that domain up the scale?
options: A longer verbatim transcript of the patient's answers
Information on the psychosocial context of this individual patient
A five-sentence rather than a two-sentence summary of the encounter
A list of differential diagnoses with DSM criteria counts for each
questions.explain: Why: the Data collection anchors run from "insufficient information to identify the major problem" at 1, to "obtains sufficient information to identify the major problem" at 3, to "obtains complete information including psychosocial context of individual patient" at 5. In every domain the jump from meets to outstanding is a jump from completeness to synthesis. Not the others: length of transcript is not a rubric anchor; the summary block explicitly requires 2–3 sentences naming the most pertinent historical and mental-state findings, so lengthening it would work against the form; and criteria counting sits under Approach to the problem, which is already described as recognizing the problem with a good description of the illness.
