questions.stem: You are completing a biopsychosocial-cultural formulation grid for a newly arrived asylum seeker. He lives with a cousin who drives him to appointments, he has completed a trade qualification, and he has found part-time work. Into which row do these belong?
options: Predisposing
Precipitating
Perpetuating
Protective
questions.explain: Why: in the 4-P grid, protective factors are the patient's strengths and supports — a supportive relative, education and occupational skills, employment and connection with healthcare are the standard social-column protective entries. Not the others: predisposing factors are longstanding vulnerabilities that pre-date the presentation; precipitating factors are the triggers for this episode; perpetuating factors are what maintains the symptoms now, such as housing instability or ongoing legal uncertainty.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man with a known personality disorder is medically cleared in the emergency department after a superficial laceration to his forearm. The emergency physician asks the on-call team to admit him. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Admit him, because self-harm has occurred
Advise that admission is unlikely to help patients with his diagnosis
Assess his current mental state and suicidality
Discharge him with an outpatient psychiatry referral
questions.explain: Why: after medical stabilization, psychiatric assessment must establish the current mental state and risk of suicidality; every disposition decision follows from that assessment. Not the others: automatic admission, automatic discharge and dismissing the admission request are all described as inappropriate without assessment. The second option is a half-truth trap: the teaching point about chronic fluctuating suicidal ideation and admission is real, but stating it before assessing is the error. Note too that deliberate self-harm is tissue damage without suicidal intent — believe the patient's account of intent and still assess risk.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman describes three weeks of low mood and poor sleep since her mother's death. She continues to work, manages the household, and her relationships are unchanged; she says she feels sad but that it comes and goes and she can be distracted by her grandchildren. Which feature would most strongly support calling this a mental disorder rather than a normal response?
options: The presence of a clear precipitating stressor
Symptoms persisting beyond two weeks
Clinically significant impairment of her day-to-day functioning
A previous episode of an anxiety disorder in her twenties
questions.explain: Why: a mental disorder involves clinically significant disturbance with functional impairment, and that is the key distinguishing feature from a normal emotional response — here it is exactly what is absent. Not the others: a precipitating stressor does not by itself establish disorder (and the definition excludes an expectable or culturally approved response to a loss); duration alone does not; and a comorbid or past history is not a criterion. This is also why the CS2 history makes impact on day-to-day function at work and at home a core severity domain.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman who recently migrated presents with insomnia and intrusive memories. She tells you, through her teenage son who is interpreting, that she believes her symptoms are a punishment sent by her late grandmother. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Explain that this belief is a symptom and offer psychoeducation to correct it
Arrange a trained interpreter and explore what she thinks is happening
Start an antidepressant immediately and review in six weeks
Reassure her the symptoms will settle and diagnose PTSD
questions.explain: Why: two rules apply at once. Use trained interpreters, not family — a teenage son interpreting for his mother about trauma is exactly the situation the rule addresses. And explore the explanatory model ("What do you think is happening?"), which builds trust and informs culturally sensitive care. Not the others: challenging cultural beliefs is the direct opposite of exploring the explanatory model; starting medication before engagement skips the negotiation the patient has not yet been invited into; and reassurance plus a label neither engages her model nor addresses the interpreter problem.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old student reports two months of anhedonia, insomnia, poor concentration and fatigue. She has failed two courses and stopped seeing friends. She meets four of the nine DSM criteria for a major depressive episode, so the diagnosis is not made. Which limitation of the DSM system does this best illustrate?
options: Comorbidity produces multiple overlapping labels
Arbitrary diagnostic thresholds exclude clinically significant cases
Dimensional models are too rigid to capture symptom clusters
Heterogeneity means two patients with the same diagnosis differ
questions.explain: Why: the categorical approach can miss meaningful distress and impairment when the symptom count falls just below threshold — 4 of 9 is not an MDE while 5 of 9 is, which is the lecture's own worked illustration. Not the others: comorbidity and heterogeneity are also listed limitations of categorical systems, but neither is what this vignette shows; and the third option inverts the models, since it is categorical rather than dimensional systems that are rigid. The four listed limitations are arbitrary thresholds, comorbidity, heterogeneity and subthreshold illness.

guide.s: what you see in their face

cards.prompt: On the MSE, what is the difference between mood and affect, and by which three descriptors is affect described?
cards.answer: Mood is what the patient says — their reply when you ask how their mood is. Affect is what you see in their face as an expression of internal feeling state. Describe the affect, the range, and its appropriateness to content.

guide.s: in the absence of any obvious stimulus

cards.prompt: Define hallucination and illusion, and give the source's example of each.
cards.answer: Hallucination = a sensory experience perceived in the absence of any obvious stimulus (hearing voices with no auditory input). Illusion = misperceiving an existing stimulus as something else (hearing your name called when your phone rings).

guide.s: Both insight and judgment are required to have capacity

cards.prompt: What are the three tasks that make up insight, how does judgment differ, and what do the two together determine?
cards.answer: Insight: (1) accurately recognize new or unusual symptoms; (2) accurately identify them as due to a specific pathological process; (3) accurately recognize the benefits of treatment. Judgment is using that insight to make decisions in one's best interest. Both are required to have capacity to make decisions in one's medical care.

cards.text: Social scientists found inter-rater reliability in psychiatric diagnosis was very low — as low as {{30%}} — and the St. Louis group's symptom-based checklists were developed by {{1972}}.

Freud published his comparison of hysterical versus stroke-related paralysis in {{1893}}, and with Josef Breuer published Studies on Hysteria in {{1895}} — the point at which treatment re-entered psychiatry.

cards.prompt: Of the 1930s somatic therapies, which survived appropriately conducted research, and for what did it prove most useful?
options: Insulin coma; psychosis
Electroconvulsive therapy; mood symptoms
Psychosurgery; intractable psychosis
Fever therapy; neurosyphilis

guide.s: subjective distress and/or significant impairment in function

cards.prompt: Select the three changes that DSM-III introduced.
options: A disorder must cause subjective distress and/or significant impairment in function
Diagnosis by a statistically validated checklist of reported or observed signs and symptoms, not expert opinion of meaning
A potential disorder is not included unless it can be reliably and stably identified
A primary distinction between brain tissue diseases and psychogenic diseases
Diagnoses recorded for hospital census purposes rather than treatment

cards.prompt: Match each figure to their contribution as PW03 describes it.
pairs: First described shell shock in WW1 veterans
First applied scientific method to behaviour patterns in groups; first description of chronic psychotic disorders
Projective tests in 30 gay men vs 30 age-matched controls, no difference found
Ran La Salpetiere, the giant Paris asylum for women, where Freud studied
Developed talk therapy and hypnosis for shell shock

guide.s: every era is a hope and a disappointment

cards.prompt: Put PW03's eras in the order the module presents them.
items: Neurologists and the first biological psychiatry (1840's-1890's)
The rise of psychoanalysis part 2 and the Bad Mother (1940's-1970's)
The rise of diagnostics and DSM-III (1970's-now)

guide.s: the area of skin supplied by the cutaneous sensory fibres

cards.prompt: Define dermatome and myotome as PW02 does.
cards.answer: Dermatome = the area of skin supplied by the cutaneous sensory fibres contained within a single spinal nerve, and therefore arising from a single spinal level. Myotome = the group of muscle cells controlled by the somatic motor fibres within a single spinal nerve; these cells may be distributed into several muscles and can control one or more movements.

guide.s: the spinal cord ends at L1

cards.text: The spinal cord ends at {{L1}}, which is why a lumbar disc herniation involves only the nerve roots, while a cervical disc can impinge a nerve root, the spinal cord, or {{both}}.

guide.s: inversion and eversion are both labelled L5

cards.prompt: On a UofT assessment, which root is assigned to ankle eversion?
options: L4
L5
S1
L5-S1

cards.prompt: Select the findings expected in an upper motor neuron lesion.
options: Increased tone (spasticity)
Normal muscle bulk
Increased reflexes with ankle clonus
Extensor plantar response
Myotomal weakness
Atrophy in the affected myotome

cards.prompt: Match each reflex to its root value(s).
What three features make up cauda equina syndrome, and why is it urgent?
cards.answer: Low back pain, saddle (perineal) anaesthesia, and bladder and/or bowel dysfunction (urinary retention or overflow, unrecognized fecal incontinence) — with or without lower limb pain, sensory loss or weakness. It is a CORE Back Tool red flag and a surgical emergency; bladder and bowel compromise is a surgical emergency whether the lesion is cord or root.

guide.s: a cervical cord lesion can cause leg weakness

cards.prompt: Can a cervical lesion cause leg weakness, and what determines the answer?
cards.answer: A cervical spinal cord lesion can, because it affects the upper motor neuron limb of the pathway to the leg. A cervical nerve root lesion cannot. UMN signs (increased tone, brisk reflexes with clonus, extensor plantar) point to the cord and should redirect imaging from the lumbar to the cervical or thoracic spine.

guide.s: High density → High attenuation → film = white

cards.prompt: On an x-ray, what determines attenuation, and what do high and low attenuation look like on the film?
cards.answer: Density. High density → high attenuation → white; low density → low attenuation → black.

guide.s: lead → bone → muscle → water → fat → air

cards.prompt: Order these from highest to lowest density and attenuation, as slide 2.4 prints them.

cards.text: The Hounsfield scale runs −1000 to +1000: air is {{−1000}}, water and CSF are {{0}}, and bone is {{+400 to +1000}}.

guide.s: do not need to be memorized

cards.prompt: Match each structure to the point value slide 2.15 puts on it (illustrative — the ordering is what matters).

cards.text: Slide 2.19's three parenchymal windows: brain {{W80 L40}}, stroke {{W30 L30}}, bleed {{W200 L100}}.

cards.prompt: At what level is the puncture for myelography performed, and why?
options: L3-L4 or lower, because the spinal cord ends at L1-L2
L1-L2, because the cord ends at T12
L5-S1 only, because the cauda equina ends at L4
Any lumbar level, since the contrast surrounds the cord anyway

guide.s: vascular access, usually femoral puncture, therefore invasive

cards.prompt: What three things does cerebral angiography require, and which one makes it invasive?
cards.answer: Vascular access, usually femoral arterial puncture — the invasive element — plus fluoroscopy and an injectable contrast agent.

cards.prompt: Which of these are listed as adverse effects of iodinated contrast in this module?
options: Allergy, from mild rash to anaphylaxis
Contrast-induced nephropathy
Fluid overload
Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis
Multiple parenchymal microhaemorrhages

cards.prompt: Name gadolinium's two listed toxicities, and how it appears on MR.
cards.answer: Allergy (rare) and nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in renal failure; it is bright on T1.

cards.prompt: Match each MR sequence to what the module's summary table says it shows.
pairs: CSF dark; white matter whiter than grey
CSF white; white matter darker than grey

cards.prompt: Multiple small round black dots throughout the parenchyma on a GRE sequence in an older patient indicate what?

Multiple acute infarcts with restricted diffusion

cards.text: MR can image vessels with no contrast agent at all: {{time-of-flight}} for arteries and {{phase-contrast}} for veins.

cards.prompt: Which MR brain sequences must be requested by name, and what else must go on the requisition?
cards.answer: MR angiogram and venogram — every other sequence comes automatically. Always write down the diagnoses you want to confirm or rule out.

cards.prompt: Put the stages of primary neurulation in order.
items: Induction of the neural plate by the notochord
Apposition, contact and fusion across the midline

cards.prompt: Match each neural tube vesicle to the cavity it contributes.
Which of these does slide 11 list as risk factors for open neural tube defects?
options: Family history
Diabetes mellitus
Obesity
Anticonvulsant use
Maternal age over 40

cards.prompt: Where do alar and basal derivatives sit in the spinal cord, where in the floor of the fourth ventricle, and what divides them?
cards.answer: Cord: alar dorsal, basal ventral. Fourth ventricle: alar (sensory) lateral, basal (motor) medial, after the pontine flexure everts the alar plates. The sulcus limitans is the boundary at both levels.

cards.prompt: In Chiari II, compression of which structure produces the hydrocephalus?
options: The foramen of Magendie
The cerebral aqueduct
The foramina of Luschka
The central canal

cards.prompt: Match each personality disorder to its cluster.
Match each personality disorder to its criteria threshold.

"You look like you're feeling humiliated and furious."
"Waiting is one of the biggest problems in our system."
"Of course this is frustrating, given how long you waited last time."

guide.s: Validate → both-and → offer help → suggest skill → suggest another

cards.prompt: Put the module's response to an acutely distressed patient in order.
items: Validate ("This is devastating. I see you are feeling really overwhelmed.")
Both-and statement ("I can't fix the system AND I would like to help you.")
Offer help ("Would you like to try some coping strategies?")
Suggest a skill ("How about holding an ice pack?")
Suggest another skill ("OK, let's try slow breathing instead.")

guide.s: ABCs first, and give medical treatment

cards.prompt: Put the module's four management steps for self-harm in order.
items: Encourage follow-up with mental health resources
Refer to psychiatry if unsure or for a second opinion

cards.text: General PD criterion A requires the enduring pattern to show in at least {{2}} of four areas: cognition, affectivity, interpersonal functioning and {{impulse control}}.
Antisocial PD needs {{3}} of 7 criteria, the person must be at least {{18}} years old, and there must be conduct disorder with onset before age {{15}}.

guide.t: 5 · The nine DSM criteria for BPD

cards.text: Borderline personality disorder requires {{5}} of 9 criteria, which yields {{256}} different ways to meet the diagnosis.
A course of DBT usually runs {{6-12}} months, with {{1}} hour a week of individual therapy plus {{2}} hours a week of skills group.

cards.prompt: Which statement about psychopathy is correct?
options: It is a DSM diagnosis distinct from antisocial PD
It is identified with the Hare PCL-R and is not a DSM diagnosis
Everyone with antisocial PD has psychopathy
It is a Cluster A personality disorder

guide.s: Fear of being uncared for vs fear of rejection

cards.prompt: What distinguishes dependent from avoidant personality disorder?
options: Dependent fears being alone and uncared for; avoidant fears rejection
Dependent patients avoid people; avoidant patients cling to them
Only avoidant PD is in Cluster C
Dependent PD requires onset after age 18

cards.prompt: What is the heritability of impulsivity given by the module?
options: 5–15%
20–62%
70–90%
Not established

cards.prompt: The one-year suicide rate after self-harm is roughly what multiple of the general-population rate?
options: About 3 times
About 10 times
About 37 times
About 100 times

cards.prompt: Select the three features of an emotionally sensitive temperament.
options: High sensitivity — a low threshold for reacting
Emotional intensity
Slow return to emotional baseline
Impulsivity
Extroversion

cards.prompt: Select the social factors the module counts as contributing to BPD.
options: Maternal separation at a young age
Neglect
Reinforcement of emotional outbursts
Invalidation followed by talking about it and repairing
Being able to talk about emotions

cards.prompt: Select the four skill sets taught in DBT skills groups.
options: Mindfulness
Distress tolerance
Emotion regulation
Interpersonal effectiveness
Cognitive restructuring

guide.s: cause them distress or impair their functioning

cards.prompt: When do personality traits become a personality disorder?
cards.answer: When they cause the person distress or impair their functioning.

guide.s: none are approved to directly treat PDs

cards.prompt: What causes personality disorders, and what is the mainstay of management?
cards.answer: An interaction of genetic predisposition and environmental influences; psychotherapy is the mainstay, and no medication is approved to treat a PD directly.

cards.prompt: Which schizophrenia domain does each Cluster A personality disorder resemble?
cards.answer: Schizotypal resembles positive symptoms, schizoid the negative symptoms, and paranoid PD the paranoid delusions — but with no true hallucinations or delusions.

cards.prompt: What is the "wanting" test for schizoid versus avoidant PD?
cards.answer: Schizoid patients do not want relationships; avoidant patients want them but fear rejection.

cards.prompt: Define validation and invalidation as the module uses them.
cards.answer: Validation is showing you understand someone's experience; invalidation is not understanding it — dismissing, ignoring, not responding, being confused or criticizing.

cards.prompt: What are the four consequences of repeatedly invalidating an emotionally intense person?
cards.answer: Emotions intensify; the sense of self becomes confused; emotions become hard to interpret (alexithymia); emotions become so overwhelming the person seeks escape.

guide.t: 5 · The nine DSM criteria for BPD
guide.s: a few hours to a few days

cards.prompt: How long does BPD's affective instability last, and what triggers it?
cards.answer: A few hours to a few days — the module's interview guide says minutes to hours — and it is reactive to external events, unlike a mood episode lasting weeks.

cards.prompt: What is the rationale for restricting access to means, and what should be prescribed?
cards.answer: If a person has to wait, think or problem-solve, the urge may pass before they act. Prescribe small supplies of 1–2 weeks, ask about stockpiling and adherence, and ask about insulin, opiates, bulk acetaminophen and other people's medications.

cards.prompt: On the interview road map, which mental-state section pairs with the history area "emotions"?
cards.answer: Mood and affect.

cards.prompt: Define mood and affect as the CS2 guide does.
cards.answer: Mood is subjective, reported by the patient (0–10, 0 = worst); affect is objective, observed by the interviewer (quality, intensity, range, stability, congruence).

cards.prompt: Insight versus judgment, and how are they graded?
cards.answer: Insight = realizing you have a mental health concern and appreciating its implications. Judgment = recent behaviours regarding safety, social functioning and treatment decisions. Both graded none/impaired · partial · intact/full.

cards.prompt: What three things must a management plan be, per the CS2 guide?
cards.answer: Biopsychosocial (medication, therapy, lifestyle), feasible, and mitigating of any safety concerns.

cards.prompt: What are the guide's two rules about checklists and about the order of a case presentation?
cards.answer: Never interview from a checklist — use it towards the end or after the interview. And do not confuse the order of the presentation with the sequence of information-gathering.

cards.prompt: Name the four functional domains in which you establish the impact of the current problems.
cards.answer: Personal care and survival; family functioning; occupational functioning; broad social functioning.

cards.text: The MedSIS summary block requires the encounter to be summarized in {{2–3}} sentences, naming the most pertinent {{historical}} and mental-state findings.
The hallmark of rung 1 (physical and drug-induced conditions) is {{confusion}}, while the hallmark of the psychoses on rung 2 is impaired {{reality-testing}}.

cards.prompt: "Unaware of being ill" is the guide's example descriptor for which MSE category?
options: Attitude
Thought content
Insight
Cognition

cards.prompt: A clinician notices she dreads every appointment with one patient and finds herself cutting them short. What is this?
options: Transference
Countertransference
Identification
Therapeutic alliance

options: Suicide
Other kinds of deliberate self-harm
Neglect of dependents
Financial exploitation
Inability to look after oneself

Problems pursuing leisure activities
Dissociative problems

cards.prompt: Match each MSE category to the guide's own example descriptor.
Match each anxiety syndrome to its screening question in Appendix 3.
pairs: Do you regularly worry about multiple things?
Do you develop intense physical symptoms all of a sudden?
Do you avoid situations like being in public?
Do you worry about performance or being judged?
Are there things (heights, animals) that you fear or avoid?

cards.prompt: Put the suicide screening ladder in the order the guide gives it.
items: Ideation — thoughts of death or suicide
Method — ways you would end your life
Classify acute vs chronic, active vs passive
Protective factors — reasons for staying alive

cards.prompt: Put the guide's five-item "stop, look and listen" loop in order.
items: Prompt the patient for more details
Probe for clarification of what you do not understand

cards.prompt: DSM-5 panic disorder: how many attack symptoms, over what time course, plus what second criterion?
cards.answer: ≥4 of 13 symptoms in an attack that peaks within minutes, plus ≥1 month of persistent worry about further attacks and/or significant maladaptive behaviour change after at least one attack.

cards.prompt: The 23-year-old with one-hour episodes of sadness once or twice weekly: on which two grounds did she fail MDE criteria?
cards.answer: (1) No functional impairment — she does not miss work or social events; (2) failure of the duration requirement — a depressive episode needs 2 weeks of symptoms most of the day, nearly every day.

cards.prompt: Harlow gave infant rhesus monkeys a wire mother with milk and a cloth mother without. What was the result, and what does it show?
cards.answer: The infant spent most of its time with the cloth mother, returning to the wire mother only briefly to feed — contact comfort, not feeding, drives attachment.

cards.prompt: Which substances can kill you in withdrawal, what do they cause, and what is the named management?
cards.answer: CNS depressants — alcohol, benzodiazepines, phenobarbital — can cause seizures, delirium tremens and death. Management named: diazepam plus thiamine, with admission for IV treatment. Opioid withdrawal is very uncomfortable but not lethal.

cards.prompt: After a frightening or traumatic event, what proportion of people still have post-traumatic symptoms at one year, and why does that matter?
cards.answer: About 10% — in 90% the symptoms have resolved by a year out. Post-traumatic symptoms are the norm after trauma; it is their persistence in the ~10% minority that constitutes PTSD.

cards.prompt: What risk of bipolar disorder did the lecture give for someone with a first-degree relative with bipolar disorder?
cards.answer: About 10% — the only heritability figure given anywhere in the three lectures, and it appears on no slide.

cards.text: In the Kaiser–CDC ACE study, about {{64%}} of adults reported at least one ACE and about {{12%}} reported four or more, with a {{dose–response}} relationship to later illness.
A major depressive episode requires {{5}} of 9 symptoms within the same {{2-week}} period, at least one of which must be depressed mood or {{anhedonia}}.
Each additional positive childhood experience reduces adult depression risk by {{26%}}, and Winnicott's 'good enough' parent requires {{optimal frustration}} rather than perfection.

cards.prompt: Tactile hallucinations — bugs crawling on or under the skin — are most in keeping with which cause?
options: Alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal
Schizophrenia
Temporal lobe epilepsy
Delirium

options: Papageno effect — a character in Mozart's opera The Magic Flute
Werther effect — a character in Goethe's 1774 novel
Papageno effect — a character in Goethe's 1774 novel
Werther effect — a character in Mozart's opera The Magic Flute

cards.prompt: Which statement belongs to the dimensional, not the categorical, model of psychopathology?
options: Disorders are exaggerated, inflexible versions of normal traits, differing quantitatively
Diagnoses are discrete — you either meet criteria or you don't
Mental diagnoses are qualitatively distinct from normal functioning and from each other
The DSM-5 is the standard diagnostic system currently used

options: Arbitrary diagnostic thresholds

options: Suicidal thoughts
Violent thoughts towards others
Driving safety
Child safety
Firearm registration
Financial capacity

cards.prompt: Match each MSIGECAPS letter to its depression screening domain.
Match each ASEPTIC letter to its mental status exam domain.
Put the first six headings of the psychiatric interview outline in the order taught.

items: Precipitating — the trigger for the current problem
Perpetuating — what maintains it once established
Protective — strengths that counteract the first three

cards.prompt: How many of the brain's neurons are monoamine neurons, and why does that matter?
cards.answer: Only a few million out of about 100 billion. They arise in brainstem nuclei and project diffusely to executive, limbic and sensory cortex and down to the spinal cord, acting like switches or main highways — which is why modulating them changes mood, cognition and behaviour at once, and why side-effect profiles are broad.

cards.prompt: Match each defence mechanism to its example.
pairs: Insists they do not have cancer despite clear medical evidence
Accuses others of hostility when feeling hostile oneself
Yells at family after being criticized by the boss
Adult throwing a tantrum under stress

cards.prompt: Give the nucleus of origin and the main functions for serotonin and for norepinephrine.
cards.answer: Serotonin: raphe nuclei — mood, anxiety, sleep, appetite, pain; targeted by SSRIs, SNRIs and TCAs. Norepinephrine: locus coeruleus — attention, arousal, mood, stress; targeted by SNRIs, TCAs, bupropion and stimulants.

cards.text: A typical ECT course is {{8 to 12}} seizures, given {{three times a week}}, usually over a few weeks.

cards.prompt: Why does ECT require general anaesthesia while deep brain stimulation electrodes can be placed in an awake patient?
options: Because a seizure cannot be induced in an awake person, whereas brain tissue has no pain receptors
Because ECT electrodes penetrate the skull and DBS electrodes do not
Because muscle relaxants are needed to prevent the DBS device from misfiring
Because DBS is performed only under local anaesthesia in the scalp

cards.prompt: Match each cognitive distortion to its example thought.
pairs: If I'm not perfect I have failed
Noticing our failures but not seeing our successes
None of these students liked my lecture, because nobody talked to me after
If I fail the exam I'll be kicked out, then I can't pay rent, then I'll be homeless

cards.prompt: Which of the following are the four DBT TIPP crisis survival skills?
options: Temperature
Intense exercise
Progressive muscle relaxation
Paced breathing
Thought records
Interoceptive exposure

cards.prompt: Put the slide's seven body scan meditation steps in order.
items: Find a quiet place and get comfortable
Warm up with some deep breaths
Start at one end of your body
Move to the next part of your body
Be mindful in all parts of your body
Begin to come back into the room

cards.text: About {{30-50%}} of psychiatric patients use complementary and alternative medicine, often {{without informing}} their clinician.

cards.prompt: State the mechanistic chain given for psychedelics, and what the default mode network does in depression.
cards.answer: 5-HT2A receptor agonism disrupts default mode network activity, with increased neuroplasticity and BDNF expression. In depression the default mode network becomes overactive and does not shut off, which is experienced as rumination; SSRIs and ketamine also reduce that hyperactivity, psychedelics most intensively.

cards.prompt: Which mood stabilizer is described as more effective for bipolar depression?
options: Lithium
Valproic acid
Lamotrigine
Carbamazepine

cards.prompt: Describe the physiological sigh and the two numbers attached to it.
cards.answer: Two inhales through the nose — the biggest breath of the day plus a sip of air at the top — then an extended exhale through pursed lips, at least 10 seconds. Three repetitions dropped the lecturer's own heart rate by about 15 to 20 beats per minute, and one participant fainted, so syncope is a real adverse effect.

guides.title: Week 40 · 1 Introduction to Psychiatry & the History of Psychiatry
guides.html:
PW01 · PW03 · Foundations

Introduction to Psychiatry & the History of Psychiatry

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The orientation reading's framing, statistics and mental status vocabulary, then Garcia's history module from ancient Egypt to the three rules of DSM-III.

Orientation

Week 40 opens the psychiatry block with two pre-week pieces. PW01 is a three-page orientation reading (Carla Garcia, 2019) that sets the posture of the block and tours the mental status examination in plain language. PW03 is a 24-slide self-study module by the same author — "How We Get to Now" — tracing the discipline as a chain of matched hopes and disappointments ending at DSM-III. Neither is a criteria module: what is examinable here is names, dates, numbers and structures.

Scope, from the lecturer (§7.0). On the history module: you "should look at" it — "There might be a question from it. It's kind of interesting. It's not super heavy." On the orientation reading: "It's very general. There's nothing to memorize there." And the nosology module is out: "You do not need to open that intro to nosology in psychiatry… There's no MCQ questions from it" [Byrne L1 tx 3:22, 3:53]. PW01's header reads "WEEK 46 MOOD AND ANXIETY DISORDERS" — stale numbering; its own body lists Week 40 as Introduction [PW01 p1, p3].

PW01 — how the block is framed

  • The content "will be directly referenced and built upon in your clerkship rotation next year" — foundational, not survey [PW01 p1].
  • Medications are paired with the neurobiology of mental illness via interventions such as neurostimulation techniques; even "simple behavioural techniques" work alongside a trusting relationship and a bit of education [PW01 p1].
  • The anti-dualism statement of the week: the Cartesian split of mind and body "was only ever an illusion" [PW01 p1].
  • Physicians must also be skilled communicators, collaborators, managers, and (perhaps most crucially) advocates. Note the hedge — "perhaps most crucially" does not rank advocacy outright [PW01 p1].
  • The three worries named: "Will you be safe? Will the patients and their families be nice? Will anyone ever get better?" Yes as often as in any other area of medicine, but "everyone will struggle to believe that at first due to the stigma these disorders carry". Closing principle: "be kind, be mindful, and be curious" [PW01 p1].

The five Canadian statistics (verbatim)

#Statistic
1One in three Canadians will experience a mental illness or substance use disorder in their lifetime.
2By age 40, about 50% of the population will have or have had a mental illness.
3More than 10 Canadians die by suicide each day.
4Suicide accounts for 24% of all deaths among 15–24 year olds and 16% among 25–44 year olds.
5Suicide rates among Indigenous youth are among the highest in the world.

Statistic 4 has two different denominators — 24% of all deaths in the 15–24 band, 16% in the 25–44 band. Neither is a population rate [PW01 p1].

PW01 — "a different physical examination": the MSE

The equivalent of the physical exam in psychiatry is the mental status examination — familiar because you have been reading verbal and non-verbal cues "since you were an infant", a "deeply human skill", of which the MSE is a formalized, organized way and "a cornerstone of a thorough psychiatric assessment". Emphasized in the original: "You track and evaluate these signs WHILE you are interviewing a patient" [PW01 p1].

DomainWhat it is
AppearanceBody habitus, grooming, dress — "well groomed, appropriately dressed" vs "disheveled… barefoot despite winter weather"
AttitudeThe patient's demeanor — "pleasant, engageable" vs "guarded, irritable"
Level of arousalAlert? Somnolent but rousable? Unconscious? If drowsy, oriented?
Level of activityNormal speed of motion? Fidgety = psychomotor restlessness; sluggish = psychomotor retardation
MoodThe patient's reply when you ask how their mood is — subjective, reported
AffectWhat you see in their face as an expression of internal feeling state — describe the affect, the range, and its appropriateness to content ("sad, restricted, and appropriate" vs "euphoric, labile, and inappropriate")
Thought processOrganization and clarity; the normal standard is goal-directed and logical
SpeechVolume, rate, rhythm and prosody — prosody: sarcastic, earnest, uncertain
Thought contentDelusions ("fixed, false beliefs such as people with psychotic symptoms experience"), thoughts of self harm, of suicide, of harm to others
PerceptionsHallucinations and illusions — see below
CognitionOperating with a cognitive impairment? Screen with the MoCA or the "better known (but maybe less reliable)" MMSE
Insight and judgment"Seem intuitive but are actually somewhat complex" — see below

Beyond discrete symptoms, look for "important trends or qualities to a person's thoughts, as these can speak to risk" — a depressed patient with a poor sense of the future, or one whose paranoid delusions focus on a specific person (a spouse, a boss): "Both of these can increase the risk of this person harming themselves or others" [PW01 p2].

Perceptions — the pair to keep straight
Hallucination = a sensory experience perceived in the absence of any obvious stimulus (hearing voices "while there is no auditory input"). Illusion = misperceiving an existing stimulus as something else (hearing your name called when your phone rings). Commonest in psychosis, but also mood symptoms, delirium, temporal lobe epilepsy [PW01 p2].

Insight is three tasks: (1) accurately recognize new or unusual symptoms ("I'm feeling much more sad and hopeless than usual"); (2) accurately identify them as due to a specific pathological process ("I am experiencing a depressive episode"); (3) accurately recognize the benefits of treatment ("This can be made better by restarting my anti-depressant"). Judgment is "your ability to use insight to make decisions that are in your best interest". The testable link: "Both insight and judgment are required to have capacity to make decisions in your medical care." The caveat: assessing them is difficult, "especially when you factor in clinician bias" [PW01 p2].

Across four weeks students meet five areas of focus: Week 40 Introduction, Week 41 Mood disorders, Week 42 Psychosis, Week 43 Substance abuse, and personality disorders as "a parallel course throughout the weeks" rather than a week of their own. Six reflective questions run throughout, ending on the stigma prompt: "Do I know anyone with these symptoms? If not, why not?" [PW01 p3].

PW03 — the history of psychiatry

Four background forces (s3)
1. Eugenics (degeneration; identifying "devolving" people by physical characteristics) · 2. Colonialism (asylums "across UK and its colonies, especially US and Canada"; the biramistan model from Middle Eastern medicine) · 3. Militarization of Medicine (shell shock; returning soldiers to the battlefield) · 4. Unification vs Pluralism. "Watch out for these forces working in the background" [PW03 s3].
  • Ancient Egypt (s4): two scrolls reference mood and psychotic symptoms; the first description of "wandering uterus" — the origin point of hysteria (standard knowledge, not in the module), placed in Egypt, not Greece; no association with the brain at all; treatment spiritual/magical.
  • Ancient Greece (s5): Hippocratic writings recognize melancholia, psychosis, mania; "Everything is about the humors!"; management is biopsychosocial (framed as ancient, not modern); treatment is "the 'science' of the time (bloodletting, etc)".
  • Medieval Europe (s6): illness is either dangerous immoral forces (witchcraft, possession) or imbalance of humours. Institutionalization begins in the late 1400's, "but often not separate than carceral system" — an entanglement the module returns to at the end.

Structural pattern — every era is a hope and a disappointment

EraThe hopeThe disappointment
The Asylum
1600's–1890's		Funded places from the early 1600's for safety and a humane alternative to jail or homelessness; later architecture, grounds, institutional rules, daily work thought curative; peak 1850's England [s7]Scandals: poor care, unexplained deaths, a conflict of interest between institutional productivity (free patient labour) and duty of care, prevalence rising anyway (syphilis? industrialization? diagnostic practices?). The answer adopted: "Degeneration!" [s8]
Neurologists
1840's–1890's		Brain–behaviour link confirmed in the 1860's; frontal-lobe speech localization, 1860's (Broca, unnamed (standard knowledge, not in the module)); by the 1870's the post-mortem brain exam was the main intervention; Kraepelin gave the first description of chronic psychotic disorders [s10]By the 1890's anatomical study had reached its limit; results inconsistent; normal brains with pathology in real life; cellular study in its infancy; rising demand for treatment [s11]
Psychoanalysis
1860's–1910's		"Phenomenology leads to diagnosis!"; Freud with Charcot at La Salpetiere finds hysterical paralysis differs from stroke paralysis (1893); with Breuer, Studies on Hysteria, 1895 — treatment becomes possible [s12]1897: ALL hysteria traced to a forbidden childhood sexual fantasy; by the 1910's psychoanalysis was codified — then WW1 produced shell shock (Dr. Charles Myers) [s13]
Somatic therapies
1930's		Anecdotal reports of brief lucidity after fevers or seizures. Five tried: cold showers or baths; fever-inducing treatments; insulin-induced comas; electroconvulsive therapy; psychosurgery (lobotomies, cyngulotomies, leucotomies) [s14]"Research supporting all of these except ECT was consistently negative when done appropriately". "Even ECT, developed to treat psychosis, was found most helpful for mood symptoms." Lobotomy briefly extremely popular, consent not rigourous, done by various people, not limited to trained physicians [s15]
Psychoanalysis 2
1940's–1970's		Wartime success in getting soldiers back into war gave psychoanalysis preeminence, particularly in the US; children orphaned by the wars became a source of study for "pathological behaviour" [s16]With "backlash around changing gender roles and misogyny", the "Bad Mother" was blamed for "neuroticism" and outcomes as varied as homosexuality and communism. "This is clearly untrue" — but ~20 years of effort by (mostly female) psychoanalysts and second wave feminists was needed to dismantle it [s17]
Deinstitutionalization
1950's–1990's		Shell shock's best intervention had been community and responsibility to the platoon, treated "on site" with peers as mentors. 1964: Principles of Preventative Psychiatry, after the Coconut Grove fire in Boston (492 deaths), using local churches, schools and clinics. Drugs: chlorpromazine, imipramine, diazepam. Policy: the US 1955 Joint Commission of Mental Illness and Mental Health; in Canada, provincially organized bed closures [s18, s19]"The main problems were 4 fold": insufficient scale; inflexible, one-size-fits-all care; poor hospital–community integration; stigma excluding the most disruptive patients. Result: "a surge in homelessness and repeat brief hospitalizations", and "may have also led to the surge of people with SPMI in carceral systems" [s20]

Degeneration — the five false assumptions (s9)

  1. "Evolution is a one way process, guiding species to their ideal version over time, including humans."
  2. "Some humans are not suited to the biologic and cognitive stressors of modern life, due in part to backwards or primitive traits."
  3. "It is possible for individuals within a species to devolve into a more primitive state… also possible to identify these devolving/degenerating people by physical characteristics (shapes of ears, skull, face, 'primitive races', etc)."
  4. "Mental illness is due to this degeneration process."
  5. "If mental illness is due to degeneration, then no role for treatment, but rather focus on observation and research ==> rise of Neurologists!"

Assumption 5 is the hinge: because degeneration implied illness was inherited and irreversible, treatment was considered pointless and the discipline's energy went into post-mortem research. "Most neurologists believe in degeneration, so treatment is not considered" [s9, s10].

Shell shock — why the sexual-repression model collapsed (s13)

The explanation could not survive contact with male soldiers: "the idea that these symptoms were connected to repressed sexual fantasies is quickly thrown out (hysteria is a feminine disease, present in weak women with repressed sexual fantasies)". Instead they were "somehow connected to the experience of war, possibly 'shocking' the nervous system". Menninger and colleagues used "talk therapy" and hypnosis. And the stated purpose matters: psychiatrists became crucial within military systems "in order to treat and return soldiers to the battlefield as soon as possible" — the module's clearest illustration of social assumptions, not data, shaping diagnosis.

The rise of diagnostics and DSM-III (s21–s24)

Social scientists raised four concerns: inter-rater reliability in diagnosis was very low, "as low as 30%" sometimes; Neo-Freudians thought diagnosis mattered less than the repressed ideas behind the symptoms; diagnosis was more based on behaviour considered deviant than on symptoms causing suffering and impaired function; and there was a fundamental difference between interventions for objectively confirmable derangements of biology and for theoretical constructs [s21]. Three currents converged [s22, s23]:

  • St. Louis. By 1972 a group had symptom-based checklists assessable statistically for stability and validity, until reliability was "high enough". (Neither the Feighner criteria nor Washington University is named.)
  • Pharma. Companies "needed a very accurate and effective way to identify homogenous enough groups of people" — named as a co-driver of operationalized diagnosis.
  • Homosexuality and the DSM. DSM-I was "a compendium of mental illnesses originally used as a hospital resource to identify patients for census purposes, not treatment". DSM-II "came out of WW2", was "very Neo-Freudian", distinguished "brain tissue diseases" from "psychogenic" diseases, and carried "diseases" representing behavioural deviances without clear dysfunction or distress. Dr. Evelyn Hooker, early 1950's, compared projective tests of 30 gay men and 30 age matched controls — no difference was found. At the 1972 American Psychiatric Association meeting, "a gay psychiatrist in a gas mask and wig with a voice distorting microphone spoke to the assembly" (Dr. H. Anonymous, John E. Fryer (standard knowledge, not in the module) — unnamed on the slide).
DSM-III — "completely revolutionized" (s24), the three rules verbatim
1. "For something to be considered a disorder, it MUST cause subjective distress and/or significant impairment in function." 2. "Diagnosis would be made not from expert opinion of the meaning of symptoms, but rather by a statistically validated checklist of signs and symptoms that can either be reported by the patient or observed by the examiner." 3. "A potential disorder would not be included unless it could be reliably and stably identified by such a process."

The module does not give the DSM-III publication year; the Week 40 WFQ key supplies 1980, calls DSM-III the paradigm shift, DSM-I and II narrative, and DSM-IV an update rather than a re-conceptualization [WFQ key].

Discriminators & exam traps

The ones that get missed
Mood vs affect — mood is what the patient says, affect is what you see, and affect takes three descriptors, not one.
Hallucination vs illusion — no stimulus vs misperceived real stimulus.
MoCA vs MMSE — the MMSE is "better known but maybe less reliable". Do not reverse it.
Insight vs judgment — insight is the three recognitions, judgment is acting on them, both are required for capacity.
Egypt, not Greece, for the wandering uterus.
ECT — developed for psychosis, most helpful for mood.
Myers described shell shock; Menninger treated it; Kraepelin gave the first description of chronic psychotic disorders; Hooker ran the 30-vs-30 study.
US vs Canada — a federal 1955 Joint Commission vs provincially organized bed closures.
The counts are examinable: four forces, five degeneration assumptions, five somatic therapies, four deinstitutionalization failures, four social-scientist concerns, three DSM-III rules.
Read the lecturer's "you don't need to memorize" lines carefully. Each is about rote recall of a slide as printed; none says the concept is off the exam. Treat them as "you will be given clues, not asked to regurgitate", not "skip it" [§7.0].
The module is one argument: psychiatry cycles through a unifying explanation, over-applies it and is corrected — humours, degeneration, neuroanatomy, psychoanalysis — until DSM-III replaced expert interpretation with a reliability-tested checklist that requires distress and/or impairment.

guides.title: Week 40 · 2 Dermatomes, Myotomes & the Neuro Primer: Lesion Localization
guides.html:
PW02 · NeuroPrimer · Neuro

Dermatomes, Myotomes & the Neuro Primer: Lesion Localization

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The course's own dermatome, myotome and reflex standard, and the primer that turns it into a localization method: root vs cord, UMN vs LMN, and why the imaging you order depends on getting it right.

Orientation

Week 40 is simultaneously the first Psychiatry week and the start of the Neuro block, so it carries PW02 — Summary of clinically-relevant dermatomes and myotomes for lesion localization (Ballyk & Chan, 2018), plus a file written for Week 39 but filed here: the Primer on Neuroanatomy, Neurological Examination and Lesion Localization in Back/Neck Pain (Chan, 2018). PW02 supplies the root tables; the primer supplies the reflexes, the exam and the reasoning that uses them.

This handout is the assessment standard. "The following are the dermatomes and myotomes that will be used throughout this course (including assessments)", based on a survey of clinical textbooks in electromyography and neuromuscular disease plus consensus among several neuromuscular neurologists [PW02 p1]. When a textbook disagrees with this handout, the handout wins — the primer says the same of the OSCE videos [NeuroPrimer p7].
Now examinable. The primer wrote for the MSK block — of the UMN/LMN table, "You do not need to memorize the details of this table now (you do need to know these by heart, however, during the Neuro block and for the Neuro MEs)" [NeuroPrimer p1, p9]. That block is this one.

Definitions and the method

  • Dermatome = "the area of skin supplied by the cutaneous sensory fibres contained within a single spinal nerve and therefore arising from a single spinal level" [PW02 p1].
  • Myotome = "the group of muscle cells controlled by the somatic motor fibres contained within a single spinal nerve… These muscle cells may be distributed into several different muscles, and can therefore control one or more movements" [PW02 p1].
  • Radiculopathy = a lesion affecting a nerve root. Myelopathy = a lesion affecting the spinal cord [NeuroPrimer p3]. Learn this pair verbatim.

Textbooks disagree because "the anatomy textbooks can differ from the clinical textbooks… with the former typically being more inclusive". The resolution: "most muscles are supplied predominantly by one (or at most, two) myotome(s), which allows for more precision in lesion localization" [PW02 p1].

The localization method is intersection
Weakness in the biceps (dominant C5 and C6 supply) and the pronator teres (dominant C6 and C7 supply) makes the most likely single root lesion a C6 lesion — (C5,C6) ∩ (C6,C7) = C6. The companion fact: triceps is a predominantly C7 muscle [PW02 p1]. Find the root common to every weak muscle.
One peripheral nerve, two dermatomes
Peripheral nerves arise from "the overlapping of fibres within a somatic plexus", so "the cutaneous distribution of a peripheral nerve will include portions of multiple dermatomes". The pad of the thumb is C6 and the pad of the middle finger C7, yet both reach the hand via the same peripheral nerve, the median nerve [PW02 p3]. That is the conceptual difference between a peripheral nerve lesion and a root lesion.

Myotomes (PW02 p2, p4)

Upper limb movementRoot(s)Lower limb movementRoot(s)
Abduction of shoulderC5Flexion of hipL2, L3
Flexion of elbowC5, C6Extension of hipS1
Extension of elbowC7Abduction and medial rotation of hipL5
Pronation of forearmC6, C7Adduction of hipL3, L4
Supination of forearmC6Extension of kneeL3, L4
Extension of wristC7Flexion of kneeL5, S1
Flexion of wristC7Dorsiflexion of ankleL5
Extension of digitsC7Plantarflexion of ankleS1
Flexion of digitsC8Inversion of ankleL5
Flexion of thumb at IP jointC8Eversion of ankleL5
Abduction and adduction of digitsC8, T1——

Figure detail an exam could use: wrist flexion and extension are drawn as a pair of opposed arcs (blue = extension, orange = flexion), each separately labelled C7 [PW02 p2].

Trap: inversion and eversion are both labelled L5 on this figure [PW02 p4]. Many clinical texts split them — eversion L5–S1, inversion L4–L5 — but PW02 is the course standard, so answer L5 for both and do not "correct" it on a UofT exam. The primer's exam table lists ankle inversion under L5 and does not list eversion at all [NeuroPrimer p6].

Dermatome test points

PW02's figures carry circled test-point markers — the points you actually touch. Upper limb: C5 lateral upper arm · C6 thumb · C7 middle finger · C8 little finger · T1 medial arm. Lower limb: L1 groin · L2 anterior mid-thigh · L3 medial knee · L4 medial malleolus · L5 dorsum of foot · S1 lateral foot · S2 posterior thigh · S3–S5/Co1 concentric perianal rings. On the upper-limb figure the medial forearm band is T1, not C8 — C8 is the medial border of the hand into the little finger. The posterior figure labels an axial line separating S2 from L5/L4: the boundary across which adjacent dermatomes are not adjacent segments. The concentric perineal rings make saddle (perineal) anaesthesia = S2–S4 a discrete, testable finding [PW02 p3, p5].

"C1" on the perianal figure is a misprint for Co1 (first coccygeal). The primer's Figure 1 runs the nerve roots C1 through Co1, confirming the reading [PW02 p5; NeuroPrimer p2].

Consolidated root → movement → reflex → dermatome

RootKey movement(s)ReflexDermatome
C5Shoulder abductionBiceps (C5, C6); brachioradialis (C5, C6)Lateral upper arm
C6Elbow flexion (C5, C6); supination; pronation (C6, C7)Biceps; brachioradialisThumb
C7Elbow extension, finger extension; wrist flexion and extensionTricepsMiddle finger
C8Finger flexion; thumb flexion at IP; finger abduction (C8, T1)—Little finger
T1Abduction/adduction of digits (C8, T1)—Medial arm
L1——Inguinal/groin
L2Hip flexion (L2, L3)—Anterior mid-thigh
L3Hip flexion; hip adduction; knee extension (L3, L4)Knee (L3, L4)Medial knee
L4Knee extension, hip adduction (L3, L4)Knee (L3, L4)Medial malleolus
L5Ankle dorsiflexion, big toe extension, ankle inversion, hip abduction; also eversion, knee flexion (L5, S1)—Dorsum of foot
S1Ankle plantarflexion, hip extension; knee flexion (L5, S1)AnkleLateral foot
S2–S4——Saddle/perineal

Reflexes come entirely from the primer — PW02 lists no reflexes of its own. "Big toe extension" appears only in the primer's L5 list; the documents are consistent, the primer is simply more granular [PW02 p2, p4, p5; NeuroPrimer p6].

The neuro primer — anatomy that drives localization

  • The cervical canal holds the cord and the exiting nerve roots, so a cervical disc can impinge a nerve root (most common), the spinal cord, or both, depending on direction (central vs lateral) and size [NeuroPrimer p1, p3].
  • The lumbar canal holds the lumbosacral nerve roots — the spinal cord ends at L1 — so a lumbar disc "almost never affects the small portion of the spinal cord at L1 and involves only the nerve roots" [NeuroPrimer p1, p2].
  • Commonest degenerative levels: cervical C5-C6 and C6-C7, then C4-C5; lumbar L4-L5 and L5-S1, then L3-L4 [NeuroPrimer p1].
  • The anatomical cauda equina is called lumbosacral nerve roots throughout, to keep it distinct from cauda equina syndrome, "a clinical syndrome due to compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots" [NeuroPrimer p1].
Cauda equina syndrome — a surgical emergency and a CORE Back Tool red flag
(a) Low back pain + (b) saddle (perineal) anaesthesia + (c) bladder and/or bowel dysfunction (urinary retention/overflow, unrecognized fecal incontinence) — with or without lower limb pain, sensory loss or weakness [NeuroPrimer p1]. Regardless of localization: "both are considered surgical emergencies when bladder and bowel functions are compromised" [NeuroPrimer p9].

Radiculopathy on history, "one or more of the following": radicular pain ("shooting" or "sharp, shock-like"), numbness/tingling (paresthesia), weakness, impaired bladder and/or bowel control. A root lesion gives sensory loss in a dermatomal distribution and weakness in a myotomal distribution [NeuroPrimer p3].

Acute mechanism: the nucleus pulposus "pops out". In the lumbar spine herniations impinge a single nerve root (lateral) or a whole bunch of nerve roots (central), "but almost never the spinal cord" — so central → multiple roots → cauda equina syndrome risk; lateral → a single root → a discrete radiculopathy. Chronic mechanism: degenerative change narrows canal and foramen over years — lumbar spinal stenosis, presenting as neurogenic claudication (CORE Back Tool pattern 4): "pain, numbness and/or weakness/fatigue in their legs brought on by prolonged walking, exacerbated by extension of the back and improves with forward flexion or sitting down". Three structures narrow the canal at once: thickened ligamentum flavum, hypertrophied facet joints, bulging intervertebral disc [NeuroPrimer p4, p5].

The neurological examination

ComponentWhat to do / look for
ToneRule out spasticity
BulkAtrophy in muscles of the same myotome — triceps for C7, gastrocnemius for S1
Power — upper limbsShoulder abduction (C5) · Elbow flexion (C5, C6) · Elbow extension, finger extension (C7) · Finger flexion and abduction (C8)
Power — lower limbsKnee extension, hip adduction (L3, L4) · Ankle dorsiflexion, big toe extension, ankle inversion, hip abduction (L5) · Ankle plantarflexion, hip extension (S1)
ReflexesBiceps (C5, C6) · Brachioradialis (C5, C6) · Triceps (C7) · Knee (L3, L4) · Ankle (S1) · rule out ankle clonus
Functional testsWalking on heels (dorsiflexion) · walking on toes and single-leg toe raises (plantarflexion) · tandem gait for balance
Plantar responseRule out an extensor response — big toe extends with or without fanning of the other toes, the Babinski sign
Sensory examReduced sensation (pinprick) in a dermatomal distribution · rule out saddle (perineal) anaesthesia (S2-S4) · rule out a sensory level, "a dermatomal level below which sensation is lost, which suggests a spinal cord lesion"
Provocative testsLumbar: straight leg raising (L4-S1), femoral stretch test (L2-L4) · Cervical: Spurling's test
In the source table the functional tests are printed inside the Reflexes row, not as a row of their own; split out above only for legibility [NeuroPrimer p6].

Worked example — S1 radiculopathy, "one of the most common radiculopathies that you will encounter clinically": tone normal; atrophy of the gastrocnemius; weakness in ankle plantarflexion and hip extension; reduced or absent ankle reflex; flexor plantar response; decreased sensation over the lateral aspect of the foot. That constellation is what the primer calls lower motor neuron signs [NeuroPrimer p5, p6].

UMN vs LMN — the table to know by heart

The motor pathway is "a two-neuron chain that spans both the CNS and PNS": the upper motor neuron, cell body in the primary motor cortex, descends to synapse on the lower motor neuron, whose cell body sits in the ventral horn and whose axon runs via a peripheral nerve to the muscle at the neuromuscular junction. The CNS/PNS boundary sits between the LMN cell body and its axon, i.e. at the root exit [NeuroPrimer p8].

Sub-componentUpper motor neuron lesionLower motor neuron lesion at a nerve root
Muscle toneIncreased (spasticity)Normal or reduced
Muscle bulkNormalReduced (atrophy)
PowerDiffuse weakness in an UMN pattern — extensors weaker than flexors in the upper limb; flexors weaker than extensors in the lower limbMyotomal
ReflexesIncreased; ankle clonus presentDecreased or absent; no clonus
Plantar responseExtensor (pathological)Flexor (normal)

Spasticity is "a velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone… a sudden resistance to quick passive movement of a limb". Ankle clonus is elicited with the hip and knee flexed at the same time, quickly dorsiflexing the ankle [NeuroPrimer p7, p9].

Leg weakness — lumbar spine or cervical spine?
Two things make the obvious answer unsafe: back and neck pain often co-exist, and both a cervical spinal cord lesion and a lumbar nerve root lesion can cause only lower limb symptoms. A cervical cord lesion hits the UMN component of the pathway to the leg; a lumbar root lesion hits the LMN component. So a cervical cord lesion can cause leg weakness — but, stating the obvious, "a lesion of the cervical nerve roots will not cause leg weakness!" This is why the CORE Neck Tool asks about changes in walking and gait [NeuroPrimer p7, p8].

Why localization changes management

Correct localization lets you image the correct region: "if we localize incorrectly… we may be falsely reassured that there is no significant radiologic lesion and miss the culprit". The worked error case — a cervical disc herniation compressing the cord causes progressive bilateral leg weakness and difficulty walking needing urgent surgery; the examiner misses the UMN signs, assumes a lumbar lesion, orders a lumbar MRI and misses the pathology, "a delay in diagnosis and treatment, which could in turn lead to permanent disability!" Why not image everything? Resource stewardship; time and tolerability (whole-spine imaging takes double to triple the time — a claustrophobic patient may tolerate a single region at about 15–20 minutes but not up to an hour); and specificity — two-thirds of asymptomatic subjects had radiological degenerative disc [NeuroPrimer p9]. The closing discipline is three questions for every back or neck pain patient: (1) signs of a specific nerve root, and if so which? (2) signs of the spinal cord rather than roots? (3) signs of a surgical emergency such as compressive myelopathy or cauda equina syndrome? [NeuroPrimer p10]

Discriminators & exam traps

The ones that get missed
C7 does a lot — elbow extension, wrist flexion and extension, digit extension, triceps reflex, middle finger. C8 is digit flexion and the little finger.
Elbow flexion is C5, C6 but supination is C6 alone; pronation C6, C7.
Dorsiflexion L5, plantarflexion S1; hip flexion L2, L3 but hip extension S1; hip abduction L5 but hip adduction L3, L4.
Knee reflex L3–L4, ankle reflex S1; no reflex is listed for C8, T1 or L5.
L4 medial malleolus, L5 dorsum of foot, S1 lateral foot — the commonest three to swap.
Straight leg raise L4–S1, femoral stretch L2–L4, Spurling's cervical.
Cord ends at L1 → lumbar disc disease hits roots, not cord; cervical disc disease can hit root, cord, or both.
A sensory level suggests a cord lesion; dermatomal loss suggests a root.
The p5 root constellation says tone "normal (i.e., not increased)" while the p9 table says "normal or reduced" — not a contradiction, the table is the more complete version.
Localize before you image: pick the single root that all the weak muscles share, then ask whether tone, reflexes and plantar response say root (LMN) or cord (UMN) — because a cervical cord lesion and a lumbar root lesion both present as leg weakness, and only one of them is on the MRI you were about to order.

guides.title: Week 40 · 3 Imaging of the Nervous System I: Basics of CT and MR
guides.html:
SLM02 · Neuroimaging

Imaging of the Nervous System I: Basics of CT and MR

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

How CT and MR generate image contrast, what every sequence shows, and when to order which.

Orientation

SLM02 (Alshafai and Rawal, Medical Imaging) teaches how CT and MR images are made, so a greyscale value can be read backwards to a tissue property. Its five objectives: the x-ray-based and non-x-ray-based modalities; the basic differences between CT and MR acquisition; the MR sequences, with the instruction to be able to identify them; the contrast agents, their indications and common adverse effects; and CT- and MR-based non-invasive vascular imaging [CT-MRI 1.2 / 3.1]. Objective 3 alone says "be able to identify them" — recognition from an image is expected. Dr. Byrne disclaimed this material ("brain and imaging, that's neuro, so I won't comment") [Byrne L1 tx 3:53].

1 · Attenuation: how x-rays make contrast

Modalities are classified by whether or not they use x-rays. X-ray based, with radiation: x-rays, cerebral angiography, myelography, CT. Not x-ray based: MRI, the only entry. Ultrasound and nuclear medicine appear nowhere in this classification [CT-MRI 2.1]. A heated cathode (−) produces electrons that accelerate to the anode (+) and strike the tungsten target, releasing x-rays — they arise at the target, not the cathode [2.2]. The image depends on attenuation: the degree of absorption of x-rays, which depends on the density of the material traversed, not on thickness or tissue type as such [2.3, 2.4]. The rule, verbatim: High density → High attenuation → film = white; Low density → Low attenuation → film = black. The six materials above the greyscale bar, by decreasing density: lead → bone → muscle → water → fat → air. Both quizzes and the whole Hounsfield section are built on that order [2.4].

2 · CT acquisition and Hounsfield units

CT uses a moving x-ray source, detectors and patient bed: rotating source + rotating detectors + moving table = composite 3-D image [CT-MRI 2.12]. That is the CT half of objective 2 — still x-ray attenuation, sampled from many angles. Hounsfield units (HU) convert x-ray attenuation values of tissues into visual gray scale, on a scale from −1000 to +1000 [CT-MRI 2.14].

MaterialHU range [2.14]On brain CT [2.15]
Bone+400 to +10001000
Soft tissue+40 to +80muscle 60
Grey / white matter—80 / 50
Water, CSF00
Fat−60 to −100−100
Lung−400 to −600—
Air−1000−1000

Slide 2.15 states HU values are illustrative and do not need to be memorized — but the ordering is fair game: grey matter (80) is denser, so brighter on CT, than white matter (50), the opposite of the T1 relationship [2.15, 2.27]. The HU axis beside the window slides ranks, densest first: iodinated contrast > clotted blood > liquid blood > grey matter > white matter > CSF > fat — hence clotted blood is denser than unclotted, which is why acute haemorrhage is hyperdense [2.17, 2.18].

That axis is schematic: labels are in correct density order but ticks are approximate — the fat leader lands at −250 while 2.15 gives fat = −100 HU. Use 2.15 for values, the axis for rank order.

3 · Windowing

Whiter pixels = higher HU. Display monitors cannot demonstrate the entire range of HU at one time, so changing the window/level settings allows the whole gray scale range to be displayed and interpreted [2.16]. Windowing changes nothing about the data — 2.17 and 2.18 are the identical slice.

Naming caution — the module reverses standard usage. Slides 2.16–2.18 define windowing as adjusting "the center point (window) and range (level)", calling the centre the window and the range the level. Standard practice, and slide 2.19's own labels, use W = window width = the range, L = level = the centre. Both spellings are printed; study both.
Conflict — the brain window is given twice with different numbers. Slide 2.17 prints "Window (center) = 40; Level (range) = 100"; slide 2.19 prints "W80 L40". The centre of 40 agrees; the range does not (100 vs 80) and the letters are inverted. W80 L40 is conventional and is what 2.19 prints — but be able to quote 2.17. Both confirmed on the rendered pages.
Window [2.19]SettingFor
BrainW80 L40routine parenchymal review
"Stroke"W30 L30subtle early ischemic hypodensity
"Bleed"W200 L100hyperdense acute blood

The bone window is printed as "Window (center) = 100; Level (range) = 2000" and allows the bones of the skull to be well-displayed, resolving trabecular detail, where the brain window allows the brain parenchyma to be well-displayed [2.17, 2.18]. Narrow window = high contrast, amplifying the few-HU loss of grey–white differentiation in early stroke; wide window = low contrast but a wide range shown, giving headroom for blood. The module prints only that different window/level settings help identify specific pathologies; "no single window shows all pathology optimally" is a restatement [std, from 2.19].

4 · Blood by age on CT

The module does not teach this. It teaches only that clotted blood is denser than liquid blood and that a bleed window (W200 L100) finds hyperdense acute blood. Minimal standard line: acute haemorrhage is hyperdense (roughly 50–70 HU), becomes isodense over days to a couple of weeks, and is hypodense when chronic (standard knowledge, not in the module) — do not attribute that to this module. It likewise never states MR signal of blood by age; its only claim is the blanket rule that most pathologies are bright on T2 and dark on T1 [CT-MRI 2.42].

5 · Contrast agents, the blood–brain barrier and safety

For all x-ray-based modalities, including CT, contrast is iodine-based: high density → high attenuation, easily seen, generally non-toxic [2.7].

Iodinated (CT)Gadolinium (MR)
Why visiblehigh density → high attenuationbright on T1
Allergyyes — mild rash to anaphylaxisyes, but rare
Renalcontrast-induced nephropathy; renal insufficiency is the most important risk factornephrogenic systemic fibrosis in renal failure
Otherfluid overloadnone listed
Vessels without it?no — CTA/CTV need IV contrastyes — time-of-flight (arteries), phase-contrast (veins)

CT head with contrast images cerebral arteries (CTA), cerebral veins (CTV), and regions of blood–brain barrier breakdown — tumour, infection, active inflammation. The mechanism line is the most examinable in the module: the integrity of the vessel wall is compromised, resulting in contrast leaking out of the intravascular space [2.20]. The same mechanism explains gadolinium enhancement, where MR adds the meninges and names meningitis [2.36]. CTA vs CTV is purely timing — same injection, same machine: early = arterial, late = venous [2.13]. The key MR-specific advantage: on MRI it is also possible to image the vessels WITHOUT contrast, with quality "similar to contrast-enhanced angiography or venography" [2.36].

The 2×2 MRA/MRV figure does not cleanly support "contrast is always better": the MRV pair does, but the non-contrast time-of-flight MRA is the crisper image. Answer from 2.36's "similar to" [2.36, 2.38].
MR metal safety is not in this module — no screening or contraindication list. The only contraindication-type material in the source is iodinated-contrast allergy, renal insufficiency/failure and pregnancy; radiation is a listed disadvantage of every x-ray-based modality [2.8]. Minimal standard line: ferromagnetic implants and retained metallic foreign bodies are screened for before MR because the static field can move or heat them (standard knowledge, not in the module).

6 · The other x-ray-based modalities

Plain films are the best way to screen bone anatomy quickly but give minimal information for the CNS [2.8]. Cerebral angiography images intracranial vessels dynamically and needs vascular access, usually femoral puncture, therefore invasive, plus fluoroscopy and injectable contrast [2.9]. Myelography images the spinal canal via lumbar puncture at the L3-L4 level or lower, to avoid the spinal cord, which ends at L1-L2; contrast opacifies CSF around the cord and cauda equina, so a mass or stenosis shows as an indentation or block in the white column [2.10, 2.11]. Invasive is the pivot word: CTA/CTV and MRA/MRV are the non-invasive counterparts and the initial tests of choice for cerebral vascular abnormalities [2.13, 2.41].

7 · How MR images are acquired

The patient is placed in a magnetic field; spinning hydrogen ions (protons) align with it; a radiofrequency (RF) pulse shifts their alignment away; the pulse is turned off and the protons relax back, releasing energy that is detected and converted into images [2.23]. Two relaxation types are measured, T1 and T2, and each type of tissue has its own characteristic rate of T1 and T2 relaxation — the answer to objective 2 [2.24]. Signal intensity of a voxel (a three-dimensional volume of brain tissue) depends on the number of protons in it, its T1 and its T2. Images come from pulse sequences: gradients and RF pulses turned on and off in a choreographed fashion, designed to interrogate specific tissue attributes [2.25].

Ordering rule, verbatim
An MRI of the brain automatically includes all of the sequences and you do not have to specify them, EXCEPT MR angiogram and venogram. You must still write down on the requisition the diagnoses you would like to confirm or rule out [CT-MRI 2.26].

8 · Every sequence and what it shows

T1 vs T2: CSF is dark on T1, white on T2; white matter is whiter than grey on T1 and darker on T2 [2.27, 2.42]. The one-second discriminator: look at the CSF. Dark CSF = T1. Bright CSF = T2. The module's blanket rule: most pathologies are bright on T2 and dark on T1 [2.42].

  • FLAIR is T2-weighted but suppresses CSF signal. It images edema and demyelination because it enhances detection of T2-bright lesions, especially those near CSF-filled spaces such as the ventricles [2.28]: CSF is bright on T2 too, so a periventricular lesion is camouflaged until FLAIR suppresses it — shown on MS plaques [2.29].
  • DWI/ADC: DWI measures random Brownian motion (diffusion) of water; the unit, in mm²/s, is the apparent diffusion coefficient. If ADC is low = restricted diffusion — bright on DWI and dark on ADC. Causes, in the module's order: acute ischemia/stroke, most commonly, via cellular swelling; densely cellular tumours (typically malignant); abscesses. Cellular swelling is accumulation of intracellular water (cytotoxic edema due to cell death) restricting free water movement between intra- and extra-cellular spaces. The two are always done together [2.30, 2.42].
  • GRE / SWI: identifies hemorrhage or calcifications, which show up as dark, being susceptible to field distortion by paramagnetic (blood products) or diamagnetic (calcium, bone) substances — it does not distinguish the two by signal [2.33]. Multiple small round black dots = microhaemorrhages of cerebral amyloid angiopathy, a cause of intracerebral haemorrhage in older patients [2.34].
  • MRA / MRV: the only two sequences that must be requested by name [2.26, 2.36].

Enhancement patterns: one thalamic tumour shows two at once post-gadolinium — a blush (diffuse, hazy) and a ring (bright rim, non-enhancing centre) [2.37].

9 · Signal cheat sheet

Module-sourced unless marked (standard knowledge, not in the module).

Tissue / findingCTT1 / T2FLAIR · DWI-ADC · GRE
CSF / water0 HU, darkdark / brightFLAIR dark (suppressed); ADC bright (standard knowledge, not in the module)
Grey matter80 HU, brighter than WMrel. dark / rel. whiteFLAIR keeps T2-type contrast
White matter50 HU, darker than GMrel. white / rel. dark—
Bone / air / fat+400 to +1000 / −1000 / −60 to −100air black, fat bright on T1 (standard knowledge, not in the module)GRE: bone diamagnetic
Iodinated contrast / gadoliniumdensest item on the axisgadolinium bright on T1—
Blood, clottedhyperdense, above liquid blood; bleed windowblanket rule only — the module never states blood signalGRE dark (paramagnetic)
Chronic microhaemorrhageoften invisible (standard knowledge, not in the module)—GRE: black dots — CAA
Oedemahypodense (standard knowledge, not in the module)dark / brightFLAIR bright
Demyelination—dark / bright but camouflaged near CSFFLAIR bright and conspicuous
Acute infarctsubtle hypodensity; stroke window—DWI bright / ADC dark
Malignant tumour / abscessenhance — BBB broken; ring enhancement post-contrastblush and/or ring post-gadcan restrict diffusion
Calcificationdense/bright (standard knowledge, not in the module)—GRE dark (diamagnetic)

10 · CT vs MR: when to order which

AxisCTMR
Radiation / basisyes; attenuation and density, in Hounsfield units; windowing; iodineno; proton relaxation (T1, T2) and proton number per voxel; pulse sequences; gadolinium
Availabilitymore widely available, much easier to obtain urgently (e.g. in the ED)slower; typically the outpatient study
Subtle abnormalitylower sensitivityhigher sensitivity
Common usesbone pathology (fractures, dislocations, metastases); acute haemorrhage; trauma; acute strokebrain pathology, using sequence-specific information
Urgent vessel questionpreferred — CTA or CTV (e.g. occlusion in acute stroke)not preferred when urgent
Contrast allergy / pregnancyavoidpreferred — and can be done with no contrast at all
Ordering mechanicsspecify contrast and phaseall sequences automatic except MRA and MRV

In most situations the information from CT and MR vascular imaging is comparable, so yield is usually not the deciding factor. The four deciders: urgency and availability → CT; already getting an MRI and needing higher sensitivity → MR; prior iodinated-contrast allergy → MR; pregnancy or radiation avoidance → MR [2.39].

11 · Every in-module question, worked

Quiz 1 (2.5), lateral skull x-ray, two arrows on the cranial vault — keyed: High. Both arrows sit on skull bone: high density → high attenuation → white. "Low" is wrong because low attenuation appears black and the arrowed regions are white.

Quiz 2 (2.6), lateral cervical spine, one arrow on the dark area anterior to the vertebral bodies — keyed: Low. The arrow is on the air-filled airway: low density → low attenuation → dark. Together the two test one idea — map the arrow's greyscale value onto the density scale.

Worked case (2.21): a 36-year-old man in the ER after a seizure; CT, two panels, each asked "Normal?" Non-contrast: no, there is subtle hyperdensity in the right occipital lobe — at your level you would not be expected to pick this up. Post-contrast: no, and the pathology is no longer subtle after intravenous contrast injection — there is a right occipital arteriovenous malformation; you are expected to recognize it is abnormal and that contrast unmasked it, but not to diagnose the specific pathology based on imaging alone.

Self-test (2.32) asks, behind a "Reveal the answers" button: which panel is the DWI and which the ADC, where the restricted diffusion is, and the differential.

There is no key for slide 2.32. The reveal layer was not exported, so the module's own answers are unavailable. Only an inference is possible: the panel with dark CSF and bright parenchyma is the DWI, the one with bright CSF is the ADC map, and the lesion is bright on DWI and dark on ADC (the two panels are not the same slice). The only defensible answer to the third question is the module's own differential from 2.30 — acute ischemia/stroke, densely cellular malignant tumour, abscess. Treat no specific diagnosis as keyed.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Renal disease matters for both agents, with different names: iodinated → contrast-induced nephropathy, renal insufficiency the most important risk factor; gadolinium → nephrogenic systemic fibrosis. Fluid overload is a distinct third iodinated effect.
  • Grey/white brightness flips between modalities — grey brighter on CT, white brighter on T1.
  • Dark CSF is not uniquely T1 — FLAIR has dark CSF but keeps T2-type parenchymal contrast.
  • GRE does not tell haemorrhage from calcification — both dark; only the adjective differs.
  • Enhancement is leakage, not uptake; and MR can image vessels with no contrast at all, CT cannot.
Density decides CT (high density → high attenuation → white, in Hounsfield units, shown through a chosen window); proton relaxation decides MR (dark CSF = T1, bright CSF = T2, FLAIR = T2 with CSF suppressed, DWI bright with ADC dark = restricted diffusion, GRE dark = blood or calcium, gadolinium bright on T1) — and enhancement on either modality means contrast has leaked through a broken blood–brain barrier.

guides.title: Week 40 · 4 Development of the Brain
guides.html:
SLM06 · Embryology

Development of the Brain

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Neurulation, neural tube defects, the five vesicles and their cavities, and how grey matter ends up on the outside.

Orientation

SLM06 (Dr. Michael Wiley, Division of Anatomy) is a 22-slide narrated module taking the neural tube from induction to the adult ventricular system.
