Its four end-of-week objectives: describe primary and secondary neurulation and their contribution to the adult brain; explain the embryology of open neural tube defects; describe the brain vesicles, their contributions to the adult CNS, and the contribution their cavities make to the ventricular system; and understand the histogenesis of the grey and white matter [DevBrain s3]. Hydrocephalus is deferred to week 41, epilepsy to week 43 [narr 13:36, 15:21]. Dr. Byrne named only "brain and imaging" as not hers, so extending that to this module is an inference, not a quote [Byrne L1 tx 3:53].

1 · Where the nervous system comes from

The origin flow chart makes one examinable claim: the CNS has a single embryological source, the neural tube; the PNS has two — neural tube and neural crest [DevBrain s6]. The brain is part of the CNS, which is why the module begins with the tube [narr 0:29].

2 · Two neurulations

Slide 7, verbatim: the neural tube forms from 2 separate tissue sources, by distinctly different morphogenetic mechanisms. In primary neurulation the primary neural tube forms from the ectoderm; in secondary neurulation the secondary neural tube develops from the mesoderm of the remains of the primitive streak [DevBrain s7].

Primary neurulationSecondary neurulation
SourceEctoderm, induced over the notochordMesoderm of the remains of the primitive streak
Mechanismfolding: plate → folds → groove → fusion → tube, then delaminationcondensation into a solid medullary cord, cavitation, mesenchymal-to-epithelial transformation (MET)
Productprimary neural tube (brain and most of the cord (standard knowledge, not in the module))secondary neural tube (the most caudal cord (standard knowledge, not in the module))
Timingclosure completed in the 4th week; rostral neuropore ~25 days, caudal ~28 daysafter the caudal neuropore has closed
Slide 7 prints "morphologenetic"; the narrator says morphogenetic. A slide typo, not a second term.

3 · Primary neurulation, step by step

Induction takes place in the ectoderm overlying the notochord, is organized by the notochord, and creates a neural plate of neuroectoderm — a pseudostratified columnar epithelium, also called the neuroepithelium [DevBrain s8]. A figure annotation never spoken aloud: surface/epidermal ectoderm expresses L-CAM and E-cadherin, induced neuroectoderm switches to N-CAM and N-cadherin.

The three named stages are elevation of the neural folds, apposition, contact and fusion, and delamination from the surface ectoderm [s9]. Narrated: the edges of the neural plate elevate into neural folds, which border a neural groove, move together into apposition and contact, then fuse across the midline forming the neural tube, which delaminates or separates from the surface [narr 1:35–2:24]. The dorsal view is captioned about 22 days, with somites flanking the groove, and shows neural crest arising at the crest of the folds and becoming the dorsal root ganglion.

Narrator-only, high yield
Delamination creates the coverings of the CNS: separation lets the surface ectoderm fuse across the midline, contributing the skin over the CNS, and opens a space for mesoderm to migrate between tube and ectoderm, contributing bone and the other connective tissues. Neither is on the slide [narr 2:18–2:40].

Timing. The slide: closure begins in what will be the cervical part of the spinal cord, proceeds rostrally and caudally together, and is completed in the 4th week, often before pregnancy is recognized; the last parts to close are the rostral and caudal neuropores [s9]. The narration is more precise: rostral neuropore ~25 days after fertilization, caudal ~28 days — complementary, both in week 4, and the only hard timing data in the module [narr 2:48–3:15].

4 · Secondary neurulation

Slide 10, verbatim: the mesoderm of the primitive streak condenses, forming the medullary cord; the cells undergo mesenchymal to epithelial transformation; these cells become radially arranged around a cavity which then becomes continuous with the cavity of the primary neural tube. The narration adds position and trigger: the primitive-streak remnant lies just caudal to the caudal neuropore, and once the caudal neuropore has closed it condenses into the rod-like medullary cord; a lumen develops; the surrounding cells lose their unpolarized stellate mesenchymal appearance for a polarized epithelial one, forming a pseudostratified columnar neuroepithelium; the secondary lumen then joins the primary to complete neural tube development [narr 3:23–4:13].

Conflict — the order of cavitation and MET. The slide's bullets run condensation → MET → cells radially arranged around a cavity, i.e. MET first [s10]. The narration runs condensation → a lumen develops → the cells around it then undergo MET, i.e. cavity first [narr 3:34–4:04], and the figure supports the narration (panel 1 a solid cord, panel 2 "lumen develops"). The end state is identical either way. Do not pick a side without naming which source you are quoting.

5 · Open neural tube defects

Slide 11, titled "Open Neural Tube Defects Cluster", carries four bullets and nothing else — learn the block verbatim [DevBrain s11]:

  1. 1:1000 pregnancies
  2. Risk factors: family history, diabetes mellitus, obesity, anticonvulsant use
  3. Most cases have unknown etiology
  4. Folic acid supplementation reduces risk

The embryology is spoken: when the neural folds fail to come together an open NTD results, and these defects tend to cluster around the rostral and caudal neuropores — the title word "Cluster", since the neuropores close last and are the most vulnerable [narr 4:18–4:36].

Neuropore that failsShould closeOpen NTDRegion
Rostral (= anterior (standard knowledge, not in the module))~25 daysAnencephalycranial — brain and vault; incompatible with life
Caudal (= posterior (standard knowledge, not in the module))~28 daysMyeloschisisspinal cord — an open mid-/lower-back lesion

The mechanism of tissue loss in anencephaly is the most testable narration-only statement here. It is not that the brain never forms: the neural plate of the rostral neuropore remains exposed to the amniotic fluid, the tissues begin to deteriorate, and the condition is incompatible with life [narr 4:36–4:46].

Folate, exactly as the source states it. The only preventive statement in the deck or narration is "Folic acid supplementation reduces risk" — no dose, no timing, no duration, no mechanism; standard periconceptional dosing has deliberately not been added [s11]. The deck separately notes closure is complete by ~28 days, "often before pregnancy is recognized", but does not itself join the two facts. Discussing Chiari II the narrator also calls meningocele an open NTD [narr 12:59]; it is conventionally a closed, skin-covered defect (standard knowledge, not in the module). Take the slide's own two examples as the open NTDs.

6 · Flexures

After closure the tube undergoes a series of bends and dilatations at the rostral end — bends are flexures, dilatations are vesicles [narr 5:03]. The cervical flexure forms where the future spinal cord joins the future brain; the cephalic (mesencephalic) flexure where the midbrain will develop — both ventral bends; the pontine flexure in the region of the developing pons, described as a very acute or sharp bend. The pontine flexure is the only flexure this deck gives a histogenetic consequence for, eversion of the alar plates [DevBrain s12, s17].

7 · Vesicles, derivatives and cavities

Slide 14's table, reproduced verbatim [DevBrain s14]:

Neural Tube VesicleDerivativeCavity
TelencephalonCerebral hemisphereLateral ventricles
DiencephalonDiencephalonThird ventricle
MesencephalonMidbrainCerebral aqueduct
MetencephalonPons and CerebellumFourth ventricle
MyelencephalonMedullaFourth ventricle
Rest of the neural tubeSpinal cordCentral canal

Three "only" facts hide there: the diencephalon is the only vesicle whose name does not change; the metencephalon is the only vesicle with two derivatives; the fourth ventricle is the only cavity from two vesicles. The last row is the link to the ventricles — the ventricular system is simply the lumen of the neural tube, regionally dilated. The optic vesicle is drawn budding from the diencephalon on s12 but is absent from the table and the narration.

This deck never names or shows the three primary vesicles. It goes straight to the five secondary ones. The standard mapping — prosencephalon → telencephalon + diencephalon; mesencephalon unchanged; rhombencephalon → metencephalon + myelencephalon — is (standard knowledge, not in the module) and is not examinable from this module's own material.
At narr 7:06 the narrator says "caudal to the mesencephalon lies the myelencephalon" — a misspeak; caudal to the metencephalon lies the myelencephalon. Both s12 and s14 give telencephalon → diencephalon → mesencephalon → metencephalon → myelencephalon → spinal cord. Trust the slide.

Expansion of the hemispheres (s13): photographs at 5, 6, 7, 8 months and term show the brain essentially smooth until about the 5th–6th month, gyrifying in the last trimester. The cause is spoken only: the telencephalic vesicles cover over most of the other vesicles, then, expanding further but constrained by the developing skull, their edges fold — the insula first, then the gyri and sulci [narr 7:22–7:58].

8 · Histogenesis: the three zones

Slide 15, verbatim: migration of newly born neuroblasts and glioblasts toward the outer wall creates the intermediate zone; extension of axons from the neuroblasts even further outward creates the marginal zone; the cells which remain adjacent to the neural tube lumen form the ventricular zone and develop into ependymal cells.

ZonePositionCells / fateAdult identity
Ventricularinnermost, against the lumenproliferating neuroectodermEpendyma
Intermediate (mantle)middleneuroblasts → neurons, glioblasts → glia; neuroblast cell bodies stop hereGrey matter
Marginaloutermostaxons extended outward; later glioblasts → oligodendroglia → myelinWhite matter

Mantle zone appears only in the figure, not in the bullets or narration. The narration alone explains why the marginal zone becomes white matter: some glioblasts move out there, differentiate into oligodendroglia and form myelin around those fibres, converting the marginal zone to white matter [narr 8:57–9:07].

9 · Alar and basal plates, and the pontine flexure

Slide 16, verbatim: accumulation of neuroblasts in the dorsal part of the intermediate zone creates the alar plates, whose neurons develop into interneurons that receive input from the fibres of primary sensory neurons in the periphery; accumulation ventrally creates the basal plates, giving rise to motor neurons which grow their axons out into the periphery.

Alar plateBasal plate
Position in the cordDorsal; midline partner the roof plateVentral; midline partner the floor plate
NeuronsInterneurons receiving primary sensory inputMotor — somatic motor and preganglionic autonomic [narr 10:08]
At the fourth ventricle after eversionLATERALMEDIAL
Boundary at both levelsSulcus limitansSulcus limitans

A trap worth naming: the primary sensory neuron cell body is not in the alar plate — it sits in the spinal ganglion and is neural-crest-derived; the alar plate holds the interneuron receiving its input [s16]. Slide 17, verbatim: at the level of the fourth ventricle (metencephalon and myelencephalon), the pontine flexure causes the alar plates to evert. So in the spinal cord the arrangement is sensory dorsal / motor ventral, but in the floor of the fourth ventricle it becomes sensory lateral / motor medial, the sulcus limitans still the boundary.

Narrator-only, high yield
Three named alar-plate-derived, laterally-displaced brainstem nuclei: the vestibular nucleus, the spinal nucleus of CN V, and the solitary nucleus — "all derived from the alar plates, but they were forced laterally by the pontine flexure" [narr 11:53–12:01]. None appear on the slide.

10 · The cerebellum

Slide 18's only text: the cerebellum develops at the dorsal edges of the metencephalon and grows to cover the fourth ventricle. The hemispheres begin dorsally, eventually merge with each other, and the cerebellum becomes so large it covers the fourth ventricle [narr 12:08–12:28]. The figure labels the rhombic lip, the dorsolateral tip of the everted alar column, as the cerebellar origin, and also derives the pontine nuclei and the olivary nucleus from the alar column, migrating ventrally — but those two are figure labels only, in neither the slide text nor the narration.

11 · Chiari II and hydrocephalus

Slide 19, verbatim: "Arnold-Chiari Malformation (Chiari II) often Accompanies NTDs in the Spinal Cord — downward displacement of parts of the cerebellum and medulla into the foramen magnum leading to compression of the foramen of Magendie and resulting in hydrocephalus". The narrated chain: an open spinal NTD → the cerebellum and medulla are displaced inferiorly into the foramen magnum → the cerebellum compresses the foramen of Magendie against the medulla → CSF produced in the ventricles cannot escape into the subarachnoid space → it builds up within the ventricles, producing hydrocephalus → relief is a shunt placed into the ventricles and tunneled under the skin into a body cavity, draining to the abdomen or in some cases the heart [narr 12:37–13:36]. Note the specificity: slide and narrator name only the foramen of Magendie (the median aperture of the fourth ventricle (standard knowledge, not in the module)), not the foramina of Luschka; and neither classifies the hydrocephalus as obstructive or non-communicating, which is (standard knowledge, not in the module).

12 · Radial glia and migration disorders

The problem posed: the neural tube plan puts grey matter inside and white outside, yet the cerebral and cerebellar cortices are grey and outermost. How does that grey matter get there? [narr 13:47] Slide 20's answer, verbatim: radial glial cells in the cerebrum and cerebellum conduct migrating neuroblasts to the cortex. They span the full width of the neural tube, from the ventricular surface all the way out to the marginal zone; neurons born in the ventricular zone migrate along them until they can go no further [narr 14:12–14:51]. The cortical-wall figure adds two layers to the three-zone scheme — from the ventricle outward, ventricular → subventricular → intermediate → cortical plate → marginal; the subventricular zone and the cortical plate appear only in this figure [s15, s20].

Slide 21: neuronal migration disorders often manifest in patients as epilepsy and developmental delay. Two MRI examples with their genes:

DisorderCaption, verbatimGene
Subcortical band heterotopia ("double cortex")bands of gray matter are interposed in the white matter between the cortex and the lateral ventriclesDCX
Periventricular nodular heterotopiagray matter fails to migrate and remains located along the lateral ventriclesFLNA

The position of the ectopic grey matter tells you how far the migration got: periventricular nodular heterotopia means migration failed at the ventricle (FLNA); subcortical band heterotopia means it arrested part-way (DCX). Both are recognized on the grey/white signal pattern, not the gyral pattern.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • CNS = neural tube only; PNS = neural tube + neural crest.
  • Ectoderm vs mesoderm is the cleanest primary/secondary discriminator, and secondary neurulation happens only after the caudal neuropore has closed.
  • Rostral 25 days → anencephaly; caudal 28 days → myeloschisis — both in week 4, at the last regions to close. Anencephaly is degeneration of tissue that did form and was exposed to amniotic fluid, not failure to form.
  • Grey matter is inside in the cord but outside in the cortex; radial glia are the reason.
  • Sensory dorsal / motor ventral becomes sensory lateral / motor medial at the fourth ventricle, sulcus limitans the boundary at both levels.
  • There are no quiz or self-test items anywhere in this deck, and no molecular content beyond the CAM annotation.
The neural tube is built twice — ectoderm by folding, primitive-streak mesoderm by condensation and cavitation — but ends as one lumen; its rostral dilatations become the five vesicles whose cavities are the ventricular system; and its wall is three zones, ventricular to ependyma, intermediate to grey, marginal to white. Everything clinical follows: neuropores close last so defects cluster there, the pontine flexure everts alar into lateral, and radial glia carry grey matter to the outside.

guides.title: Week 40 · 5 Personality Disorders: Definitions, General Criteria & the Ten PDs
guides.html:
SLM07 · PD Module 1

Personality Disorders: Definitions, General Criteria & the Ten PDs

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

What separates a personality trait from a personality disorder, the general criteria A–F that apply to all ten PDs, the three clusters, and the criteria and threshold for every PD except borderline.

PD Module 1 (SLM07, Sonley/Wiebe/Yang) defines personality trait and personality disorder, sets out the general diagnostic criteria that apply to every personality disorder, and walks the ten DSM personality disorders cluster by cluster — all of them except borderline, which the module explicitly defers to PD Modules 2–5 [PD1 §7.1]. Dr. Byrne named modules 07–11 as the required pre-reads for the Sept 18 personality-disorders workshop with Dr. Sonley: "please do look at those", and "if you haven't looked at these things, it's going to be a total waste of time" [Byrne L1 tx 4:24, 4:57].

1 · Trait vs disorder

TermDefinition (module, verbatim)
Personality traitAn enduring pattern of perceiving and relating to the environment that is exhibited across a wide range of contexts [PD1 §2]
Personality disorder (PD)Present when a person's personality traits cause them distress or impair their functioning [PD1 §2]
The trait itself is never the diagnosis. The step from trait to disorder is distress or functional impairment — nothing else [PD1 §2].

Having a PD does not mean someone has a "bad personality". A person with a PD can still be kind, entertaining, charismatic, passionate and engaging [PD1 §2].

2 · General diagnostic criteria A–F (apply to ALL personality disorders)

Criterion [PD1 §3]
AAn enduring pattern of inner experience and behaviour that deviates markedly from the expectations of the individual's culture, manifested in ≥2 of these 4 areas: 1. Cognition — ways of perceiving and interpreting self, other people and events; 2. Affectivity — range, intensity, lability and appropriateness of emotional response; 3. Interpersonal functioning; 4. Impulse control
BThe pattern is inflexible and pervasive across a broad range of personal and social situations
CIt leads to clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational or other important areas of functioning
DIt is stable and of long duration, with onset traceable to at least adolescence or early adulthood
ENot better explained as a manifestation or consequence of another mental disorder
FNot attributable to the physiological effects of a substance (drug of abuse, medication) or another medical condition (e.g., head trauma)
Memory hook — criterion A
The 4 domains are "CAIr": Cognition, Affect, Interpersonal, impulse Regulation. Need 2 of 4 [PD1 §3].
Exam traps on the general criteria [PD1 §3]
→ A pattern that began after a head injury, or only while using a substance, fails E/F — not a PD.
→ A pattern confined to one setting (only at work) fails "pervasive" (B).
→ Recent onset in mid-adulthood with no earlier history fails D.
→ (standard knowledge, not in the module) DSM-5-TR allows a PD diagnosis under age 18 if the traits are pervasive, persistent (≥1 year) and not limited to a developmental stage — except antisocial PD, which requires age ≥18.

3 · Etiology and management of PDs in general

  • Etiology (all PDs): an interaction between genetic predisposition and environmental influences [PD1 §4].
  • Medications: none are approved to directly treat PDs. They may be used for comorbidities or specific symptoms [PD1 §4].
  • Mainstay of management: psychotherapy, for most PDs [PD1 §4].
  • Management in depth is deferred to the clerkship PD course [PD1 §4]; BPD-specific management is in PD Module 4.

4 · Classification — the three clusters

ClusterOne wordFriends characterPDs
AEccentric (odd)PhoebeParanoid, Schizoid, Schizotypal
BIntense (dramatic)RachelAntisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, Narcissistic
CAnxiousMonicaAvoidant, Dependent, Obsessive-compulsive

Count check: A = 3, B = 4, C = 3 → 10 PDs [PD1 §5]. The module's "Funny Nicknames" slide pairs the three Friends character stills with the cluster labels; the examinable content is the character-to-cluster pairing and the one-word nicknames [PD1 §14].

The module explicitly discourages "mad, bad and sad" as a cluster mnemonic — it is somewhat derogatory and not particularly accurate. Use "eccentric, intense, anxious" instead [PD1 §5].

5 · Cluster A — Eccentric (Phoebe)

Key idea: Cluster A criteria resemble features of schizophrenia but are similar to, NOT the same as schizophrenia — no actual hallucinations or delusions. Schizotypal resembles the positive symptoms (odd beliefs, perceptual distortions, odd speech); schizoid the negative symptoms (detachment, flat affect, anhedonia, asociality); paranoid PD the paranoid delusions (suspicion, mistrust) [PD1 §6]. (standard knowledge, not in the module) DSM-5-TR adds for all three that the pattern does not occur exclusively during schizophrenia, a bipolar or depressive disorder with psychotic features, another psychotic disorder, or (schizoid/schizotypal) autism spectrum disorder (standard knowledge, not in the module).

Schizotypal PD — 5 of 9

Acute discomfort in close relationships, cognitive or perceptual distortions, and eccentricities of behaviour [PD1 §6.1].

  1. Ideas of reference (excluding delusions of reference)
  2. Odd beliefs or magical thinking inconsistent with subcultural norms (superstitiousness, clairvoyance, telepathy, "sixth sense")
  3. Unusual perceptual experiences, including bodily illusions
  4. Odd thinking and speech (vague, circumstantial, metaphorical, overelaborate, stereotyped)
  5. Suspiciousness or paranoid ideation
  6. Inappropriate or constricted affect
  7. Behaviour or appearance that is odd, eccentric or peculiar
  8. Lack of close friends or confidants other than first-degree relatives
  9. Excessive social anxiety that does not diminish with familiarity, tied to paranoid fears rather than negative self-judgement

Schizoid PD — 4 of 7

Detachment from social relationships and a restricted range of emotional expression [PD1 §6.2].

  1. Neither desires nor enjoys close relationships, including being part of a family
  2. Almost always chooses solitary activities
  3. Little, if any, interest in sexual experiences with another person
  4. Takes pleasure in few, if any, activities
  5. Lacks close friends or confidants other than first-degree relatives
  6. Appears indifferent to praise or criticism of others
  7. Emotional coldness, detachment or flattened affectivity

Paranoid PD — 4 of 7

Distrust and suspiciousness such that others' motives are interpreted as malevolent [PD1 §6.3].

  1. Suspects, without sufficient basis, that others are exploiting, harming or deceiving them
  2. Preoccupied with unjustified doubts about the loyalty or trustworthiness of friends
  3. Reluctant to confide in others, for unwarranted fear the information will be used maliciously
  4. Reads hidden demeaning or threatening meanings into benign remarks or events
  5. Persistently bears grudges
  6. Perceives attacks on character or reputation not apparent to others; quick to react angrily or counterattack
  7. Recurrent unjustified suspicions about a partner's fidelity

6 · Cluster B — Intense (Rachel)

Borderline PD is deferred. Module 1 gives only the core pattern — instability in interpersonal relationships, self-image and affects, and marked impulsivity — and sends the criteria to PD Modules 2–5 [PD1 §7.1]. Threshold 5 of 9 (standard knowledge, not in the module).

Narcissistic PD — 5 of 9

Grandiosity, need for admiration, and lack of empathy [PD1 §7.2].

  1. Grandiose sense of self-importance (expects recognition as superior without commensurate achievement)
  2. Preoccupied with fantasies of unlimited success, power, brilliance, beauty or ideal love
  3. Believes they are "special" and unique, understandable only by other special or high-status people
  4. Requires excessive admiration
  5. Sense of entitlement
  6. Interpersonally exploitative
  7. Lacks empathy — unwilling to recognize others' feelings and needs
  8. Often envious of others, or believes others are envious of them
  9. Arrogant, haughty behaviours or attitudes

Antisocial PD — 3 of 7, plus age and conduct-disorder requirements

Disregard for, and violation of, the rights of others [PD1 §7.3].

  1. Failure to conform to social norms re: lawful behaviour — repeated acts that are grounds for arrest
  2. Deceitfulness — repeated lying, aliases, conning for personal profit or pleasure
  3. Impulsivity or failure to plan ahead
  4. Irritability and aggressiveness — repeated physical fights or assaults
  5. Reckless disregard for safety of self or others
  6. Consistent irresponsibility — failure to sustain work or honour financial obligations
  7. Lack of remorse

Mandatory: at least 18 years old, and evidence of conduct disorder with onset before age 15 [PD1 §7.3].

Psychopathy is not a DSM diagnosis
It is identified with the Hare Psychopathy Checklist–Revised (PCL-R). Most people with psychopathy probably also have ASPD, but many people with ASPD do not have psychopathy [PD1 §7.3].

Histrionic PD — 5 of 8

Excessive emotionality and attention seeking [PD1 §7.4].

  1. Uncomfortable when not the centre of attention
  2. Inappropriate sexually seductive or provocative behaviour
  3. Rapidly shifting and shallow expression of emotions
  4. Consistently uses physical appearance to draw attention to self
  5. Speech excessively impressionistic and lacking in detail
  6. Self-dramatization, theatricality, exaggerated emotional expression
  7. Suggestible
  8. Considers relationships more intimate than they actually are

7 · Cluster C — Anxious (Monica)

Obsessive-compulsive PD (OCPD) — 4 of 8

Preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism and control [PD1 §8.1].

  1. Preoccupied with details, rules, lists, order or schedules to the extent that the major point of the activity is lost
  2. Perfectionism that interferes with task completion
  3. Excessively devoted to work to the exclusion of leisure and friendships (not explained by economic necessity)
  4. Overconscientious, inflexible about morality, ethics or values (not explained by culture or religion)
  5. Unable to discard worn-out or worthless objects
  6. Reluctant to delegate unless others submit to exactly their way
  7. Miserly spending style; money hoarded for future catastrophes
  8. Rigidity and stubbornness

(standard knowledge, not in the module) OCPD vs OCD: OCPD is a pervasive personality style, usually ego-syntonic ("the right way"), with no true obsessions or compulsions; OCD is discrete, usually ego-dystonic, with them (standard knowledge, not in the module).

Avoidant PD — 4 of 7

Social inhibition, feelings of inadequacy and hypersensitivity to negative evaluation [PD1 §8.2].

  1. Avoids occupational activities with significant interpersonal contact, fearing criticism or rejection
  2. Unwilling to get involved with people unless certain of being liked
  3. Restraint within intimate relationships, fearing shame or ridicule
  4. Preoccupied with being criticized or rejected in social situations
  5. Inhibited in new interpersonal situations because of feelings of inadequacy
  6. Views self as socially inept, personally unappealing or inferior
  7. Unusually reluctant to take personal risks or try new activities that may prove embarrassing

Dependent PD — 5 of 8

Excessive need to be reassured and taken care of [PD1 §8.3].

  1. Difficulty making everyday decisions without excessive advice and reassurance
  2. Needs others to assume responsibility for most major areas of life
  3. Difficulty expressing disagreement for fear of losing support — do not count realistic fears of retribution
  4. Difficulty initiating projects on their own, from lack of self-confidence, not lack of motivation or energy
  5. Goes to excessive lengths to obtain nurturance, even volunteering for unpleasant things
  6. Uncomfortable or helpless when alone, fearing being unable to care for self
  7. Urgently seeks another relationship when a close one ends
  8. Unrealistically preoccupied with fears of being left to take care of self

8 · Threshold cheat sheet — all ten

PDThresholdSpecial requirements
Paranoid4/7—
Schizoid4/7—
Schizotypal5/9—
Antisocial3/7Age ≥18 and conduct disorder before 15
Borderline5/9 (standard knowledge, not in the module)Covered in PD Modules 2–5
Histrionic5/8—
Narcissistic5/9—
Avoidant4/7—
Dependent5/8Don't count realistic fear of retribution (crit. 3)
OCPD4/8Work devotion not due to economic necessity; morality not due to culture or religion
Pattern to remember
The three 4/7s are Paranoid, Schizoid, Avoidant. The 5/9s are Schizotypal, Narcissistic and Borderline. The 5/8s are Histrionic, Dependent. OCPD 4/8. Antisocial 3/7 — the lowest [PD1 §10].

9 · "In a nutshell" clip cues

Each PD carries a short video clip with a "spot these criteria" list. The audio was not transcribed; the cue lists below are the module's own [PD1 §14].

  • Schizotypal — Luna Lovegood: unusual perceptual experiences (illusions), odd beliefs/magical thinking, odd thinking and speech, eccentric behaviour and appearance
  • Schizoid — Lurch: emotional coldness/flat affect, no desire for close relationships, no close friends, few pleasurable activities
  • Paranoid — Dale (King of the Hill): suspects others are exploiting or deceiving; reads hidden demeaning meaning into benign remarks
  • Narcissistic — Alex (In Treatment, about 2 min): grandiose self-importance, belief in being "special", arrogant/haughty behaviour
  • Antisocial — Patrick (American Psycho): acts that are grounds for arrest, conning for pleasure, lack of remorse
  • Histrionic — Scarlett O'Hara (to 1:25): discomfort when not the centre of attention, overestimating intimacy, shifting shallow emotions, self-dramatization
  • Avoidant — Lars (to 3:15): inhibition in new situations from inadequacy, restraint in intimate relationships from fear of shame, reluctance to take risks
  • OCPD — in-house role-play "Surgeon – Ankle": preoccupation with details and rules, perfectionism interfering with completion, rigidity
  • Dependent — in-house role-play "At Doctor's Office": difficulty with everyday decisions without reassurance, helplessness when alone, preoccupation with being left to care for self

10 · Discriminators and look-alikes

PresentationThink…Not…Why
Loner, flat affect, doesn't want friendsSchizoidAvoidantNo desire for relationships
Wants friends, avoids them for fear of rejectionAvoidantSchizoidDesire present; fear of criticism
Magical thinking, odd speech, ideas of reference, no fixed delusionsSchizotypalSchizophreniaNo true hallucinations or delusions
Suspicious, grudges, sees insults in benign remarks, no fixed delusionsParanoid PDDelusional disorderPervasive trait, not psychotic
Social anxiety persisting with familiarity, paranoid in flavourSchizotypalAvoidantParanoid fears vs negative self-judgement
Seeks admiration, entitled, no empathyNarcissisticHistrionicAdmiration and superiority vs any attention and emotionality
Rigid perfectionist who never finishes tasks, won't delegateOCPDOCDPersonality pattern, no true obsessions or compulsions
Can't decide anything without reassurance; can't be aloneDependentAvoidantFear of being uncared for vs fear of rejection
16-year-old with repeated theft, fights, lyingConduct disorderASPDASPD requires age ≥18
Two discriminators the module states outright
Why do they want attention? Histrionic → attention itself, emotions shallow. Narcissistic → admiration that confirms superiority, lacks empathy. Borderline → instability plus impulsivity, with fear of abandonment [PD1 §7.4].
Dependent criterion 4: poor initiation from low confidence → dependent; from low energy or motivation → think depression [PD1 §8.3].

11 · Activity keys (module's own answers)

The matching exercise key is simply the ten core patterns given above, one per PD [PD1 §9]. Practice vignette keys [PD1 §13]: solitary tester indifferent to praise or criticism → schizoid (avoidant patients want relationships; no odd beliefs, so not schizotypal). Energy fields, metaphor-laden speech, uneasy at book club after two years → schizotypal. 19-year-old with three arrests → the missing requirement is conduct disorder before age 15. Accountant who redoes spreadsheets, won't delegate, hoards broken electronics and sees nothing wrong → OCPD. Suspiciousness beginning 6 months after a traumatic brain injury → fails criterion F (and D). Cannot order without her partner, moved in with a new partner within a week → dependent PD, Cluster C. Management → psychotherapy is the mainstay, medications target comorbidities or specific symptoms; etiology is a gene–environment interaction, not primarily environmental. Flirtatious, shifting emotions, calls a new acquaintance her "best friend", no detail about a "terrible" week → histrionic.

Ten PDs, three clusters, one set of general criteria: an enduring, inflexible, pervasive pattern in ≥2 of 4 domains causing distress or impairment, present since adolescence or early adulthood, not explained by another disorder, a substance or a medical condition. Then count the disorder-specific criteria against its own threshold — antisocial 3/7 is the lowest, and the only one with an age floor.

guides.title: Week 40 · 6 Borderline Personality Disorder: Etiology and Criteria
guides.html:
SLM08–09 · PD Modules 2–3

Borderline Personality Disorder: Etiology and Criteria

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Why BPD earns four modules, the biosocial theory of an emotionally sensitive temperament meeting an invalidating environment, and the nine DSM criteria with the 5-of-9 threshold, worked through Victoria's case.

PD Modules 2 and 3 are the etiology and criteria halves of borderline personality disorder, the one PD that Module 1 deliberately left out. A single longitudinal case — Victoria — runs through Modules 2 to 5 [PD2][PD3]. Module 2's objective is to explain BPD etiology using the biosocial theory; Module 3's is simply to list the diagnostic criteria [PD2 §1][PD3 §1].

1 · Why BPD gets so many modules: common, serious, treatable

You will meet patients with BPD whatever area of medicine you go into [PD2 §2.1].

SettingPrevalence of BPD
General population2–6%
Primary care6%
Psychiatry outpatient clinics10%
Psychiatric inpatients20%

No sex difference in prevalence in community samples [PD2 §2.1]. Memory hook: 2–6 → 6 → 10 → 20.

  • Health-care use: people who self-harm use emergency services more than people with other chronic conditions — 232 ED visits per 100 person-years vs 117.6 for asthma. Compared with other PDs, BPD patients have higher health-care use: more visits, phone calls, prescriptions and referrals [PD2 §2.1].
  • Suicide: 8–10% lifetime rate of completed suicide, similar to other serious mental illnesses such as schizophrenia and depression [PD2 §2.2].
  • Self-harm: seen in about 3/4 of patients with BPD — cutting, burning, overdosing — causing significant disfigurement and morbidity [PD2 §2.2].
  • Quality of life: ratings similar to serious medical illness and schizophrenia [PD2 §2.2].
  • Treatable: 75% of people improve with Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (DBT) [PD2 §2.3].

2 · Victoria — the case that runs through Modules 2 to 5

You are a family doctor in downtown Toronto. Victoria, 18, the daughter of one of your patients, asks for an urgent appointment. She has been cutting herself and thinking more and more about ending her life: "Please help me doctor, why am I so weird? I feel like I'm going crazy!" [PD2 §3].

From her mother, over the years: as a baby she was colicky and often cried inconsolably, very different from her older sister Laura, "such an easy child". As a child and teen she was "so sensitive and moody", slammed doors and threw things. When Victoria was upset her mother tried to reassure her that things weren't so bad and told her she was overreacting. This didn't help [PD2 §3].

3 · The biosocial theory

BPD = a child with an emotionally sensitive temperament (BIO) interacting with an invalidating environment (SOCIAL) [PD2 §4].
BIOSOCIAL
Genetics: emotionally intense temperament, family historyInvalidating environment
Inherited trait of impulsivityTrauma
Bullying
Maternal separation

BIO — the emotionally sensitive temperament

Most natural traits follow a normal distribution. The module shows a height histogram (about 5'1" to 6'4", peaking around 5'7"–5'8") and then an emotional-reactivity histogram in adults with mean about 100, SD about 13, N = 10,000 — the same bell shape. The examinable readings are the normal shape, the mean and SD, and the point that extreme sensitivity is a tail position, not a categorical illness. Temperament is likely established in the first few years of life and probably relates to genetic predisposition; being emotionally intense is not a problem in itself [PD2 §5.1].

Feature of the temperamentMeaning
High sensitivity to emotional stimuliLower threshold; emotions easily triggered
Emotional intensityReactions are more intense
Slow return to emotional baselineReactions last longer

Memory hook: easily triggered → intense → long-lasting [PD2 §5.2]. Impulsivity is a separate biological feature, very common in BPD and one of the most heritable personality traits (heritability 20–62%); BPD patients often have a family history of substance use, especially alcohol, anger problems and other impulsive behaviour [PD2 §5.3].

Review Quiz 1 has no printed answer key in the module. The biological factors to select follow from the module's own lists: emotions easily triggered, intense, lasting longer than average; impulsivity; family history of impulsive aggression; family history of substance use problems. Distractors: A+ blood type, extroversion, family history of diabetes — the reasoning for why they are wrong is supplied by the study guide, not the module [PD2 §5.4, §13] (standard knowledge, not in the module).

SOCIAL — the invalidating or "poor fit" environment

Not everyone who is emotionally intense and impulsive develops BPD — these traits are risk factors, not causes on their own [PD2 §6]. Validation is showing you understand someone's experience; invalidation is not understanding it — dismissing, ignoring, not responding, being confused, criticizing [PD2 §6.3].

Children with especially sensitive temperaments experience emotions as overwhelmingly intense, confusing and painful. The optimal environment is attuned enough to help them cope while still giving them space to feel distress and learn to manage it themselves. Even very well-intentioned parents find this hard: it is easy to feel helpless, hopeless, invalidating and frustrated, and upset parents lose empathy and attunement and respond by giving up, turning away, or criticizing [PD2 §6.1–6.2].

Examples of invalidating environments [PD2 §6.4]: not understanding why the child is reacting as they are; getting angry with the child for being emotional; maternal separation for about 4 months before age 5; neglect and all forms of abuse. Trauma is a severe form of invalidation — childhood sexual abuse runs 10–20% in the general population vs 40–70% in inpatient BPD samples. Worked example: a child cries when her grandparents leave and is told "Stop that crying or I'll give you something to cry about"; she learns that her inner emotional experience must be wrong in some way [PD2 §6.5].

What repeated invalidation does, in the module's order [PD2 §6.6]: emotions intensify → sense of self becomes confused → emotions become hard to interpret (alexithymia) → emotions become so overwhelming the person looks for ways to escape. With the inherited trait of impulsivity, the escape is impulsive: alcohol and drugs, self-harm or suicide attempts, binge or emotional eating, overspending, gambling, shoplifting [PD2 §6.7].

Review Quiz 2 — the module's own key
Correct social risk factors: maternal separation at a young age · neglect · lack of caregiver attunement · reinforcement of emotional outbursts · dismissal of a child's emotions, needs or identity · trauma.
Incorrect: caregiver suggesting healthy coping strategies · invalidation followed by talking about it and repairing · being able to talk about emotions.
Trap: invalidation followed by repair is protective; reinforcement of emotional outbursts is a risk factor [PD2 §6.8].

The balance of bio and social

The bell curve is redrawn with two people marked on the right-hand tail. Person A, only "somewhat" sensitive (about 2 SD above the mean), may develop BPD only with severe invalidation such as trauma. Person B, at the extreme tail, may develop BPD with more subtle invalidation. Principle: the more biological vulnerability, the less environmental invalidation is needed, and vice versa — a diathesis–stress interaction (standard knowledge, not in the module). The figure's exam point is that BPD risk is a product of two dimensions, not a threshold on either alone; asked which patient needed more severe invalidation, the answer is Person A, the less sensitive one [PD2 §7].

Dandelion childrenOrchid children
Temperament"Easy""Spirited" / emotionally intense
EnvironmentDo fairly well in most environments; it takes a large insult to stop them growingFinicky, hard to grow; need the right amount of water and sun
OutcomeRobustThrive in the right environment, wither in the wrong one
BPD riskLowAt risk in invalidating environments
Victoria — the matching key
BIO: emotionally sensitive temperament · inconsolable crying · temper tantrums · colic. SOCIAL: mother offered reassurance · told her she was overreacting · felt confused and overwhelmed · felt helpless.
Trap: well-meant reassurance ("things aren't so bad") counts as invalidation, not support [PD2 §8.1].

4 · Victoria, first year at U of T — the criteria case

Break-up: her high-school boyfriend Mark went to McGill and broke up with her during Frosh Week. She phones and texts him constantly and asks whether he'd stay if she dropped out and moved to Montreal. She feels out of control: she has slept with 3 different guys in her frosh group (felt better in the moment, regretted it after, not interested in any of them) and has been getting drunk most nights and missing classes. Mood: usually "up and down"; thinking about the break-up makes her sad for hours or the whole day; she keeps getting really angry with her roommate and regrets it; she still enjoys new friends and competitive dance; she calls Mark both "the best thing to happen to me" and "the worst person alive". Suicidality: thoughts on and off since age 12, more frequent since the break-up; wants to "escape from it all" but doesn't "really want to die"; no plan, no past attempts. Self-harm: cutting her upper thighs since about age 13, now daily since the break-up; worried about scarring and wants to stop [PD3 §2].

Physical exam: BP 115/70, HR 71 regular, T 36.9 °C; thyroid, cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal exams normal; skin shows superficial cuts on the left upper thigh plus scarring, no signs of infection. MSE: co-operative and calm; speech normal; mood "up and down"; affect euthymic, congruent, full range, reactive; no hallucinations; urges to self-harm but wants help, passive SI without active ideation, intent or plan; thought process organized; insight articulate; judgment seeking help [PD3 §2]. (standard knowledge, not in the module) A euthymic, reactive, full-range affect at interview fits BPD's reactive mood instability rather than a sustained mood episode (standard knowledge, not in the module).

5 · The nine DSM criteria for BPD — need 5 of 9

Stem, verbatim: a pervasive pattern of instability of interpersonal relationships, self-image and affect, and marked impulsivity, beginning by early adulthood and present in a variety of contexts, shown by five (or more) of the following [PD3 §3].

Affect — 3 criteria

  1. Affective instability due to marked reactivity of mood — intense feelings lasting a few hours to a few days, up and down in response to external events
  2. Inappropriate intense anger or difficulty controlling anger — frequent displays of anger, recurrent physical fights
  3. Chronic feelings of emptiness — patients usually understand what this means and simply endorse or deny it; asked about it they often point to their chest or stomach, so it seems to be a physical sensation

Behaviour — 2 criteria

  • 4. Impulsivity in at least two potentially self-damaging areas — spending, sex, substance abuse, reckless driving, binge eating. Does NOT include suicidal or self-harming behaviour, which are counted in criterion 5
  • 5. Recurrent suicidal behaviour or self-harm — high associated morbidity and mortality

Cognition — 2 criteria

  • 6. Identity disturbance — markedly and persistently unstable self-image or sense of self; they seem like a completely different person with one group of friends versus another, values and interests changing with company
  • 7. Transient, stress-related paranoid ideas or severe dissociative symptoms — derealization (things seem unreal) and depersonalization (feeling like a spectator in your own life, watching from the ceiling). "Micropsychosis" can include auditory or visual hallucinations

Interpersonal relationships — 2 criteria

  • 8. Unstable and intense relationships alternating between the extremes of idealization and devaluation — people are either "good" or "bad" instead of "good and bad" (splitting)
  • 9. Frantic efforts to avoid real or perceived abandonment — threats, extreme accommodation. Self-harm does not count toward this criterion either

Domain count: Affect 3 + Behaviour 2 + Cognition 2 + Interpersonal 2 = 9. Threshold: 5 of 9, which gives 256 different ways to meet criteria for BPD — and a history of self-harm does not by itself mean BPD [PD3 §3, §5].

6 · Both mnemonics

"ARMS ASIDE""IMPULSIVE"
AngerImpulsive
Relationships (unstable)Moody
Mood (unstable)Paranoid under stress
Self (unstable)Unstable self-image
AbandonmentLabile, intense relationships
Suicide or self-harmSuicidal ideation and self-harm
ImpulsivityInappropriate anger
Dissociation (and transient paranoia)Vulnerable to abandonment
EmptinessEmptiness

7 · Asking the questions — the module's interview guide

The module says you aren't expected to know these yet. Screening strategy: start with affective instability, a fairly sensitive and specific screening question for BPD. If a patient has several behavioural indicators — anger outbursts, self-harm or suicidality, impulsivity such as substances or an eating disorder — ask enough questions to see whether they meet 5 criteria [PD3 §6].

CriterionSuggested question, and what to look for
Affective instability"Do you have intense moods that change rapidly, say from neutral to irritated to really anxious?" "How long do they last?" "Are they usually a reaction to something?" — reactive; get examples
Anger"Do you have anger outbursts where you yell and scream, throw things, or break things?"
Chronic emptiness"Do you often feel empty inside?" — a visceral sensation, different from being lonely, bored or dissociated, that leads to damaging behaviour
Self-damaging impulsivitySubstances · binge and purge · reckless driving · gambling · shoplifting · impulsive spending · impulsive sex regretted afterward — need ≥2 areas
Suicidal / self-harm behaviour"Have you ever harmed yourself deliberately, like cutting, scratching, headbanging, hitting yourself?"
Identity disturbance"Do you have a solid sense of who you are as a person?" — supported by frequent changes in friend groups, career or school focus, morals and values
Paranoia / dissociation"When you get really stressed out, do you have strange experiences, like going fuzzy or numb, losing time, feeling like you aren't real?" — stress-related, transient
Abandonment"Do you find yourself frantically trying to stop someone close to you from leaving?" — "leaving" can mean breaking up or just leaving the room
Unstable relationships"Do you have intense and stormy relationships where you run hot and cold?" — idealization and devaluation
Conflict — duration of affective instability. The module's criteria box says intense feelings last "a few hours to a few days" [PD3 §3]; the module's own interview guide says "minutes to hours" [PD3 §6]. Both are internal to Module 3 and both describe short, reactive mood shifts rather than mood episodes lasting weeks. For an exam, quote the criteria-box figure (a few hours to a few days) unless the stem is clearly asking about the interview teaching.

8 · The Victoria quiz — module answer key

Constant phoning and texting, and the offer to drop out and move to Montreal → abandonment. Three guys she isn't interested in, drunk most nights, missing classes → impulsivity. Mood up and down, sad for hours, angry at her roommate → anger + mood (unstable), two answers. Mark as best and worst → relationships (unstable). Suicidal thoughts since 12, and cutting since 13 → both suicide and self-harm. Does Victoria have BPD? Yes [PD3 §7].

The ARMS ASIDE tally: anger, relationships, mood, abandonment, suicide/self-harm and impulsivity are all confirmed; self, dissociation and emptiness were not assessed. Longstanding and impairing: yes. 6 confirmed criteria, so BPD [PD3 §7].

Source error in the module. PD Module 3's "incorrect" feedback on Q7 wrongly repeats "Suicide and Self Harm" — a copy-paste error. The intended answer to "Does Victoria have BPD?" is "Yes" [PD3 §7].
Quiz traps
Drinking and impulsive sex count as impulsivity; self-harm would not count there. Frantic contact to prevent the break-up is abandonment, not unstable relationships. Passive SI and cutting both fall under criterion 5, so together they count once [PD3 §7].

9 · Discriminators and exam traps

  • Criterion 4 needs ≥2 areas and excludes self-harm and suicidality; criterion 9 (abandonment) also excludes self-harm — the two classic miscounting traps [PD3 §8].
  • "Micropsychosis" — brief, stress-related hallucinations or paranoia — fits criterion 7 and does not automatically mean a primary psychotic disorder [PD3 §8].
  • Self-harm alone is not BPD. It also occurs in teen depression and neurodevelopmental disorders [PD3 §8][PD5 §4].
  • A two-week episode of low mood with anhedonia and early-morning waking is a depressive episode, not BPD's reactive affective instability [PD3 §10].
  • Onset by early adulthood and pervasive across contexts are in the stem, and the general PD criteria still apply on top [PD3 §8] (standard knowledge, not in the module).
  • Practice-vignette arithmetic: shoplifting + binge eating + cutting = 2 criteria, not 3 [PD3 §10]. Self-harm, suicidal threats, impulsive spending in a single area and anger outbursts = only 2 criteria confirmed — screen the rest [PD3 §10].
BPD is 5 of 9 criteria across 4 domains (affect 3, behaviour 2, cognition 2, interpersonal 2) in someone with a pervasive pattern beginning by early adulthood, and it arises from an emotionally sensitive temperament meeting an invalidating environment — the more biological vulnerability, the less invalidation it takes.

guides.title: Week 40 · 7 BPD Management, Self-harm and Risk Assessment
guides.html:
SLM10–11 · PD Modules 4–5

BPD Management, Self-harm and Risk Assessment

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Psychotherapy over medication, DBT in numbers, the six ways to validate and the in-office distress sequence, then deliberate self-harm: how it differs from suicide, how not to reinforce it, and how to assess and manage risk.

PD Modules 4 and 5 close the borderline sequence. Module 4's objectives are referring for psychotherapy (e.g., DBT), validation, and suggesting coping skills [PD4 §1]. Module 5 covers self-harm and risk assessment — distinguish self-harm from suicide, respond without reinforcing it, encourage reducing access to means, and offer referral [PD5 §1]. A fuller approach to suicide risk assessment sits elsewhere in the curriculum; this module is about self-harm, especially in the ED [PD5 scope]. Dr. Byrne deferred DBT and BPD to these modules and the Sept 18 workshop, and promised "a whole workshop on validation next week" [Byrne L3 tx 30:48, 19:21].

1 · "Doctor, how do you treat BPD?"

Victoria returns: "My emotions are all over the place, I'm always kind of depressed, and I just keep getting overwhelmed and can't handle things." You present the diagnosis of BPD, and she answers: "Wow, I can't believe this is actually a thing — I just thought I was a freak or something. What a relief!" Naming the diagnosis can bring relief, not stigma [PD4 §2].

Conflict — Victoria's age at onset of self-harm. Module 4 states self-harming since age 11 [PD4 §2]; Module 3 states cutting her upper thighs since about age 13 [PD3 §2], and Module 5's assessment table also records age started 13 [PD5 §7]. The discrepancy is in the source — 2 of 3 modules say 13. Use 13 unless the stem is drawn from Module 4.
OptionModule verdictKey points
NothingWrong"Fortunately there are helpful treatments for BPD"
MedicationMaybeNo specific medication treats BPD, though medications may help comorbid conditions. Antidepressants can help when there are significant depressive and anxiety symptoms. Antipsychotics and mood stabilizers are sometimes used, but their use is controversial and they are probably best prescribed by psychiatrists. Dangerous, or at least unhelpful, polypharmacy is all too common in BPD and should be avoided. Some patients get better with no medication at all
PsychotherapyCorrectPatients may respond both to therapies designed specifically for BPD and to general therapeutic approaches

This matches Module 1's statement for personality disorders generally: no medications are approved to directly treat PDs; psychotherapy is the mainstay [PD1 §4][PD4 §3].

2 · Dialectical Behaviour Therapy in numbers

DBT is a structured psychotherapy rooted in CBT, focused less on thoughts and more on understanding behaviour, experiencing emotions, and using skilful coping strategies. It runs 6–12 months at 1 h/week individual therapy plus 2 h/week skills group, and about 75% of patients have significant reductions in self-harm, ED visits and hospital admission days [PD4 §4].

The 4 required modes: individual therapy · skills group · between-session skills coaching by phone · weekly therapist team meetings. The 4 skill sets: mindfulness · distress tolerance · emotion regulation · interpersonal effectiveness [PD4 §4] — hook "MDEI", "My Distress Eases Instantly" (standard knowledge, not in the module).

The "D" is Dialectics: synthesizing apparent opposites — two opposites can both be true at the same time, which is the basis of the "both-and" statements below [PD4 §4]. (standard knowledge, not in the module) Other evidence-based BPD psychotherapies include MBT, transference-focused psychotherapy, schema therapy and Good Psychiatric Management (standard knowledge, not in the module). Scholar's Corner names Linehan, DBT Skills Training Manual, 2nd ed. (Guilford, 2015), useful for everyone, not just patients with BPD [PD4 §4].

3 · The waitlist — where management stops being referral

You explain that therapy exists — a specialized BPD/DBT clinic, general therapy, or psychiatry referral — but there will be a wait. Victoria becomes upset: "now you say there's nothing to be done for MONTHS!? What am I supposed to do?!" Signs of distress to notice: speaking louder and faster with higher pitch, bigger gestures, slapping the arms of the chair [PD4 §5].

Teaching you to treat BPD is beyond the medical-school curriculum, but management includes more than referral. These DBT-derived techniques are indispensable in the ED and anywhere you meet an emotionally overwhelmed person [PD4 §5].

4 · Technique 1 — validation, the six ways

#WayExample to Victoria
1Show interest — eye contact, don't look bored or distracted, don't look at your computer—
2Reflective statements — summarize what the patient said"You're really upset about the wait lists."
3Mindreading statements — an educated guess about what they think or feel, based on what they've said or how they look"You're feeling hugely let down and disappointed — and angry! — because of the waitlists."
4"Makes sense in a context" — use knowledge of the individual"Of course this is incredibly frustrating given how long you had to wait the last time I made a referral for you."
5Normalizing statements — most people would react the same way"Waiting is one of the biggest problems in our entire health care system — it IS incredibly frustrating!"
6Be genuine, authentic, cheerleading"I wish this was a problem I could fix! I think you can get through this, and I will do my very best to help you get through it."
What NOT to say [PD4 §6.1]
"You are overreacting, please calm down." · "A few months is nothing!" · "I know waiting is frustrating, but it's not that bad. You've done it before." · anything dismissive, patronizing or blandly reassuring.
"Wait lists are a normal part of our system, of course you have to wait" is NOT normalizing — it normalizes the system, not the patient's reaction.

Why it works, and when it doesn't [PD4 §6.1]: people often calm down as soon as you validate, as long as you are sincere, insistent and emphatic — half-hearted validation doesn't help. The mechanism is that we get more upset when we feel challenged, doubted or disagreed with, and relax when we feel understood. If validation calms them, you don't need to teach skills. Sometimes people get more upset with validation, because they focus more on painful feelings, or stay upset because they feel they're right to be — then ask whether they'd like to learn a coping skill.

5 · Technique 2 — both-and statements

A both-and statement links your validation to something you can offer or a problem you can help solve [PD4 §6.2]:

  • "I hear how hard it is to tolerate having to wait AND I believe you can get through it."
  • "Waiting is massively frustrating AND I'd like to help you tolerate the frustration."
  • "Your overwhelm makes perfect sense AND I'd love to help you get less overwhelmed right now."

Use "AND", not "BUT" — "but" cancels the validation that came before it (standard knowledge, not in the module); all of the module's examples use AND [PD4 §6.2].

6 · Technique 3 — suggest coping skills

  1. Validate and offer help: "You look really distressed and overwhelmed. I can't fix the wait list issue, AND, maybe I can help you manage how you're feeling right now — would you be willing to try them out with me?"
  2. Make specific suggestions — the module's four: hold something cold (an ice pack) against the temples · breathe together, focusing on a longer exhalation · get exercise (jumping jacks in your office) · squeeze something very hard
  3. Offer lots of praise for their willingness to try
  4. Don't be discouraged if the first one or two don't work; keep trying
  5. Expect to repeat all your validating statements several times

(standard knowledge, not in the module) These map to DBT's TIPP distress-tolerance skills: Temperature, Intense exercise, Paced breathing, Paired muscle relaxation (standard knowledge, not in the module).

Sequence to memorize
Validate → both-and → offer help → suggest a skill → suggest another [PD4 §7]. The module's drag-and-drop key: "This is devastating. I see you are feeling really overwhelmed." → "I can't fix the system AND I would like to help you if I can." → "Would you like to try some coping strategies?" → "How about holding an ice pack?" → "OK if that isn't helpful, let's try slow breathing."

How the encounter can branch [PD4 §7]: if validation lands, she unclenches her jaw and breathes easier but cries more loudly — validate the sadness too, then offer skills. If she declines skills, respectfully back off, keep validating, give her space. If she tries the cold temperature skill, coach her ("just feel the cold on your skin, bring your focus to it") and review that she can use it at home. If a skill doesn't help, move to the next one and keep going until you run out of ideas. If she is still distraught and you are out of time: do a brief risk assessment to decide whether she needs the ED, then gently end the meeting, encourage home practice, and give handouts or websites (dbtselfhelp.com, ilovedbt.com).

7 · Monitoring your own reactions, and stigma

  • Don't do things for patients that they can do themselves in an attempt to be helpful — keep a coaching and cheerleading mindset. Polite gestures are fine (a cup of water for an anxious patient); think twice about making phone calls on their behalf that they could make themselves [PD4 §8].
  • It's common to feel confused or surprised. In an unfamiliar situation — being followed on social media, being asked a lot of personal questions — take time to think and consult a colleague [PD4 §8].
  • Frustration is common, because change is hard and patients may be hostile, demanding or stubbornly withdrawn; this has produced considerable stigma against BPD among health professionals, particularly mental health professionals [PD4 §8].
The anti-stigma dialectic
The lives of suicidal people are unbearable as they are currently being lived; people are doing the best they can, they want to improve, AND they need to try harder [PD4 §8].

8 · Deliberate self-harm

You're on call. Victoria comes in with her boyfriend, who convinced her to come because he was extremely worried. After a fight earlier that day, he found she had made five superficial cuts to her wrist with an X-ACTO knife. He is afraid she was trying to kill herself. The question of the hour: should you certify her and keep her in hospital because she is at imminent risk of killing herself? Answering it requires distinguishing self-harm from suicidal intent [PD5 §2].

Deliberate self-harm (DSH) is deliberately causing tissue damage in the absence of suicidal intent. Common methods: superficial cutting, burning, hitting self, head banging, overdosing on prescribed or OTC medications. It serves two functions — avoid intense affect or anxiety, by providing an intense stimulus that is distracting or promotes endorphin release, and communicate distress, because people who self-harm often find it hard to express pain in words or ask for help and often feel dismissed when they try. Treatment takes a lot of work in psychotherapy; the goal is to tolerate feelings without escaping, avoiding or distracting [PD5 §3].

Self-harm is not BPD, and self-harm is not suicide — but don't dismiss it

  • Self-harm is one of the BPD criteria but is not pathognomonic; it also occurs in teens with depression and neurodevelopmental disorders. Even when it isn't BPD it signals difficulty regulating emotions, so consider referral to therapy [PD5 §4].
  • If a patient says they cut to avoid emotions or relieve stress and weren't trying to kill themselves, they are most likely telling the truth. Deliberate self-harm often occurs without imminent suicide risk [PD5 §5.1].
  • But self-harm and suicidal ideation or attempts often co-occur in the same person, and people who self-harm have a higher suicide risk: the 1-year suicide rate after self-harm is 439.1 per 100,000 person-years, 37.2 times the general-population rate of 11.8 per 100,000 [PD5 §5.2].
  • Accidental death is possible — taking too many pills or not realizing how dangerous they are, cutting deeper than intended and hitting an artery [PD5 §5.2].
Self-harm is never "unimportant": it is a sign of emotional dysregulation that needs treatment, and it signals the patient could be at risk of suicide even if not directly from the self-harm [PD5 §5.2].

9 · Avoiding reinforcement

Reinforcement = a consequence that makes a behaviour happen more frequently [PD5 §6]. For most patients self-harm is reinforced by internal relief from painful emotions; for some it is also reinforced by soothing and caring from other people. Calling that "attention-seeking" is unfair and judgmental — the intent is rarely to get attention — but if attention, positive or negative, follows self-harm it may make it happen more often [PD5 §6].

In the acute setting (e.g., suturing the cuts), too infantilizing sounds like "You poor thing, you must REALLY be in pain to do this to yourself"; too hostile sounds like "And what were you hoping this would accomplish?" or "I don't know why I'm bothering, since you'll just do this again next week". The right approach is kind, respectful, neutral and matter-of-fact, with no less civility than for any other patient — and note that anger and contempt can also reinforce self-harm, because they're still attention [PD5 §6.1].

Longer term: the sooner you give warm, caring contact after self-harm, the more likely you are to reinforce it. What helps is genuine happiness, warmth and caring when they have NOT recently self-harmed, and genuine disappointment or less warmth — not punitive anger — when they have. More frequent appointments during a crisis can reinforce crisis behaviour; consider not increasing frequency, or increasing it only if they can stay away from self-harm and suicide threats [PD5 §6.2].

10 · Assessment and management

The module's 5-point assessment [PD5 §7]: 1. take the history of self-harm — age started, methods, frequency, precipitants; 2. ask explicitly about intent at the time of the self-harm; 3. ask about suicidal ideation, but don't presume they are suicidal; 4. screen for other BPD criteria; 5. remember not everyone who self-harms has BPD, especially adolescents — but self-harm is a dangerous way of avoiding emotion, so get a diagnostic assessment and some form of treatment regardless.

The module's 4-step management [PD5 §8]: 1. ABCs first, and give medical treatment; 2. suicide risk assessment; 3. encourage follow-up with mental health resources; 4. refer to psychiatry whenever unsure or you want a second opinion.

Assessing Victoria [PD5 §7]: age started 13; methods cutting, scratching; frequency 2–3 times per month; precipitants usually fights with her boyfriend, sometimes other interactions leaving her feeling rejected or alone; intent relief from awful feelings (despair, fear, shame, worthlessness); suicidal sometimes, but not this time — while cutting, she didn't want to die. The doctor establishes that her suicidal thoughts come without intent, and she is future-oriented, so the plan is discharge with an offer of mental health support.

Frequency differs across modules. Module 3 records Victoria's cutting as daily since the break-up [PD3 §2]; Module 5's ED assessment records 2–3 times per month [PD5 §7]. These are different points in the longitudinal case — Module 3 is the acute post-break-up period in first year, Module 5 the later ED presentation — so most likely a timeline difference rather than a contradiction, but the numbers should not be quoted interchangeably.
Admission caution
Many patients with chronic, fluctuating suicidal ideation do not benefit from psychiatric admission. Hospitalization can become an escape behaviour that interferes with coping in regular life, and a potent reinforcer of suicidal thinking, communication and behaviour. This call is usually made by psychiatrists [PD5 §8].

Managing means — "one of the best ways to reduce risk"

Rationale: if a person has to wait, think or problem-solve, the harmful urge may pass before they act [PD5 §8.1].

MeansWhat to do
HeightsHigh-rise? Balcony? Someone can lock or block it
Medications in the homeReduce supply as much as possible — "people don't really need 100 tabs of acetaminophen at home"
SharpsSome knives are needed for cooking, "but do you really need 10?"
Weapons / firearmsIdeally remove from the premises; if not, locked, key inaccessible, ammunition locked separately
Prescribing practicesSmall amounts, 1–2 weeks; ask about stockpiling; ask whether they're actually taking it
Dangerous medicationsAsk specifically about insulin, opiates, bulk acetaminophen, and other people's medications dangerous in overdose (e.g., cardiac medications)

11 · Victoria's disposition — the module's key

Is her risk high or low? Low. She has suicidal thoughts but says she won't act on them, has no current suicidal intent, and is planning to attend a friend's party — future-oriented [PD5 §9].

What do you do next? A, D, G, H [PD5 §9]:

OptionModule rationale
A. Discharge home — yesNot at imminent risk of suicide; doesn't need to stay in hospital
B. Certify — noUnnecessary; she isn't intending to act on suicidal thoughts
C. Admit — noUnnecessary intervention for self-harm
D. Refer to therapy — yesTherapy is the best intervention for learning healthy coping
E. Contemptuously tell her to manage her feelings — noHostility is unprofessional and can reinforce self-damaging behaviour
F. Warmly invite her back whenever she's upset — noLeads to multiple unnecessary visits; encourage coping skills instead, the hospital remaining available for emergencies
G. Crisis lines and distress-tolerance skills — yesCrisis lines are a source of validation; skills help her cope independently
H. Psychoeducation for partner/family — yesHelps the partner feel less panicked and suggest therapy rather than insisting she come to hospital
Trap: "warmly invite her back whenever you're upset" sounds kind, but it reinforces crisis-driven ED use. The correct version is "for emergencies" [PD5 §9].

12 · Cross-module cheat sheet

ItemKey fact
First-line BPD treatmentPsychotherapy, BPD-specific or general
MedicationsNone specific for BPD; treat comorbidities; avoid polypharmacy; antipsychotics and mood stabilizers controversial and best left to psychiatrists
DBT rootsCBT, focused on behaviour, emotion and skills rather than thoughts
DBT duration / intensity6–12 months; 1 h individual + 2 h group per week
DBT 4 modesIndividual · skills group · phone coaching · weekly team meeting
DBT 4 skillsMindfulness · distress tolerance · emotion regulation · interpersonal effectiveness
DBT outcomeAbout 75% with significant reductions in self-harm, ED visits and admission days
"D" in DBTDialectics — two opposites can both be true
6 ways to validateInterest · reflection · mindreading · makes sense in context · normalizing · genuine/cheerleading
Crisis skillsCold to temples · paced breathing with a long exhale · exercise · squeeze hard
Distress sequenceValidate → both-and → offer help → suggest skill → suggest another
DSH definitionDeliberate tissue damage without suicidal intent
Two functionsAvoid intense affect (distraction or endorphins) · communicate distress
Self-harm vs BPDA BPD criterion but not pathognomonic — also teen depression, neurodevelopmental disorders
Suicide risk after self-harm439.1 vs 11.8 per 100,000 person-years (37.2 times) at 1 year
ReinforcementInternal relief plus soothing or attention, positive or negative
Acute stanceNeutral, matter-of-fact, civil; not infantilizing, not hostile
Long-term stanceWarmth when not self-harming; don't escalate appointment frequency in a crisis
AssessmentAge of onset, methods, frequency, precipitants, intent, SI (don't presume), BPD screen
ManagementABCs and medical care → suicide risk assessment → MH follow-up → psychiatry if unsure
AdmissionOften unhelpful for chronic fluctuating SI (escape plus reinforcement); the psychiatrist's call
Means restrictionBalcony · meds in 1–2 week supplies, stockpiling, insulin/opiates/acetaminophen/others' meds · sharps · firearms
Victoria's dispositionLow risk → discharge + therapy referral + crisis lines and skills + family psychoeducation

13 · Discriminators and exam traps

  • Family therapy is not one of DBT's four modes — the fourth is between-session phone coaching [PD4 §11].
  • Telling the validations apart: "So you've been waiting three months" is reflection; "Anyone would be frustrated by that" is normalizing; "Given how hard you worked to get here, of course this stings" is makes sense in context; only "You look like you're feeling humiliated and furious right now" is mindreading [PD4 §11].
  • An SSRI plus an antipsychotic plus a mood stabilizer at the first visit is polypharmacy — the priority is a psychotherapy referral [PD4 §11].
  • Overly soothing responses while suturing are as much a problem as hostile ones — both can reinforce [PD5 §12].
Refer for psychotherapy, don't reach for medication; validate sincerely before you offer a skill, and use AND rather than but; and treat self-harm as real without treating it as an emergency — neutral tone, explicit intent question, means restriction, therapy referral, with admission reserved for the psychiatrist's judgement.

guides.title: Week 40 · 8 The Psychiatric Interview, Mental Status Examination and Case Report (ICE CS2)
guides.html:
Clinical skills · ICE CS2

The Psychiatric Interview, Mental Status Examination and Case Report (ICE CS2)

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The ICE CS2 student guide end to end: the interview road map, the 33 process steps, every history domain, the 13 MSE categories with their descriptors, the session format and the MedSIS case-report rubric.

ICE Clinical Skills 2 is a four-session sequence running Weeks 40–43, and everything in it is built on two instruments: the psychiatric history and the mental state examination. The student guide (Grek) calls these "the essential means to psychiatric diagnosis", and the MedSIS case-report form is how your write-up is marked. This guide follows the CS2 guide's own order — introduction, road map, range of problems, principles of diagnosis, the "how" and the "what" of the interview, the MSE, session format, evaluation, the Appendix 1 feedback checklists, the case report, and the Appendix 3 history template.

The history is what the patient reports; the mental state is what you observe, in the same domains, at the time of the interview. Session 1's stated learning outcome is to describe exactly that difference.

1 · What the psychiatric interview is, and the course's stance on it

Psychiatry, as this guide defines it, is concerned with disorders of behaviour, thought, emotion and motivation, and like medical and surgical sicknesses these may have physical, social or psychological causes or complications [CS2 guide p2]. Four domains — a highly testable list. All physicians will meet these problems in their patients and perhaps in their own lives, and all physicians require the skills to help patients with psychiatric illnesses.

The framing sentence worth holding verbatim: "In all branches of medicine, the history and examination are crucial to the understanding that underlies the doctor's ability to reach a diagnosis, offer a prognosis, and treat his/her/their patient" [CS2 guide p2]. Three outputs. Psychiatrists "tend to emphasize the nuances of history-taking and observation" because they use few gadgets — but they do not have a monopoly on looking, listening and talking, or on raising sensitive topics, "and nor should they".

Interviewing is a technique to be acquired. It requires no special intuition or talent: the only requirements are interest, attention, a willingness to practise, and the gradual accretion of experience — no more or less true than for any medical skill "from measuring the blood pressure to separating conjoined twins" [CS2 guide p2–3]. Techniques break into behavioural steps that can be precisely described, observed in oneself and others, and modified until perfected — which is why the course runs on standardized self-evaluation guides that peers and preceptors use to score the same interview.

Two rules the source states outright
Never interview from a checklist — you will sound more interested in your agenda than in the patient, and no checklist is long enough for every unimagined eventuality. Use the checklist towards the end or after the interview, to make sense of what you saw and heard and of what you do and don't have for the write-up. And: there is a conventional, predictable order for presenting a case, which you must learn — but take care not to confuse the order of the presentation with the sequence of information-gathering [CS2 guide p3].

2 · The road map: history domain → MSE section

The single most compressed table in the guide. Each broad symptomatological area you ask about in the history is paired with the major section of the mental state you observe [CS2 guide p4, after IGDA/WPA 2003].

Broad symptomatological areas (history)Major sections of mental state (examination)
Behaviour and adaptive functioningOvert behaviour
Physical manifestations of mental disorderAppearance
EmotionsMood and affect
Consciousness, orientation, memory and intellectSensorium or alertness, memory
Speech, thinking, perception and self-experience and/or self-understandingSpeech and thought processes, thought content, perception

3 · The range of psychiatric problems — symptoms and predicaments

The guide offers a "brief and practical — rather than exhaustive or mutually exclusive" list, adapted from HoNOS, of what usually counts as a psychiatric problem complained of or discovered during a psychiatric history. 23 items as printed [CS2 guide p4–5]:

  1. Overactive, aggressive, violent, disruptive or agitated behaviour
  2. Non-accidental self-injury, suicidal thoughts, suicidal acts
  3. Substance misuse
  4. Physical illness or disability problems — either the cause or the result of psychiatric symptoms or psychosocial predicaments
  5. Cognitive problems, including confusion and memory loss
  6. Changes in speech and behaviour associated with delusions and hallucinations
  7. Problems with depressed mood
  8. Problems with elated or expansive mood
  9. Mental strain, tension, worry
  10. Anxiety
  11. Fears, phobias
  12. Obsessions, compulsions
  13. Somatoform problems — physical symptoms without physical cause
  14. Dissociative problems, sometimes including unexplained physical symptoms; depersonalization, derealization
  15. Fatigue
  16. Sleep problems, insomnia
  17. Eating problems
  18. Sexual problems
  19. Problems with activities of daily living, poor self-care and hygiene
  20. Problems with relationships, social isolation or withdrawal, conflict
  21. Problems with living conditions
  22. Problems at work, inability to work, underemployment, unemployment
  23. Problems in the pursuit of leisure activities, including insufficient opportunities

The last three — living conditions, work, leisure — are predicaments, not symptoms. The heading "Symptoms and Predicaments" is doing real work.

4 · Principles of psychiatric diagnosis

"Your goal is to make a diagnosis, in order to arrive at a plan of management" [CS2 guide p5]. A working diagnosis needs three things (after Taylor 1979):

What you doThe word for it
Classification of the symptoms and signs the patient bringsIllness
Discernment of the context in which they are to be understoodPredicament
Discovery, if possible, of the pathophysiological processes underlying themDisease
