And the plan itself has three requirements: it must focus on biopsychosocial aspects including medication, therapy and lifestyle change; it must be feasible; and it must mitigate any safety concerns [CS2 guide p5].

The hierarchical diagnostic scheme

Imagine a hierarchy of the major psychiatric disorders. The hierarchy carries no moral implication — no disorder, and no person suffering one, is worthier than another. Its value is diagnostic: disorders higher on the ladder often feature the symptoms and signs of disorders lower down; those lower down rarely feature the clinical signs of the categories above them [CS2 guide p6].

RungCategoryHallmarkPrognosis / treatment
1 (uppermost)Physical conditions — physical disease or drug-inducedConfusion; may also show all the features of everything belowIdentifiable physical and chemical pathology → most reliably recognized, most open to specific and sometimes life-saving treatment
2The psychoses — schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorderImpaired reality-testing: delusions and hallucinations; unlikely to show confusionReliable diagnosis and prognostication across cultures; disabling and sometimes dangerous; good evidence for effective drug treatment
3 (lowest)Depression and anxiety, in their manifold varieties, often togetherAffective symptoms without confusion or impaired reality-testingVery common; much distress and social/occupational disability; often in stressful situations; medication plus psychological, environmental and behavioural approaches; prognosis generally less sinister

Exam use: delusions plus confusion should push you up the ladder toward a physical or drug-induced cause, not down to a primary psychosis — confusion is rung 1's hallmark and the psychoses are "unlikely to feature" it. The operational version of this appears later in the template: always ask about concurrent substance use, and about symptom intensity when abstinent.

Course, and the five appraisal questions

"The course of the sickness is of vital importance", and its discovery relies entirely on the history. "Cross-sectionally, signs and symptoms may not have the same significance as they do longitudinally" [CS2 guide p6]. Accurate appraisal then depends on five questions [CS2 guide p6–7]:

  1. How dangerous is the condition? Is the patient, or anyone else, at risk of life or limb, or the necessities of life?
  2. How great is the functional impairment? Has the person's capacity changed — basic and instrumental activities of daily life, work, self-sustenance, care of dependents, participation in family and community?
  3. What is the immediate psychosocial context — the circumstances, including loss or change — of the presentation and of prospective treatment?
  4. What physical factors are at play? Concurrent physical illness or disability; concurrent medications, drugs and alcohol.
  5. Who is the person with the sickness? Characteristic psychological make-up — intelligence, capacity for enduring reciprocal relationships, capacity for work and independence.

5 · The "how" — process of the interview (33 steps)

Attend to technique the way you attend to suturing or auscultation: as you incorporate it, "your diagnostic accuracy will increase, because you will be paying attention" [CS2 guide p7].

Stop, look and listen — the five-item core loop
1 Slow down, stop, think · 2 Look, see, notice, observe · 3 Listen, hear · 4 Prompt the patient for more · 5 Probe for clarification of what you do not understand. Re-iterate it, each pass bringing you closer to the goal: a diagnosis, so that you can make a safe, practical plan [CS2 guide p7].

Don't rush to talk, ask or explain. It is more efficient to let the patient disclose and explain than to keep poking with one question after another, which suggests that asking is what you want to do rather than listening. "A clinical interview should not feel like an interrogation" — a patient who feels misunderstood, judged or patronized may clam up, leaving you to pick through every conceivable possibility. On empathy: paying attention is the first step; showing that you are paying attention is the second. Both are observable behaviours, unlike imagination [CS2 guide p7–8].

A · How to start (1–7)

  1. Greet the patient and let them know more about the interview set-up.
  2. Tell the patient your name and that you are a medical student.
  3. Ask the patient's name.
  4. Ask the patient's understanding of the reason for the interview.
  5. If they do not know, briefly explain the purpose: to practise your interviewing technique, in front of your classmates.
  6. If appropriate, tell the patient how much time is available for the interview.
  7. Start with open questions, so the patient tells the story of the current problems in his own words.

B · Eliciting the spontaneous account (8–16)

  1. Listen attentively.
  2. Allow the patient to complete statements without interruption.
  3. Leave space for the patient to think before answering, without filling the silence too quickly.
  4. Once the chief complaint is complete, use an open question to find out whether there is anything more or anything else.
  5. Prompt the patient to speak more — repeat or paraphrase what you have heard.
  6. Notice and respond to things the patient says which hint at unexplored problems.
  7. Notice and respond to non-verbal clues (body language, tone of voice, facial expression, affect) that reinforce, supplement or contradict what is said — acknowledge them and explore their meaning with the patient.
  8. Encourage the patient to tell you his feelings about what he is describing.
  9. Encourage the patient to tell you his thoughts about it.

C · Getting more of the information you need (17–26)

  1. Continue with open questions if they are productive.
  2. Move from open to closed questions if open ones aren't yielding coherent, succinct, relevant, consistent information: resolve ambiguities, clear up points you don't understand.
  3. Encourage the patient to give precise information, particularly where it can be dated or quantified.
  4. Ask the patient to explain technical or obscure words they use.
  5. Use concise, easily understood questions. Single, brief questions rather than long complex ones.
  6. Ask one question at a time; don't stack questions.
  7. Avoid leading questions, which contain the answer you expect or desire.
  8. Avoid jargon: avoid technical or ambiguous words.
  9. Show calm interest in emotionally loaded material, even if you or the patient are disturbed or embarrassed. Named difficult topics: suicide, domestic abuse, money, sex, death and dying.
  10. Raise emotionally loaded topics yourself, even if the patient doesn't, when there are verbal or non-verbal clues to their relevance.
The language rule, stated explicitly in the source
Choose vocabulary wisely and replace words carrying a negative connotation: "commit suicide" → "complete suicide / die by suicide"; "drug abuse" → "drug use" [CS2 guide p9].

D · Managing your time (27–30)

  1. Keep track of the time.
  2. Avoid repetition: don't ask for information already elicited — it can be perceived as rude or inefficient.
  3. Keep yourself flexibly on task. Structure the interview logically, but the logic of your questions and changes of direction should be clear to the patient as well as to you.
  4. Allow the patient time to respond fully, but if the information is unnecessary or repetitious, redirect them tactfully.

E · Closing (31–33)

  1. Don't wait until the end of the interview to raise potentially important or sensitive topics.
  2. Summarize the main points briefly.
  3. Thank the patient for their time.
The "commonly omitted" list is counter-intuitive. The guide states that "in bold face are things that are surprisingly often omitted", and the bold falls on a fragment of most steps. Bold appears in steps 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 17, 18, 19, 21, 22, 23, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32 and 33. Steps 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 15, 16, 20 and 24 carry no bold at all — so "greet the patient", "tell the patient you are a medical student", "ask the patient's name", "listen attentively" and "avoid jargon" are not on the surprisingly-often-omitted list, despite being the intuitive candidates [CS2 guide p8–10].

6 · The "what" — content of the history

The five-item minimum of what you require from the patient (and other informants, if necessary) [CS2 guide p10]: (1) the reason the patient is here — current problems and the expectations of the patient and others; (2) the development and course of the problems, including prior psychiatric illness and treatment; (3) severity — effect on day-to-day function at work and home, and impact on the safety of the patient and of others; (4) factors that may plausibly have caused the illness; (5) factors that may plausibly affect management and prognosis.

These expand into 19 numbered content items:

DomainItems
Reason the patient is here (1–3)Elicit the current problem(s) · elicit hopes for or expectations of treatment · elicit the patient's opinion about the nature and cause of the problem(s)
Course of the illness (4–8)Define the onset of this episode · elicit main precipitants · elicit key chronology, fluctuations, progression and events · cover treatment of the current episode · find out whether psychiatric problems have occurred in the past
Severity (9–10)Impact on patient and family in four functional domains; degree of risk under six headings (below)
Current personal and social circumstances (11–12)Nine sub-items: partner · other family · other people · housing · occupation · finances · legal involvement · leisure · recent changes or losses. Then: what support is currently available
Active physical factors (13–15)Active medical problems · medications (which, why, what dose) · alcohol or drug use and how much
Systematic enquiry (16–19)Screening questions, if necessary, for: cognitive function · hallucinations or delusions · mood · anxiety

The four functional domains: personal care and survival · family functioning (spouse, children, parents, other relatives) · occupational functioning (paid or volunteer worker, student, homemaker) · broad social functioning (roles, activities and interactions in the community at large).

The six risk headings in the guide's content list: suicide · other kinds of deliberate self-harm · violence towards others · inability to look after oneself · self-neglect · neglect of dependents [CS2 guide p11].

The staging rule for the personal and developmental history
A detailed life history — developmental milestones across the lifespan, markers of the capacity for love, work and self-sufficiency, adverse experience and achievement — is "a usual and important part of a psychiatric assessment". But at this stage of your training, first make sure you can get the basic problem, its immediate biopsychosocial context, and its impact. Even advanced practitioners sometimes wait for a subsequent interview for the earlier life [CS2 guide p12].

7 · The mental status examination

"The mental status exam is the 'physical exam' in psychiatry. It is a summary of your observations, which paired with history, will lead to a diagnosis" [CS2 guide p12]. The guide's one worked contrast, and a likely stem: a patient with pressured speech, distractibility and affect lability is more indicative of mania than one presenting as dysphoric, with delayed thought processing and poverty of speech.

#CategoryExample descriptors given in the guide
1Appearanceuntidy, unsteady, gaunt
2Attitudeuncooperative, suspicious, hostile
3Behaviourrestless, hyperactive, slowed down, socially withdrawn
4Sensorium or alertnessdrowsy, distractible
5Speechexcessive, monotonous, sparse, loud, fast, slow
6Form of thoughtrambling, disorganized, incoherent
7Cognitiondisorientated, forgetful
8Moodanxious, depressed, elated
9Affecttense, depressed, elated, blunted
10Thought contentunusual, somatic concern, grandiose, guilty, helpless, hopeless, suicidal
11Perceptionhallucinatory statements, hallucinatory behaviour
12Insightunaware of being ill
13Judgementimpulsive, vulgar, lewd
The count of MSE headings differs between sources — learn the domains, not a count. The guide's own section 8 prints 13 rows with Behaviour separate; the Session 3/4 timetable line prints 11, folding Behaviour in; Appendix 2 prints 12; and the live MedSIS form splits "Speech/thought form" into two, giving Speech and Thought form/process as separate items [CS2 guide p12–13, p18–19, p24] [Case report form p1–2].
Flagged inference — the unlabelled MedSIS row. On the live form an unlabelled radio row sits between Appearance and Behavior: 13 radio rows against 12 printed labels, the extra one occupying an empty line slot with no text at all. Because the guide's Appendix 2 puts Attitude in exactly that position, the missing label is identified as Attitude — a high-confidence inference from position and count, not a direct reading. Include attitude in your write-up regardless [Case report form p1] vs [CS2 guide p24].

The expanded descriptors (Appendix 3) — what to use for the write-up

DomainDescriptors to report
Appearance / BehaviourAge (chronological vs apparent), gender, heritage; posture, grooming/hygiene, dress, body habitus, distinguishing features; eye contact, facial expression; attitude (polite, collaborative, uncooperative, guarded/suspicious, evasive, agitated, aggressive/hostile); reliability and ease of building rapport; gait, psychomotor slowing/agitation, mannerisms, tics, tremors, tardive dyskinesia, dystonia, catatonia
CognitionLevel of consciousness, orientation (name, place, time); attention, memory, intellect; MMSE or MoCA if applicable
SpeechRate (normal, pressured, slowed), rhythm, volume, tone; quantity, spontaneity, latency; fluency, articulation
MoodSubjective emotional state as reported by the patient; scale 0–10 (0 = worst, 10 = well)
AffectObjective emotional state as observed; quality (euthymic, depressed, elevated, anxious, irritable) and intensity; range (full, restricted, flat, blunted); stability (fixed to labile); congruence with mood and thought content
Perceptual disturbancesHallucinations as reported — visual, auditory, olfactory, tactile; observed "responding to internal stimuli" in the absence of a sensory stimulus
Thought processOrganized/coherent, logical/goal-directed, circumstantial, tangential, loosening of associations, word salad; flight of ideas, thought blocking, repetition
Thought contentThemes, preoccupations, over-valued ideas, delusions, obsessions, suicidal/homicidal ideation (intent, plan)
Insight / JudgmentGraded none/impaired · partial · intact/full. Insight = realizing you have a mental health concern and appreciating its implications. Judgment = recent behaviours as they relate to safety, social functioning, treatment decisions
Mood is subjective (what the patient reports, 0–10 with 0 = worst); affect is objective (what you observe: quality, intensity, range, stability, congruence). Insight is recognizing the illness and its implications; judgment is recent behaviour around safety, social functioning and treatment decisions.

Example screening questions

Depression. "Have you ever had 2 weeks or more when you felt sad or low — for most of the day, nearly every day?" and the same stem for lost interest. Anchor an episode (worst, most recent, best recalled, first, longest) — "during that period, did you have…" — then screen suicidal ideation, guilt/worthlessness, energy, concentration, appetite, psychomotor, sleep.

Mania. "Have you had an unusually high mood for many days in a row? How many days?" and "Did you have increased energy during this time? Were you more active?" Then grandiosity, sleep, talkativeness, pleasurable activities, goal-directed activity, flight of ideas/irritability/impulsivity, distractibility.

Anxiety syndromeScreening question
GeneralizedDo you regularly worry about multiple things? Do you find it difficult to control these worries?
Panic disorderDo you develop intense physical symptoms of anxiety all of a sudden?
AgoraphobiaDo you avoid situations like being in public?
Social anxietyDo social situations provoke intense anxiety? Do you worry about performance or being judged?
Specific phobiaAre there any specific things (heights, closed spaces, animals) that you fear or avoid?

Delusions all run off one stem — "Has it ever seemed that…": people are after you or doing bad things to you (persecutory) · some outside force is controlling your actions or thoughts (control) · others know what you think, or you can read others' minds (mind reading) · you have special traits or abilities (grandiosity) · things happen because of you, or people are talking about you (reference) · something outside yourself controls your thoughts against your will (thought insertion) · your thoughts are taken out of your head (thought withdrawal) · something has changed in your body (somatic). Teaching point: in depression with psychosis, delusions tend to be mood congruent — nihilistic, somatic, guilty [CS2 guide p29].

Hallucinations: auditory ("do you ever hear things that others don't hear, like a voice speaking to you?"), then quality (conscience? inside or outside the head?), number and recognizability, commentary, command ("are they telling you to hurt yourself or others?"), and visual. Other screens: obsessive-compulsive (intrusive thoughts that keep coming back; behaviours you repeat and struggle to resist) and post-traumatic (something horrific seen or experienced causing intense fear; recurrent dreams, nightmares or flashbacks).

The suicide ladder — the most OSCE-relevant list in the guide
1 "Has life seemed so stressful that you think about death or suicide?" → 2 "Are you thinking about ways that you would end your life?" → 3 "Have you prepared or acquired the means?" → 4 "How would you describe your level of intent?" → 5 "Have you attempted suicide in the past? When?" → 6 acute vs chronic → 7 active (plans) vs passive (thoughts of death) → 8 "What are some reasons for staying alive (protective factors)?" The order is ideation → method → means → intent → past attempts, then the two classifications, then protective factors [CS2 guide p29].

8 · Session format, absence policy and evaluation

Each of the four four-hour sessions runs: group discussion led by the preceptor → interviews of standardized patient → group feedback. In Session 1 the tutor's demonstration is on a real patient while the student interviews a standardized patient (SP) — note the asymmetry. Sessions 2–4 all run two interviews with feedback after each, and the SP may be invited to give feedback.

SessionWeekLearning outcomes
140Develop a structure to a psychiatric assessment · describe the difference between the history and mental state examination · describe the basic approach to psychiatric diagnosis
241Describe what is meant by the "process" of a psychiatric interview · complete, observe and reflect on interviews · systematically and constructively discuss technique and findings
342Describe the content of an initial psychiatric interview · complete, observe and reflect · discuss technique and findings
443Describe the constituents and organization of the mental state examination · complete, observe and reflect · discuss technique and findings
Sessions 2 and 3 have swapped emphases relative to their outcomes: Session 2's outcome is about process while its group discussion covers content; Session 3's outcome is about content while its discussion covers the mental state — and Sessions 3 and 4 carry an identical group-discussion line [CS2 guide p17–19].

Absence policy. Clinical Skills sessions are mandatory; missing any session, even with approval, requires a written make-up assessment. If you cannot attend: submit an absence request to the University, and notify the tutor and site coordinator as soon as possible, ideally before the session — failure to do so may result in a poor professionalism assessment. For planned absences, forward the approval to the tutor and site coordinator. Repeated absences, regardless of reason, may prompt a check-in with the CS Director [CS2 guide p14].

Evaluation. Each student submits a case write-up based on their own interview, to the preceptor, no later than two weeks after the final psychiatric session (stated dates: Tuesday Oct 27 for Tuesday groups, Thursday Oct 29 for Thursday groups). The write-up consists of (1) the history, (2) the mental state examination, (3) a diagnostic impression, (4) a plan of management. The preceptor evaluates it on MedSIS and a "satisfactory" score is required to pass the course. And: interview skills are examined in the OSCE at the end of ICE Clinical Skills 2 — not only in the psychiatry stations, but in the global assessment of interview skills in every station [CS2 guide p20].

9 · Appendix 1 — the interview-evaluation guides

"The group discussion of each interview should be based on these items." The interviewer uses them for self-evaluation; the group uses the same items to guide observation and evaluation. Both checklists are scored Yes / No [CS2 guide p21].

Process (23 items) — greets and obtains the name · gives own name and medical-student status · asks the patient's understanding of the reason, explains if not known · states time available · uses open questions · listens attentively, allows completion, leaves space · facilitates verbally and non-verbally (encouragement, silence, repetition, paraphrasing, interpretation) · encourages expression of feelings and thoughts · picks up verbal clues · picks up non-verbal clues (body language, speech, facial expression, affect) and checks them out · moves open → closed appropriately · concise single brief questions · handles emotionally loaded material · encourages precision (datable, quantifiable) · avoids jargon · asks for the definition of the patient's jargon · keeps the interview on task in a logical sequence · attends to timing · avoids repetition · closes by summarizing briefly · then the three global items.

The three global items — the only ones with their own definitions
Self-assurance: the interviewer appears confident, open and relaxed; does not show confusion, hesitancy, shyness or embarrassment. Empathy: shows, by asking appropriate questions and making appropriate responses, that he/she/they understands the nature of the patient's illness, its effect on his life, and the way the patient themself perceives their problems. Warmth: by smiling, sitting attentively, facilitating responses and other verbal and non-verbal behaviour, shows regard and concern for the patient. Memorize these — they are the qualitative items an examiner is most likely to quote [CS2 guide p21].

Content (19 items) — "Did the interviewer…" current problem(s) · onset of this episode · main precipitants · key chronology, fluctuations, progression, events · treatment of current episode · support currently available · impact on the four functional domains · the patient's opinion about nature and cause · hopes for or expectations of treatment · active medical problems · medications (which, why, doses) · substance use and how much · the nine personal and social circumstances · degree of risk · history of psychiatric problems, psychiatric treatment, or suicide attempts · and the four "ask screening questions, if necessary" items (cognition, hallucinations/delusions, mood, anxiety).

Differences between the Appendix 1 content list and the guide's section 7 list. Appendix 1 says "uses substances" where section 7 says "uses alcohol or drugs"; its risk list has four headings (self-harm and suicide · violence towards others · self-neglect · neglect of dependents) against six in section 7; its past-psychiatric item adds "psychiatric treatment, or suicide attempts"; and it lists non-verbal clues as "body language, speech, facial expression, affect" where step 14 says "body language, tone of voice, facial expression, affect" [CS2 guide p9, p11, p21, p23].

10 · The case report and how it is marked

Part 1 is a formative feedback checklist — "this checklist will provide the student with constructive feedback about the report. The formal assessment for the report will be generated using Part 2." Part 1's columns on the live form are Not Done ("item missing entirely") · Inadequate ("included but information missing and/or described inappropriately") · Adequate ("included; described appropriately") · N/A [Case report form p1].

The HISTORY block scores 22 items: patient's expectations / chief complaint · current problems · course of the illness · expectations of the doctor · active physical illnesses · current medications · substance use · current personal and social circumstances · recent losses or changes · impact on personal care and survival, occupational, family and social functioning · risk of self-harm or suicide, self-neglect, neglect of dependents, aggression or violence · previous psychiatric problems · screens for cognitive impairments, psychosis, depression/mania, anxiety. The SUMMARY block scores two things: a summary of the encounter in 2–3 sentences pointing out the most pertinent historical and mental state findings, and an attempted diagnostic impression within the limits of your knowledge to date.

Write to the live MedSIS form, not to the guide's reprint. The live form adds "Patient's expectations / chief complaint" as a separate first item, renames "Use of alcohol or drugs" to "Substance use", "Screen for cognitive problems" to "Screen for cognitive impairments", "Screen for hallucinations and delusions" to "Screen for psychosis", and "Screen for changes in mood" to "Screen for depressin / mania" (sic) — i.e. it now asks you to screen for mania as well as depression and to state a chief complaint [Case report form p1] vs [CS2 guide p24].

Part 2 generates the mark. Five points — live form: Unsatisfactory · Below Expectations · Meets Expectations · Exceeds Expectations · Outstanding; the guide's reprint numbers them 1–5 with 3 = "pass, meets expectations". Both have five points, both put "meets expectations" third, and the pass mark is the third point.

Domain1 — Unsatisfactory3 — Meets expectations5 — Outstanding
Data collectionInsufficient information to identify the major problem, or on the wrong trackObtains sufficient information to identify the major problemObtains complete information including psychosocial context of the individual patient
LanguageInappropriate use of termsAppropriate use of terms with few errors in expression or languageCommand of language and terminology; applies all terms in the appropriate categories
Approach to the problemLittle or no thinking about the problem; unable to describe the patient's illnessRecognizes problem with good description of the illnessHighly relevant and accurate description of the illness
Global assessmentIncomplete history and MSE; case report disorganizedComplete history and MSE with succinct presentation and approachSophisticated synthesis of history and MSE; emerging ability to apply information

How to read the rubric as a study tool: in every domain the jump from "meets" to "outstanding" is a jump from completeness to synthesis — psychosocial context, correct categorization of terms, relevance and accuracy, and synthesis plus application. Domain 2 in particular rewards putting each observation in the right MSE category: don't report a thought-content finding as an affect finding.

11 · Appendix 3 — the psychiatric history template as a checklist

The practical interview scaffold, attributed to Dr. Jerome Perera. Work through it in this order.

  • Intro: name/role · purpose · circumstances · limits of confidentiality · thank the patient if appropriate.
  • Identifying data: name, age, gender (preferred pronouns) · living situation · relationship status and gender of partner · children · source of income/support, occupation · outpatient or inpatient (voluntary/involuntary).
  • Chief concern: "Please tell me about the concerns that you've had recently" — the patient's subjective report, symptom and duration.
  • History of present concern: context (events, problems, stressors, losses, changes, precipitants, social determinants) · symptoms by onset, duration, progression, intensity, with "describe for me what that's like; how do you experience it?" · fluctuation with day, reproductive cycle, season · impact on ADLs/IADLs and on occupational, social, family and relationship functioning · supports, treatments, coping · similar past experiences and longitudinal course (first onset, worst episode, typical duration/frequency) · last period of wellness · changes to usual personality when unwell · reason for seeking help · opinions about cause, willingness to engage, hopes of treatment.
  • Review of systems: mood · anxiety · psychosis · other (compulsions, post-traumatic, disordered eating).
  • Risk assessment: suicide/self-harm/self-neglect · homicide/aggression/violence · dependents · safe driving and cooking — the last two are routinely omitted and are explicitly listed.
  • Past psychiatric history: previous diagnoses and contacts (counselling, case manager) · ED visits · hospitalizations (approximate total, date of last discharge) · suicide attempts (number, severity, medical intervention, most recent) · self-harming behaviour · aggression, legal charges · treatments, non-pharmacological and pharmacological, with effectiveness and side effects.
  • Substance use: tobacco, cannabis, alcohol, other stimulants, hallucinogens, prescriptions, caffeine — and gambling and online use are included here · first, typical, last use and periods of abstinence · withdrawal including seizures and DTs · previous treatment · impact on symptoms and motivation to change.
  • Past medical history: medical problems, especially endocrine and neurological (seizures, head injuries) · pregnancies · surgeries and hospitalizations · impact of prior health concerns.
  • Medications: generic name, dose, frequency · contraceptives · over-the-counter and herbal/naturopathic · adherence, effectiveness, side effects. Allergies: anaphylactic reactions to medications.
  • Family psychiatric history: "Does anyone in your family have mental health concerns?" — diagnosis, treatments, hospitalizations, suicide attempts, substance use, legal.
  • Past personal history: birthplace, time in current location, heritage, religion/spirituality · family members (age, occupation, personality, quality of relationships) · trauma — abuse (verbal, physical, sexual), neglect, domestic violence · prenatal/perinatal · early childhood (milestones, temperament, caregivers, home stability) · school age (academics, socializing, bullying, inattention, behaviour, extra-curriculars) · sexuality (puberty, identity, orientation, dating) · adulthood · and the template's only explicit strengths item: hobbies, interests, sources of meaning, accomplishments, aspirations, hopes.

"Look for" — six interpretive themes: emotional development in early life and its context · major events and themes · recurring patterns of behaviour and experience · identity formation · experience of failure or loss · impact of experience on beliefs about self, other and world, and on trust, intimacy, anger and self-esteem.

Six key phrases, verbatim: "Help me to understand…" · "Let's work together to…" · "You're doing well, let's keep going." · "In the interest of time, I may ask questions more quickly." · "I apologize for interrupting / if I interrupt you." · "What you're talking about is important." Convey at the end: your understanding of the concerns, validation, and if appropriate hope — plan, finding meaning, improving.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • History vs mental state — same domains, different source: reported vs observed. Do not describe an observation in the history section.
  • Presentation order is not interview order. The write-up is conventional and predictable; the interview follows the patient.
  • Checklists are for after the interview, never during it.
  • Confusion + delusions sends you up the hierarchy, not down — look for a physical or drug-induced cause.
  • Mood vs affect and insight vs judgment are the two definitional pairs most likely to be quoted at you.
  • Risk headings are six in the content list but four on the marking form — and the template adds safe driving and cooking. Know which list you are being asked for.
  • The bolded "surprisingly often omitted" fragments are not the obvious courtesies — greeting, naming yourself and avoiding jargon carry no bold at all.
  • Interview technique is assessed in every OSCE station, not only the psychiatry ones.
Interview for a diagnosis so you can make a safe, practical plan: classify the illness, discern the predicament, look for the disease — then write a plan that is biopsychosocial, feasible, and mitigates safety concerns.

guides.title: Week 40 · 9 Introduction to Psychiatry (Byrne, Lecture 1)
guides.html:
Lecture 1 · Byrne

Introduction to Psychiatry (Byrne, Lecture 1)

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

What psychiatry is, how a disorder is separated from ordinary distress, the DSM-5 categories and their limits, and what makes a person vulnerable — diathesis–stress, ACEs and attachment.

Dr. Roisin Byrne (acute care psychiatrist at CAMH) opened the Week 40 block with the first of three consecutive lectures. Lecture 1 answers four questions: what psychiatry is, how a mental disorder is separated from ordinary distress, how the DSM-5 carves psychopathology into categories and where that carving fails, and what makes a given person vulnerable in the first place (diathesis–stress, biopsychosocial, ACEs, attachment). Everything below is on a slide, in a slide image, or said aloud in the room; standard knowledge added to repair a misstatement is marked (standard knowledge, not in the module).

What she said is and isn't testable (§7.0)

2 · What psychiatry is, and why every physician needs it

Definition (s10): "Psychiatry is the branch of medicine focused on diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of mental, emotional, and behavioral disorders" — framed on the same slide as biology + psychology + social context.

  • "Most of you will not become psychiatrists, but mental health disorders will impact your patients no matter what field of medicine you study" — she put the CaRMS figure at ~95% of the class.

  • Against the stereotype of the specialty: "I prescribe medications all the time. We do neurostimulation treatments. I order labs, I do investigations, I occasionally physically examine my patients."

3 · Stigma, and the two media effects

  • In high-income settings only 1/3 of people with depression receive treatment (s13).
  • Three levels of stigma, in her own words: individual (internalized) — "that shame — I shouldn't be this way, I should work harder, I shouldn't be imperfect"; interpersonal — "worrying that if you told someone how you're feeling, they would judge you or shame you"; structural — "this is racism; barriers for getting time off of work because of mental health."
  • Consequences of internalized stigma: worse symptoms, lower self-esteem / hope / empowerment, poorer treatment adherence, and earlier discontinuation of antidepressants if stigma is high. "You can measure stigma in people. If stigma is high, they're less likely to stay on treatment."
  • Awareness campaigns (s14): social media, online campaigns and #activism → ↓ stigma, ↑ help-seeking. 65% of studies of high-income-country social-media mental-health campaigns observed positive behaviour change; #TherapyTok has 2 billion views.

4 · What is a mental disorder?

"A syndrome characterized by clinically significant disturbance in cognition, emotional regulation, or behavior that reflects a dysfunction in psychological, biological, or developmental processes." (s19) — "That's the definition that comes from the DSM."

The three qualifiers printed underneath:

  1. Condition causes significant psychological pain or functional impairment. Her gloss: "To have a million terrible mood problems, but you're still working, you have relationships, you're living life — that's unlikely to be a psychiatric disorder."
  2. Not an expectable or culturally approved response to a common stressor or loss (e.g. grief after a death). "If something terrible happens in your life and you develop mood problems, that doesn't mean you have depression. We would expect that to happen."
  3. Symptoms arise from underlying psychological, biological, or developmental abnormalities — not just a response to external stressors.

(WFQ Q12: the keyed discriminator for "this is a disorder" is functional impairment — not the presence of a stressor, not comorbid history, not duration.)

Student question — where the "culturally expected" exclusion actually lives
A student pointed out that the expectable-response criterion belongs to the general definition of a mental disorder but is not one of the DSM's criteria for major depressive disorder. She agreed. Her worked answer: someone could have nine of nine for depression after "something horrible, like experiencing a flood" that anyone in their shoes would react to — would she diagnose it? "Probably not." The alternative she named is adjustment disorder (it appears on no slide). The duration guard still applies: "you need at least two weeks for them to be persistent." Her closing line: "One psychiatrist might diagnose depression, another not. There's a lot of grey in psychiatry too."

What also mattered was the earlier class discussion on the two TikTok clips (s18, "So, is this a psychiatric condition?"). A student answered that what matters is how often and how long it happens; her endorsement is the examinable line: "the frequency, intensity and duration of these difficulties matters as to whether it's a condition or not."

5 · Categorical vs dimensional classification

DSM-5-TR = Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th ed., Text Revision, published by the American Psychiatric Association. ICD-11 = International Classification of Diseases, 11th Edition, published by the WHO — "the DSM is our sort of diagnostic Bible… it's an American publication. The ICD is the kind of more international one."

The categorical premise (s21): mental diagnoses are qualitatively distinct from normal functioning and from each other; diagnoses are discrete — you either meet criteria, or you don't. Her punchline after the two worked cases: "You either have depression or you don't. You have panic disorder or you don't."

6 · Worked case 1 — Panic Disorder

Vignette (s22): 20-year-old male, taking two online grade 11 courses, lives with father, mother died last year. Panic attacks daily for 9 months, calling EMS weekly for chest pain; sudden chest pain, sweating, SOB, tremor, sense of doom. Lives in fear of panic attacks; does not leave home alone; avoids crowded and enclosed spaces. No suicidal ideation, no substances, FHx anxiety.

DSM-5 Panic Disorder criteria (s23). A. Recurrent unexpected panic attacks — an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort that peaks within minutes, with ≥4 of 13 symptoms: palpitations · sweating · trembling · shortness of breath or smothering · feelings of choking · chest pain · nausea or abdominal distress · dizziness or faintness · chills or heat sensations · paresthesias · derealization or depersonalization · fear of losing control or "going crazy" · fear of dying. B. At least one attack followed by ≥1 month of persistent worry about further attacks or their consequences, and/or significant maladaptive behaviour change. C. Not attributable to substances or another medical condition. D. Not better explained by another mental disorder.

Threshold to hold: ≥4 of 13 symptoms, peaking within minutes, plus ≥1 month of worry and/or behaviour change after at least one attack.

Poll (s24): "Does he meet criteria for Panic Disorder?" Key: YES — "Yes, he does." She walked it against the vignette aloud: four or more symptoms, present, plus one attack followed by worry or avoidance; and she called back the earlier student's frequency point — "so to your point, my friend over there, it's daily for nine months."

Plan as written (s25): (1) fluoxetine 20 mg po QAM; (2) refer to CBT with in vivo and interoceptive exposures. Aloud: "I know how to treat panic disorder — you use an SSRI, you use CBT, you do exposure therapy… It's really treatable and it goes away. But it doesn't tell you why." That question — "Does the diagnosis tell us why he developed panic disorder?" — is the hand-off to formulation in Lecture 2.

Unsourced clinical figure. Aloud: "10% of people go to the emergency room thinking they're having a heart attack — it's panic." She gave no source and it is on no slide. Treat it as an illustrative clinical figure, not a citable statistic.

7 · Worked case 2 — the Major Depressive Episode that isn't

Vignette (s26): 23-year-old female, full-time manager in a clothing store. Low self-esteem since childhood; avoids closeness in relationships; avoids promotions at work; periods of sadness that come on intensely and last a maximum of one hour, once or twice per week. Binge drinking of alcohol. No suicidal ideation. Does not miss work or social events because of these mood changes.

DSM-5 MDE symptom list (s27) — 5+ symptoms in the same 2-week period, representing a change from previous functioning: (1) depressed mood most of the day, nearly every day; (2) markedly diminished interest or pleasure; (3) significant weight loss when not dieting, or weight gain; (4) insomnia or hypersomnia; (5) psychomotor agitation or retardation; (6) fatigue or loss of energy; (7) feelings of worthlessness or excessive/inappropriate guilt; (8) diminished ability to think or concentrate, or indecisiveness; (9) recurrent thoughts of death, suicidal ideation, or a suicide attempt or specific plan.

A DSM rule the slide leaves off. s27 prints only "5+ sx … same 2-week period", but the DSM-5 criterion also requires that at least one of the five be (1) depressed mood or (2) loss of interest/pleasure (standard knowledge, not in the module). She assumed it aloud — "one person has to have low mood and loss of interest" — but it is printed nowhere in the deck. Do not build an "any 5 of 9" flashcard from s27 alone.

Poll (s28): "Does she meet criteria for MDE?" Key: NO, on two grounds she stated aloud: (1) no functional impairment — "she doesn't really have functional impairment. She's still managing to do things"; and (2) failure of the duration requirement — "the periods of sadness are kind of an hour or two. That's not in keeping with a depressive episode. In depression it's at least two weeks, so it's pretty much day in, day out." No answer word is printed on the slide; the transcript settles it.

The pairing of the two cases is deliberate: panic does meet criteria, depression does not — and yet the second patient is still suffering. That is the bridge into the limitations of the categorical system.

8 · Limitations of categorical systems (four, memorize by name)

  1. ARBITRARY DX THRESHOLDS — "4/9 sx ≠ MDE, but 5/9 does." Aloud: "If someone had four of nine symptoms and they were really impaired, I would still offer them treatment." The real-world cost she named: "in the US, if you don't meet the diagnostic criteria, then you don't get insurance coverage."
  2. COMORBIDITY — multiple labels. "You'll be told 'go see this patient, she has GAD, BPD, MDD, ADHD.' It's one brain. What we know neurobiologically is that it's likely one process manifesting in different symptoms."
  3. HETEROGENEITY — same label, different patients. Her two patients with the identical diagnosis: patient A — low mood and loss of interest, not sleeping at all, has lost 50 lb, catatonia and cannot physically move; patient B — binge eating and sleeping 14 hours a day. "Is this the same disorder? Do we treat it the same, even though it's the exact same label?"
  4. SUBTHRESHOLD ILLNESS — impairment without diagnosis. "The subthreshold illness ties into the arbitrary thresholds" — limitations 1 and 4 are two views of the same problem.
Number caution. She said depression has "something like 256 different presentations" because you need only 5 of 9. The commonly cited combinatorial count for a DSM-5 major depressive episode is 227 distinct symptom combinations (standard knowledge, not in the module), and she prefaced the figure with "something like". Take the order-of-magnitude point (hundreds of presentations of one label), not the number.

Stem: "A 32-year-old man reports feeling off for months with low motivation, poor sleep and trouble connecting socially. He's only got three of nine criteria for depression. He says his relationships and work have deteriorated. Which of the following highlights the limitations of the diagnostic system used in this case?"

9 · Dimensional models, and the same patient re-read

  • Psychological traits and symptoms lie on a continuum; disorders = exaggerated, inflexible, dysregulated versions of normal traits; differences are quantitative > qualitative — the exact opposite of the categorical premise.
  • HiTOP and RDoC are complex and not used in practice. "RDoC was put up by the National Institute of Health in the US… It's so complicated and really hard to clinically apply. They're more used for research."
  • The statistical claim that makes this more than an opinion: "these traits, in populations… narcissism, neuroticism — these things are measured and normally distributed. Some are heritable, some related to your early development."
  • The s31 re-reading of the depression patient by traits rather than label: low self-worth · hopelessness · alcohol misuse → "No dx of depression, but still clinically significant suffering" → plan: targeted psychotherapy (self-esteem work) and psychoeducation about alcohol.
A categorical system discharges this patient with no diagnosis and no plan; a dimensional reading generates a treatment plan anyway. "We may not say she meets depression criteria, but she's still suffering, and we could still derive a treatment plan for her."

10 · Why the brain is vulnerable: evolution, diathesis–stress, biopsychosocial

Evolutionary psychology (s32) answers the printed question "Why would the brain evolve to be vulnerable to mental illness?": traits that seem maladaptive today were possibly adaptive in ancestral environments; evolution selects for reproductive fitness, not happiness or health; some emotional responses are normally adaptive systems that become excessive, persistent, or contextually mismatched. Worked example on the slide: "being overly anxious could increase survival by avoiding predators or danger." Her line to patients: "Your brain didn't evolve to keep you happy or even at peace. This is a survival machine." (WFQ Q14 keys "they were once adaptive in ancestral environments".)

Diathesis–stress (s33–s34):

Mental illness = Predisposition (diathesis) + Stressor. Diathesis is a sliding scale rather than a binary switch: high diathesis needs very little stress to produce symptoms; low diathesis may absorb major stress without illness.
  • The figure (image only, the most important diagram in L1): x-axis predisposition for the disorder (low → high), y-axis amount of stress, and a diagonal dashed threshold line splitting the plot into "Disorder not manifested" (lower left) and "Disorder manifested" (upper right). The line is a threshold, not a point — the model is continuous in both axes.
  • Stressors listed: bereavement · job loss · divorce · academic pressure · physical illness · substance use · chronic discrimination. "It's actually pretty hard being a human being."
  • The clinical payoff, stated as the reason the model is taught: "This risk is what you're going to look at when you're interviewing someone in psychiatry… because those are the things you would generally address for treatment."
Poll 3 (SLIDO) — the two siblings
Stem: "A 29-year-old woman with chronic anxiety and low mood shares that her sibling, who grew up in the same environment, is functioning well. She wonders why her mental health is worse. Which of the following explains this disparity?"
Key: diathesis–stress interactions vary between individuals. Her reasoning is the examinable part: "She may have shared some genetics, but [she is] not an exact genetic copy — and what happened to them at school, what happened to them at recess, is different." Same household ≠ same environment, and siblings are not genetically identical, so both terms of the equation differ.

The biopsychosocial model (s35) was proposed by George Engel in 1977: biological, psychological and social/environmental factors interact dynamically, converging in the Venn diagram's centre on "Health". Aloud: "We still use it in psychiatry. We also always add culture in there as well." The three arms are then worked through as predisposing factors — which is exactly how they are entered in the Lecture 2 formulation grid.

11 · Biological predisposing factors

  1. Heritability — "If you have aunts and uncles with anxiety, you're more likely to develop anxiety."
  2. Inherited temperamental traits — "If you're a very relaxed person temperamentally, you're less likely to develop a disorder than if you have a more neurotic temperament." (WFQ Q22: temperament = innate traits influencing early interaction with the world; present from infancy, biologically based, foundational to personality, distinct from learned behaviour and from attachment.)
  3. Epigenetic changes (e.g. DNA methylation) from early life stress can modify gene expression and ↑ long-term risk.
  4. Neurodevelopmental abnormalities — "things that happen to you in childhood."
Misspeak, corrected. She offered the short/long allele of the serotonin transporter gene (5-HTTLPR) as her example of an epigenetic change. That variant is a genetic polymorphism — inherited sequence variation, not an epigenetic mark (standard knowledge, not in the module), and she half-corrected herself in the same sentence ("that's just inherited"). Keep them separate: methylation = epigenetic; short/long allele = inherited sequence variation. She also hedged that the epigenetics literature here is "a bit debated".

12 · Social predisposing factors — the ACE study

Design (s37): a 1995 Kaiser–CDC team mailed a retrospective questionnaire to >17,000 insured adults who had completed routine check-ups; childhood adversities were tallied, each "yes" = 1 point = the ACE score; participants' EMRs were then followed prospectively, linking ACE dose to later medical and psychiatric morbidity.

The 10-item questionnaire (s38, image only) asks "Before your 18th birthday, did any of the following happen to you?" and covers: neglect/basic needs unmet · loss of a parent (divorce, abandonment, death) · household mental illness or suicide attempt · household substance use · domestic violence between adults · household incarceration · verbal abuse · physical abuse · feeling unloved · unwanted sexual contact. Footer: "Your ACE score is the total number of checked responses."

Protective factors — PCEs and the "good enough" parent

  • "Not all ↑-ACE children develop illness." Each additional positive childhood experience (PCE) ↓ adult depression risk by 26%.
  • Winnicott's "good enough" parent: "Ordinary, non-ideal care is enough for healthy development — perfection is unnecessary and unrealistic."
  • Optimal frustration (lecturer-only, and the exam framing): "You actually need optimal frustration. You need some adversity or challenges in childhood to develop resilience." So "good enough" is not merely adequate care — a question offering "shield the child from all adversity" as a protective factor is wrong on this lecture's own terms.

13 · Psychological predisposing factors — attachment

The claim (s41): "Insecure attachment and adverse early caregiving are associated with increased risk of psychopathology across diagnostic categories." Two bodies of work: John Bowlby (1958–1980s) — the human infant is biologically "wired" to seek proximity to a caregiver who provides food and protection; and Harlow's monkey studies (1950s–60s) on the role of caregiving and comfort.

Her evolutionary argument for why infants are wired this way (the single largest lecturer-only block in L1, on no slide): human beings are useless when born, unlike an elephant that "pops out and it can walk". The obstetric trade-off: big brains plus bipedalism means the mother's hips cannot be wide enough to birth a developed infant — "so we birth very underdeveloped infants, to give us the advantage of bipedalism and a big head." The payoff: "if our parents didn't care about us, we would die and no one's genes would survive… We're all wired to want to be close, to want to feel secure and safe, because otherwise we would have died."

Harlow, narrated because the video would not play: infant rhesus monkeys were given a wire mother that has the milk and a soft cloth mother with no milk. The hypothesis was that the monkey would prefer the milk mother. The result — the examinable finding — is that the monkey spends most of its time with the cloth mother, returning to the wire mother only briefly for milk: contact comfort, not feeding, drives attachment. Her ethical aside first: "it was horrible what they did to these little monkeys."

From the Sprouts attachment video, played in the room: a strong bond to one primary caregiver in the first years is critical to development. Securely attached → safe to explore, with "a safe base which we can return to any time" → greater trust, connection, success. Insecurely attached → "afraid to leave or explore a rather scary-looking world, because we are not sure if we can return" → mistrust, poorer social skills, difficulty forming relationships. Three insecure types — anxious, avoidant, disorganized — and one third of us are insecurely attached, two thirds securely attached. That ratio exists only in the video and the transcript; no slide carries it.

14 · Bias and culture in diagnosis

The problem (s44): "Norms for emotion, behavior, and spirituality differ across societies. Clinicians may misinterpret culturally normative behaviors as psychopathology" — e.g. spiritual experiences (visions, hearing voices during prayer) mistaken for psychosis when religious context is ignored. And clinicians may unconsciously interpret behaviours differently across racial groups: Black patients in North America are more likely to receive a schizophrenia diagnosis than a mood disorder diagnosis, even when symptom profiles are similar.

Six strategies to minimize bias (s45) — memorize by name:

  1. Cultural humility — ongoing self-reflection on one's own biases. "We have so many biases, known and unknown."
  2. Use structured tools — the DSM-5 Cultural Formulation Interview (CFI).
  3. Elicit patient perspective — "What does this experience mean to you?"
  4. Collaborate — interpreters, cultural liaisons, or community healers. Her local example: Indigenous healers who come onto the CAMH unit "to help us understand and offer supports for patients of Indigenous background."
  5. Education — local idioms of distress and culture-bound syndromes. "The DSM has a whole section on them."
  6. Avoid assumptions — distinguish pathology from culturally accepted practices.

(WFQ Q17 keys "explore his explanatory model of illness and book a follow up" — strategies 3 and 4.)

15 · Discriminators and exam traps

  • Papageno vs Werther. Recovery-focused coverage → ↓ suicide (protective, Mozart opera); sensationalized or romanticized coverage → ↑ suicide by imitation (harmful, Goethe novel). Both named after fictional characters.
  • Suicide vs self-harm. Men die by suicide more (~3×); women self-harm more. Self-harm here means non-suicidal self-injury.
  • "Disorder" vs distress. The keyed discriminator is functional impairment, with frequency, intensity and duration as the axes that decide it — not the presence of a stressor.
  • The MDE gate. 5 of 9 over 2 weeks, and at least one must be depressed mood or anhedonia (standard knowledge, not in the module). An "any 5 of 9" option is wrong.
  • Panic threshold. ≥4 of 13, peaking within minutes, plus ≥1 month of worry or behaviour change — not 4 of 9, and not "attacks alone".
  • Limitation 1 vs limitation 4. A vignette with impairment but a sub-cutoff symptom count is keyed to arbitrary thresholds / subthreshold illness, not to comorbidity or heterogeneity. A distractor offering symptom tracking loses because tracking works in either system.
  • Categorical vs dimensional wording. "Qualitatively distinct, discrete" = categorical; "quantitative differences, exaggerated versions of normal traits" = dimensional. HiTOP and RDoC are research tools, not clinical ones.
  • Attachment. Rejecting or emotionally unavailable care → avoidant (self-sufficiency, mistrust, substance misuse); inconsistent or intrusive care → anxious (reassurance-seeking); maltreatment or frightening caregiver → disorganized (BPD, complex PTSD, self-harm).
  • "Good enough" ≠ perfect and ≠ frictionless — some frustration is actively necessary. And ACE risk is dose–response, offset by PCEs at 26% per additional positive experience.
L1 key messages, verbatim from s46: mental illness lies at the intersection of biology, psychology and social context; DSM/ICD categories are useful but imperfect maps of psychopathology; risk exists on a continuum — vulnerability × environment/stress; development, attachment and evolved emotional systems help explain vulnerability; culture, stigma and clinician bias shape who gets diagnosed and treated.

guides.title: Week 40 · 10 Assessment, Diagnosis and Formulation (Byrne, Lecture 2)
guides.html:
Lecture 2 · Byrne

Assessment, Diagnosis and Formulation (Byrne, Lecture 2)

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The psychiatric interview, alliance and empathy, the ROS mnemonics, the ASEPTIC mental status exam, and the 4 P's biopsychosocial formulation worked through on one case.

Lecture 2 is the "how" of psychiatry: how the interview is structured, how the Mental Status Examination stands in for the physical exam, and how a formulation — not a diagnosis — explains why this patient fell ill now. It runs as a three-stage pipeline: (1) Psychiatric Interview → (2) Mental Status Exam → (3) Diagnosis and Formulation, ending in the 4 P's × bio/psycho/social grid worked through on a single case.

Scope — you do not need to memorize the interview deck
Said three times over this lecture: "The slides are heavy and you don't need to memorize all of this right now"; of the 15-heading interview outline, "You don't need to memorize this. This will be you when you do your interview seminar — this can be for your reference"; and of the mnemonics and ROS screens, "You're going to have all these memorized by the time you finish clerkship." The seminar she names is ICE. That is a statement about rote recall of the slide as printed, not about the concepts: the WFQ keys tied to this week test the MSE vocabulary (Q15), transference (Q16) and the 4 P's regardless.

1 · Objectives, and the question that framed the lecture

By the end of this lecture the learner should be able to (s4):

  1. Describe the structure and goals of the psychiatric interview, including the importance of collateral information.
  2. Understand, perform and document a basic Mental Status Examination (MSE). (WFQ Q15)
  3. Differentiate between descriptive diagnosis and psychiatric formulation.
  4. Construct a basic psychiatric formulation using the biopsychosocial model.

A student asked her at the break: "in rheumatology we just learned that we would do a history and labs and ask about symptoms. Why isn't it like that in psychiatry?" Her answer, which she then returned to three more times: "So it is like that also in psychiatry… we use pretty much the same approach as all medical assessments." The HPI is "the same with psychiatry — if they have abdominal pain, what makes it worse, what makes it better, when did it start and what have you tried"; past psychiatric history is "just like… you'd want to know about their past rheumatological history."

The examinable framing: psychiatry's assessment is structurally identical to any other specialty's history. What differs is the depth of the personal/developmental history, the routine safety screen, and the MSE standing in for the physical exam.

How long it takes, in her practice: "In emerg I'll do an interview in like 7 minutes… if you're doing an outpatient assessment, the interview could be over an hour."

2 · The four goals of the psychiatric interview

Cited to Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th ed. (2022) (s6):

  1. Understand the concern — "you really want to understand what's brought the patient to the setting."
  2. Build an alliance — "It's really important in psychiatry because you're asking people to share very difficult, sensitive things. And so if they trust you, they're more likely to do that."
  3. Assess diagnosis and safety.
  4. Develop a shared plan.
The four-item safety screen, named aloud
"Every psychiatry interview we ask about safety — so suicidal thoughts, violent thoughts towards others, driving safety, child safety." This is the closest thing in the lecture to the missing "Risk assessment" slide (heading 5 of the interview outline has no slide of its own), and three of the four reappear as the statutory exceptions to confidentiality.

Before you begin — patient and interviewer must feel safe (s7)

  • In hospital or the ER, other staff or security may be present and the door is left ajar; you should have a clear, unencumbered exit path; pause, de-escalate and seek help if safety is compromised; and stay alert to the patient's comfort throughout (tissues, water).
  • The one quantified violence figure in all three lectures, transcript-only: "Someone with psychosis is at 2 times increased risk of violence compared to the general population."
  • The seating rule: "You always want to be closest to the door… if it's a little room, you put your chair closest to the door so that you could leave more easily."
  • The stop rule: "Definitely if someone seems like they're getting agitated, just stop the interview" — scoped mainly to the psychotic, agitated or manic patient. And what is expected of a clerk: "you won't be asked to go see an agitated person by yourself."
  • Why it is not hypothetical: a colleague who used to run the CAMH emergency room "was punched in the face a couple of weeks ago."

3 · Beginning the interview, and confidentiality

Three openers (s8): introduce yourself; review the nature of the interaction and the approximate amount of time; review the limits of confidentiality.

Her actual opening script, used with every patient: "Hi, I'm Dr. Byrne… Before we begin, I'd like to review confidentiality. So everything you and I talk about is confidential between us. There are exceptions that the law places on all doctors around safety: if you told me you were threatening someone's life, if the care of a child is a concern, or driving safety — those are reasons I might need to break confidentiality." Her comment: "It's literally all the time. I just repeat it. It has saved me so many times."

Worked example from the day before: a man in the ER for cocaine use disorder who was driving impaired — "I told you, if you tell me you are unsafe driving, I have to report you. And so I reported him to the ministry." The principle underneath: "You want to tell people what could happen if they're disclosing things to you" — the warning must come before the disclosure, not after.

4 · Alliance and empathy

Alliance (s9): the patient must feel the evaluation is a joint effort, that the MD is genuinely interested, and that you care — through four behaviours: listen without interrupting · acknowledge distress · explain questions · agree on priorities. Aloud: "You don't need to be this kind of clinically distant person… They're going to tell you about their trauma or their childhood — they don't want to talk to a robot."

Empathy (s10): "Understanding what the patient is thinking and feeling — when the clinician can put themselves in the patient's place while at the same time maintaining objectivity."
  • Verbal empathic intervention: "that must have been very difficult for you." Nonverbal responses: raised eyebrows, leaning toward the patient, head nodding.
  • The over-identification guard (not on the slide): "You don't want to over-identify with the patient. Early in my training… I'd be fighting tears. You still need to be the clinician and have objectivity, but it's OK to really put yourself in their shoes."
  • Her counter-example of what not to do: "you're just looking at your screen typing — 'OK, kid died. OK, yeah, next' — like that's not empathic. You want to be looking, making eye contact, raising your eyebrows, passing a Kleenex."

From the Brené Brown clip, played in full in the room (so it is lecture content):

  • "Empathy fuels connection. Sympathy drives disconnection."
  • Theresa Wiseman's four qualities of empathy: (1) perspective taking — recognizing another's perspective as their truth; (2) staying out of judgement; (3) recognizing emotion in other people; (4) communicating that recognition back to them.
  • Empathy is feeling with people. The hole metaphor: climbing down to say "I know what it's like down here, and you're not alone," where sympathy stays at the top ("…you want a sandwich?").
  • The most testable line: "Rarely, if ever, does an empathic response begin with 'at least'." ("I had a miscarriage" → "at least you know you can get pregnant.") The prescribed alternative: "I don't even know what to say right now. I'm just so glad you told me."
  • "Empathy is a choice, and it's a vulnerable choice… Rarely can a response make something better. What makes something better is connection."
Attribution caution. She introduced Brené Brown as a social worker who researches self-compassion. Brown's research programme is on shame, vulnerability and empathy; self-compassion is Kristin Neff's field (standard knowledge, not in the module). The clip's content is unaffected.

After the clip a student said that as a medical student you must sit with a lot of discomfort, because people bring you problems you cannot yet solve. Her answer is the examinable one: "Your role will be gathering history, to begin with, and holding that space… being able to sit with the discomfort, being a human being. They feel that sense of connection."

5 · The psychiatric interview outline (15 headings, in order)

  1. Identifying Data
  2. Chief Complaint & Reason for Referral
  3. History of Present Illness
  4. Review of Systems
  5. Risk assessment
  6. Substance Use History
  7. Past Psychiatric History
  8. Past Medical History
  9. Medications
  10. Allergies
  11. Family History
  12. Developmental and Social History
  13. Mental Status Examination
  14. Physical Examination
  15. Collateral

Identifying data (s13) — full name, age, sex, gender identity, pronouns · ethnicity and cultural background · marital/relationship status and children · occupation and education · living situation · referral source · date and setting. Why it is longer here than anywhere else: "In psychiatry we're obsessed with identifying data… are they married? Do they have a job? What's the source of income? Identifying data is so important in psychiatry because it contextualizes the HPI." It feeds the Social column of the 4 P's grid directly.

Chief complaint and reason for referral (s14) — the main reason for presenting, ideally in the patient's own words: "What has brought you in today?"; "What is the most pressing concern you have about your mental health?" "This should be brief and focused, not a full narrative."

HPI (s15), eight elements: onset, duration, progression · context and precipitating STRESSORS · symptom clusters (mood, anxiety, psychosis, sleep, appetite, cognition) · functional impact · suicidal or homicidal ideation, plan, intent or behaviour · safety concerns (driving, child safety) · insight into illness · coping strategies and help-seeking.

6 · Review of systems — the four core screens

Depression · Mania/hypomania · Psychosis · Anxiety, with cognitive, eating, sexual function and somatic/dissociative screens added if relevant (s16). When it is done, and the one exception: "Generally speaking at every psychiatric assessment — unless it's a psychotic person in the emergency room where I'm basically there to give medications to restrain them — I would ask about depression, mania, psychosis, and anxiety."

Depression — MSIGECAPS

LetterDomainScreening question
MMood"Have you felt sad, down, or hopeless lately?"
SSleep"How has your sleep been, sleeping too much, trouble falling or staying asleep?"
IInterest"Have you lost interest in things you usually enjoy?"
GGuilt"Do you feel guilty or blame yourself unnecessarily?"
EEnergy"How is your energy level throughout the day?"
CConcentration"How is your concentration?"
AAppetite"How has your appetite changed?"
PPsychomotor"Do you feel slowed down in your movements or thinking, or restless, like you can't sit still?"
SSuicidality"Have you had thoughts that life isn't worth living?"
MSIGECAPS has 9 letters and maps one-to-one onto the 9 DSM-5 MDE criteria of Lecture 1: M↔depressed mood, S↔insomnia/hypersomnia, I↔anhedonia, G↔worthlessness/guilt, E↔fatigue, C↔concentration/indecisiveness, A↔appetite/weight, P↔psychomotor agitation or retardation, S↔thoughts of death or suicidal ideation.

Mania — GST PAID

Mania is "a distinct period of elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy/activity" (s18).

LetterItemScreening question
GGrandiosity"Feeling unusually confident or that you have special abilities/powers?"
SSleep (decreased need)"Have you needed less sleep than usual but still felt full of energy?"
TTalkativeness / Pressured speech"Have you been talking much more than usual?"
PPleasurable but risky activities"Any impulsive/risky behaviors, like overspending or reckless driving?"
AActivity increase (goal-directed or agitation)"Have you been unusually active or started lots of new projects lately?"
IIdeas racing (flight of ideas)"Have your thoughts been racing so fast it's hard to keep up with them?"
DDistractibility"Are you more easily distracted than usual?"

Contrast to hold: the decreased need for sleep of mania (still energetic) is not the insomnia of depression (tired); mania's talkativeness and pressured speech pairs with depression's slowed speech on the MSE.

Psychosis — hallucinations, and what each modality suggests

Hallucinations = "perceptual disturbances without external stimuli" (s19): auditory (voices or sounds others can't hear), visual, olfactory (odours with no source, often unpleasant), tactile/somatic (bugs crawling, being touched).

Modality → likely cause (transcript-only, on no slide, and the highest-yield table in L2)
Auditory — "most common in schizophrenia." Visual — "typically more in keeping with delirium and a medical presentation." Olfactory — "more common in a medical cause, like a temporal lobe epilepsy" (the slide makes the same point at s36). Tactile — "more common in, say, alcohol withdrawal or benzodiazepine withdrawal."

The rule of thumb: auditory → primary psychiatric (schizophrenia); everything else → look for a medical, neurological or withdrawal cause.

Delusions = "fixed false beliefs" — five types (s20–s21):

TypeDefinitionHer real-patient illustration
PersecutoryBeing harassed, followed, spied on or harmed by others"like being paranoid — basically we call those persecutory delusions"
GrandioseExceptional abilities, fame, wealth, or a special mission
ReferentialUnrelated events, objects or people (TV, radio) have special meaning directed at the persona patient who linked a street sign starting with L and tripping on "something that looked like a laser" — "just drawing nonsensical connections between different stimuli"
ErotomanicAnother person, often of higher status or a stranger, is in love with the individuala patient who believed Roger Federer was her husband and that his wife was sending her signals and holding him captive — note how it extends into a persecutory elaboration
NihilisticOne is dead, does not exist, or the world is ending"'we're actually in purgatory', 'I'm dead, you're dead', 'my body is rotten'" — "this comes along with very severe depression"
The pairing to hold: nihilistic delusions → severe (psychotic) depression, not schizophrenia. She returns to it in Lecture 3, where her ECT patient has nihilistic delusions and a psychotic depression.
Two delusion polls (SLIDO)
(1) "A 40-year-old woman with a history of schizophrenia believes that commercials on television are speaking directly to her." Key: referential delusions — "Yeah, exactly. So those are referential delusions."
(2) "A 64-year-old man tells his doctor that his body no longer exists, that he's already dead and he's floating in a memory after the world ended. He appears perplexed, with intact understanding and short-term memory." The room answered and she moved straight on — she never said the answer word aloud. On the slide's own definitions the answer is nihilistic delusion, but treat this one as inferred from the stem, not quoted.

Anxiety — six conditions (s22–s23)

Generalized anxiety (chronic worry, physical tension) · panic (sudden episodes of intense fear peaking in minutes) · OCD (repetitive obsessions and compulsions — aloud she added tapping, counting, checking) · PTSD (hyperarousal, avoidance, re-experiencing after trauma) · social anxiety (fear of negative evaluation) · specific phobias (flying, heights, animals, needles; she added emetophobia, phobia of vomiting).

Grouping caution. OCD and PTSD sit here under "Review of Systems – Anxiety", but in the DSM-5 category table of Lecture 1 they are separate categories — Obsessive-Compulsive & Related and Trauma and Stressor Disorders. The ROS grouping is a screening convenience, not a nosological claim.
The PTSD discriminator, transcript-only: after something frightening, post-traumatic symptoms are the norm — "90% of people, a year out, those have all resolved. But there's about 10% of people who continue to have those symptoms — can't sleep, nightmares, flashbacks, hyperarousal… That is PTSD." Neither figure is on any slide.

7 · Substance use, past history, family history

Substance use history (s24) — always ask about alcohol, cannabis, tobacco, opioids, stimulants, hallucinogens, sedatives, then six probes: route/frequency/quantity/duration · last use and periods of abstinence · withdrawal, tolerance, cravings · impact on functioning · past treatments (detox, rehab, 12-step) · screening tools (CAGE, AUDIT).

Live class question — which substances kill you in withdrawal?
Lethal in withdrawal: alcohol, benzodiazepines, phenobarbital — her unifying category is central nervous system depressants. What they cause: seizure, delirium tremens, and death. Opioids are the contrast case: "Can opioid withdrawal be lethal? As far as anyone knows, not really. It's very uncomfortable… but it's not lethal." Named management: diazepam plus thiamine, with admission for IV treatment. None of this is on a slide — the slide lists only the six history probes.
  • Past psychiatric history (s25) — previous diagnoses and episodes · inpatient/outpatient treatments with dates, durations, outcomes · suicide attempts or self-harm · psychotherapy modalities, duration, perceived benefit · medication history (names, doses, response, side effects, adherence). Her four actual questions: "Have you been admitted to hospital before? Have you made suicide attempts? Have you taken medications? Have you done psychotherapy?"
  • Past medical history (s26) — chronic conditions (diabetes, epilepsy, HIV), surgical history, neurological history (head injuries, seizures), relevant labs and imaging.
  • Medications and allergies (s27) — prescribed, OTC, supplements, recent changes. Family history (s28) — depression, bipolar, schizophrenia, suicide, substance use; family medical history if relevant.
  • Personal (developmental/social) history (s29) — four domains: early life · current circumstances · relationships and supports · identity and culture. How deep to go: "In the emergency room I'm not getting into that with people, but you titrate up or down based on the relevance of it." Tied back to L1's panic patient: "We want to know why he has panic disorder."
  • Collateral history (s30), citing BMJ 2023;382:e076462 — "information gathered from someone other than the patient (family, friends, carers, or other health professionals)" across physical and mental health, social circumstances and functional abilities leading up to the assessment. "Especially in emergency psychiatry — if someone has suicidal thoughts, we want to get the perspective of other people."
The medical cause of psychosis — a worked case, transcript-only
A university student admitted with sudden-onset psychosis and complete paranoia; screening labs showed TSH sky high → myxedema psychosis. "Untreated hypothyroidism can lead to psychosis. And so then the treatment is: hey, you don't have schizophrenia, we just need to replace your thyroid." The other clues in the same young man: hypercholesterolaemia and hypertension in an otherwise healthy young person. The general rule: "you always want to think about medical conditions and their medical history." She also made the reciprocal point first: psychiatric and medical comorbidity each worsen the other's outcomes, quite apart from one causing the other.

The one heritability number in the lecture: "If you have a first-degree relative with bipolar disorder, you have a 10% chance of having bipolar disorder yourself." No slide carries a heritability figure for any disorder.

8 · The Mental Status Exam — ASEPTIC

What it is (s31): the "psychiatric equivalent of the physical examination"; it "explores all areas of mental functioning and denotes evidence of signs and symptoms of mental illnesses"; and crucially, "data for the MSE is gathered throughout the interview" — it is observational and continuous, not a separate set of questions at the end. Aloud: "basically it's a snapshot of describing someone's mental status," and "you don't have to say all of these things for every person" — the tables are a vocabulary bank, not a mandatory checklist. Psychiatrists do also examine patients: "in particular a neuro exam… and examine for side effects from medications."

LetterDomainDescriptor vocabulary (s33–s39)
AAppearance / Behaviourage (stated? younger/older?) · dress (casual, formal, inappropriate to weather or setting) · grooming/hygiene · gait (brisk, slow, intoxicated, ataxic, rigid, shuffling, staggering) · psychomotor activity (normal, reduced, excessive) · LOC (alert, confused, lethargic, stuporous) · abnormal movements (grimaces, tics, tardive dyskinesias, foot tapping, compulsions) · eye contact · attitude (cooperative, belligerent, oppositional, submissive)
SSpeechrate (rapid, pressured, slowed) · rhythm (hesitant, rambling, halting, stuttering, jerky, long pauses) · tone · volume (loud, soft, whispered, yelling, inaudible) · accent · clarity · quantity (responds only to questions, offers information, repetitive, verbose)
EEmotion (Mood and Affect)mood = subjective (what the patient says) · affect = observed · congruence (congruent/incongruent) · appropriateness to situation · quality (euthymic, elevated, depressed) · range (broad/restricted) · stability (fixed/labile)
