PPerceptual disturbanceshallucinations (auditory, visual, olfactory — classically temporal lobe epilepsy) · illusions = distortions of real images or sensations · depersonalization = the patient feels they are not real · derealisation = the patient feels the world is not real
TThought content and processprocess: circumstantial (answers eventually, after excessive detail) · tangential (moves away, never answers) · flight of ideas (rapid shifts, discernible connections) · loose associations (connections weak or hard to follow) · thought blocking (halted). content: suicidal or homicidal ideation, delusions, obsessions
IInsight and Judgementinsight = the patient's understanding of what is happening to them · judgement = can they use facts and make reasonable decisions (good, fair, impaired)
CCognitionorientation in 3 spheres (name, place, time) · attention/concentration · memory (short- and long-term). Documentation phrase given verbatim: "Cognition not formally assessed, but grossly intact."
Mood vs affect is the single highest-yield MSE distinction: mood = subjective (the patient's report); affect = objective (your observation). Her worked discrepancy: "The patient told me they're very sad, but they're laughing — so their affect might be elevated or jovial." (WFQ Q15 uses "broad affect" as the distractor, because a depressed patient would be expected to show restricted affect.)
  • Three separate affect axes, and a question can key on which one a word belongs to: quality (euthymic / elevated / depressed on the slide, plus flat, her word at the poll; blunted is the standard intermediate term but appears in neither the slides nor the transcript (standard knowledge, not in the module)) · range (broad / restricted) · stability (fixed / labile). "Flat is the quality of it, and restricted is the range."
  • Hallucination vs illusion: "A hallucination is like 'I am seeing someone standing right here.' A visual illusion would be looking at something real and what I see instead is… a ghost." The illusion needs a real object present to be misperceived.
  • Depersonalization and derealization are types of dissociation — "feeling disconnected from themselves, or disconnected from reality." Clinically they show up in PTSD and in psychosis. Neither association is on a slide.
  • Her added screening qualifier: "Are you experiencing a voice in your head that nobody else can hear, that's not your own voice?" — the discriminator from ordinary inner speech, absent from the slide.
Insight and judgement can come apart
Her example of absent insight: police bring in someone who believes they are Jesus Christ reincarnated — "they have psychosis and they can't tell that what they're experiencing isn't true." Then the dissociation, which is the testable part: "Judgement is more so based on behaviour. So you could have poor insight, but you'd still be behaving appropriately — your judgement could be OK." Insight = does the patient recognize they are ill; judgement = are their decisions and behaviour sound. They are scored separately and can move in opposite directions; the slide lists them in one row and never says this.

Why "dress" is a real MSE item — the Consent and Capacity Board anecdote. As a resident she argued at the CCB (where the patient has a lawyer and the doctor does not) that an involuntarily admitted patient with schizophrenia should stay: it was about 35 °C and she was wearing multiple jackets, so she was at risk of overheating — evidence of impaired judgement. The lawyer cross-examined: "Well, what kind of material was it? Was it fleece? Was it cotton?" Her point: "Sometimes it doesn't matter how someone dresses, but sometimes it does" — which is why the slide says inappropriate to weather or setting rather than simply "dressed oddly". The observation must be tied to a consequence.

Physical examination (s40) — "limited but important in many settings" (e.g. neuro exam for delirium): signs of intoxication, withdrawal, malnutrition, medication side effects · neurological or movement disorders (tremors, EPS) · catatonia · baseline for psychotropics (weight, BP).

Practice MSE — the film clips, and her model answer

Three clips were on the slides — A Beautiful Mind, Silver Linings Playbook, and Stepmom (1:30 to 2:30) — but only the first two were done in the room; the Stepmom clip was skipped for time.

Her own MSE of the A Beautiful Mind clip — a model answer
"This is a middle-aged Caucasian male. He was dressed in hospital clothing. He was poorly kempt, and he was actually in restraints. His gait wasn't observed. He definitely had excessive psychomotor activity — he was, if anything, agitated… He was alert. And then he was non-cooperative. And what was also obvious was that he was experiencing a visual hallucination — so you would say someone is 'internally preoccupied', attending to some internal stimuli that's not actually obvious."

Two pieces of documentation vocabulary here appear nowhere on the slides: "internally preoccupied" and "attending to internal stimuli". Note also what she does with an unobservable item — "gait wasn't observed" is stated, not omitted or guessed.

On the second clip (Bradley Cooper ranting at 4 a.m.), her feedback is the examinable part: "That mental status would be suspicious, especially the fast speech. You might even call that pressured speech. It can be pretty hard to interrupt him. That's a cardinal symptom of mania." "Hard to interrupt" is the feature that upgrades fast speech to pressured speech. And why the MSE is written down at all: "you go see a case and then you're conveying that to your staff" — the MSE exists to transmit an abnormal picture to another clinician.

Two MSE polls (SLIDO)
Depression: "A 41-year-old woman presents with low mood, lack of energy, significant weight loss. She doesn't find joy in things and sits silently during the interview. She describes passive thoughts of death but denies intent. Which MSE finding is most likely to be observed?" Key: slowed speech — "in mania the speech tends to be really fast; in depression speech can often be slow. We call it speech latency: a long pause before giving a verbal response." Why grooming loses: "they may or may not be well groomed… it wouldn't be as good a feature of depression to narrow this down." Same construct and key as WFQ Q15, but a different stem (the WFQ vignette is a 36-year-old man).

Psychosis: "A 26-year-old man brought to clinic by his family for social withdrawal, delusions and poor hygiene. He avoids eye contact and shows minimal emotional reactivity. Which best describes his affect?" She accidentally said the answer while reading the stem — flat — then caught herself. Key teaching: flat is the quality, restricted is the range.

9 · Challenges in the interview (Kaplan & Sadock 12e)

(a) Personal questions (s44). Questions about your qualifications → answer directly ("I'm a C3" — a third-year resident). A sarcastic comment ("are you even old enough to be in medical school?") → address the underlying issue: "why are they asking me this? Do they think… they don't trust people?" then "Are you worried that I'm not going to be able to help you? Rest assured, I'm going to be reviewing things with the senior resident." A surface-level question ("Do you watch football?") → answer directly, but keep the self-disclosure limited — "I'm not going to tell them 'and then I went to this, I did this with my friends'" — and redirect. Not sure how to respond → "Let's keep this assessment about you… tell me again, how is your mood?"

The pattern across all four: answer briefly and factually, redirect, and treat a hostile question as data about the patient rather than an attack on you.

(b) Resistance (s45). "Although the patient comes for help, there may be forces that impede the movement to health." Definition: "Resistances are the processes, conscious or unconscious, that interfere with the therapeutic objectives of treatment." The patient may unconsciously avoid emotionally difficult or threatening material. Worked example: asked about past relationships, the patient says "I don't really see how that's relevant… You're just a student."

What to do about resistance — the process comment (transcript-only)
"It's a phenomenon that can happen, and you don't have to just roll with it." The named technique: "interesting — I notice you really don't want to talk about your relationships. What's going on there? That's called a process focus comment." The contrast she drew: a content question (trainee level) asks about the material — "How do you feel?", "What medications are you on?"; a process comment (experienced level) asks about what is happening in the interview itself — "I notice when I ask you this, you look down at the ground." She generalized it: "especially in psychiatry, but even in other domains of medicine."

(c) Transference (s46): "when the patient unconsciously transfers feelings and behavior from past relationships (often childhood) onto the clinician, who is usually an authority figure." The patient may be angry, demanding, or obsequious because of former relationships; identify transference to avoid misunderstanding the behaviour and reacting personally. Slide example: a middle-aged male patient, very deferential, repeatedly calling the student "doctor" despite correction, seeking constant reassurance, who mentions he never felt supported by his father. Her tell: "You'll get this funny feeling when transference is activated — you're like, what's going on here?"

(d) Countertransference (s47): "when the clinician unconsciously reacts to a patient based on their own history and the current interaction." Four common signs: feeling unusually angry, protective or emotional with a patient · dreading or overly looking forward to seeing someone · feeling bored, sleepy or distracted · acting out of character (too distant, too involved). Four management tips (s48): notice your reactions · reflect or debrief with a supervisor or peer · keep boundaries · use it as a learning tool. "Countertransference is normal. Being aware of it helps you be a better clinician."

Her own countertransference, given as a worked self-disclosure
"For me, a narcissistic patient — most of the time I feel pretty confident in my skills… When I'm doing an interview and I start to doubt myself — 'do I even know anything?' — oh yeah, it's a narcissistic patient. And that's based on probably my own childhood and my father. Whereas I have a colleague who gets just angry when there's a narcissistic patient."

The generalizable rule: "When you're reacting differently than usual, that's a clue about the dynamic that's happening with that patient." The signal is the deviation from your own baseline, not any particular emotion. Her one-line definition: "when something in the patient elicits a reaction from you that's not really about that patient, but maybe about your own story." Using it as a tool: "imagine how this is impacting all the people in his life. And he's telling me nobody likes him — now I know why."
Two polls on interview challenges
Resistance vs acting out: "During a therapy session, a 60-year-old woman suddenly becomes defensive when asked about her childhood and says 'that's none of your business'. She's previously been cooperative and calm." Key: resistance — "She's literally just resisting, shutting you down." Why acting out loses (a definition the slides never give): "acting out is kind of an old-school psychiatric term… she might not just stop things, but start distracting with something else, like maybe start singing." So resistance = blocking the material; acting out = discharging it into behaviour.

Countertransference: "A clinical clerk finds herself feeling unusually irritated with a patient who reminds her of her critical older sibling." Key: countertransference. Paired with WFQ Q16, which runs the mirror-image stem and keys transference: the discriminator is always whose past relationship is being imported. The WFQ key's four definitions are worth memorizing together — transference = patient → clinician from past relationships; countertransference = the clinician's own reaction; identification = loss of objectivity; therapeutic alliance = a collaborative clinical relationship.

10 · Diagnosis vs formulation

Diagnosis (s49) is a "structured classification based on established criteria (DSM-5 TR in North America)" that "assigns a disorder label… according to specific symptoms, duration, and severity" — but it "may not explain why those symptoms occur in that individual."

Formulation (s50, citing Cabaniss et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2015): a hypothesis that answers (1) Why has this patient fallen ill now? and (2) What should we do to help this patient? "Formulations should have a 'because' in them — they are ideas about causation." The one-line contrast from s58: diagnosis describes what; formulation explains why now.

Why it changes management — the two panic patients (transcript-only): "Someone with panic — that young guy with panic disorder we saw — versus a 70-year-old with panic disorder is very different. Even though they both meet criteria for the exact same condition, we may treat them really differently." For the 70-year-old, "it might be that she had a recent stroke… and the panic serves a purpose, to keep her on some level warned of future threat"; for the 20-year-old, "it might be all about social embarrassment and anxiety." The DSM label is identical and the treatment is not. Her framing: "Formulation is not a diagnosis. Someone has depression, but I want to know why."

11 · The 4 P's grid, and the worked case

The template (s51): columns Bio | Psycho | Social (with a small superscript "*cultural" above the Social column — cultural factors fold into Social), rows Predisposing | Precipitating | Perpetuating | Protective. The four P's, defined (s52, citing Racine et al. 2016):

  1. Predisposing — "areas of vulnerability that increase the risk for the presenting problem" (genetics, life events, temperament). Hers: "attachment insecurities… the ACEs."
  2. Precipitating — "the specific event or trigger to the onset of the current problem" (death of a loved one, abuse). Hers: "the stressor — a recent divorce, the car accident."
  3. Perpetuating — "those that maintain the problem once it has become established" (substance abuse, all-or-nothing thinking). Hers: "avoidance in panic disorder", which names the maintaining mechanism of the L1 case.
  4. Protective — "the strengths that reduce the severity of problems, counteract the first 3 P's, and promote healthy and adaptive functioning."

She back-referenced Lecture 1 explicitly: the three columns are "biological factors, psychological factors and social factors, which remember we went through in that diathesis–stress" — the 4 P's grid is the diathesis–stress model with time added.

Two citation and layout cautions. The cited Racine reference is titled "Predisposing, Precipitating, Perpetuating, and Present Factors", whereas the lecture's fourth P is Protective — the slide teaches Protective. And the template orders columns Bio–Psycho–Social while every filled-in worked example orders them Bio–Social–Psych; content is unaffected.

The case (s53): a 25-year-old male presenting to the outpatient clinic with depression × 3 months following a romantic relationship breakup. He grew up with a mother who had severe depression and was often hospitalized and unavailable as a parent; his parents divorced when he was 7. He has poorly controlled type I diabetes and cannot keep regular work because of frequent DKA and admissions. Past psych history: previous good response to fluoxetine at 16, stopped 6 months ago because of cost.

BioSocialPsych
PredisposingFHx depression · type I diabetesMother's depression, frequently in hospital / away from him · father left the family at 7 yo→ insecure attachment, difficulties with trust · → "I am not good enough"
PrecipitatingStopped antidepressant due to costGirlfriend cheated on him → breakup→ reactivates feelings of inadequacy and issues with trust
PerpetuatingPoor BG controlLow income · social isolationConflict of trust and self esteem
ProtectiveWilling to take medication, previously adherent, previous good response to SSRIGood healthcare teamPsychologically-minded, self-reflective
Two slide-authoring slips in this grid, resolved by the transcript — both versions on record.
(1) The mother's diagnosis. The Predisposing/Social cell reads "Mother MDD" on s55 and s56 but "Mother had SPMI" on the final slide s57. SPMI (severe and persistent mental illness) and MDD are not the same, and the vignette itself says only "severe depression". Presenting the case aloud she said "his mother had severe depression" and later "we know that his mother had depression" — she never said SPMI. Treat severe depression / MDD as the intended fact and SPMI as a slip.
(2) The Protective/Social cell. It reads "Good healthcare team" on s55 and s56 but "Good social supports, good healthcare team" on s57 — and "good social supports" sits awkwardly beside "social isolation" in the Perpetuating row of the same column. Narrating that cell she said only "but he does have a good healthcare team". Read "good social supports" as a second s57 slip.

Her cell-by-cell reasoning is what turns the table into a formulation:

  • Bio — "biologically he's predisposed to depression because of heritability. And type 1 diabetes itself is a risk factor for depression — there's an inflammatory model of depression, and diabetes is an inflammatory condition." That mechanism is transcript-only and is what connects the two Bio/Predisposing entries the slide merely lists side by side. Precipitating: stopping the antidepressant. Perpetuating: poor glycaemic control. Protective: willing, previously adherent, previously responsive.
  • Social — the discipline to notice: the same fact (mother's depression) is entered in Bio as heritability and in Social as absence, and she says which she is using in which column. "Parents divorced, mom was in hospital a bunch — he didn't have his secure base." Precipitating: "his girlfriend cheated on him. That wasn't in this stem" — which is why that cell appears to come from nowhere.
  • Psych — "often, if a child experiences a parent basically abandoning them, they'll have self-esteem issues, because on some level the child often blames themselves and thinks 'I wasn't enough to keep my dad around'." That is the explicit derivation of the "I am not good enough" cell. The breakup then reactivates those earlier challenges; ongoing trust and self-esteem issues perpetuate.

How to read the grid as a sentence: the arrows in the Psych column show the psychological factors are derived from the social ones in the same row — the mother's illness and the father's departure → insecure attachment and "I am not good enough" → which the girlfriend's infidelity reactivates. That causal chain, plus a "because", is what makes it a formulation rather than a list.

The plan that falls out of the formulation maps one-to-one onto the columns: "We've got to get better blood sugar control. Let's start Prozac again. You need to be in psychotherapy to work on your self-esteem." Bio → glycaemic control + restart the SSRI; Psych → psychotherapy for self-esteem; Social → the healthcare team and the isolation. Her contrast: "that's really different than just saying 'he's depressed, give him Prozac'." And the buy-in argument: delivering the formulation back to the patient "really actually gets someone to buy in."
Poll — placing a factor in the grid
Stem: "A 36-year-old woman with persistent low mood feels isolated and struggles to maintain close relationships. Her parents were emotionally unavailable. She recently lost her job. Which of the following is the most appropriate psychological predisposing factor?"
Her reasoning on the distractors is the whole item: "recent unemployment is precipitating; sleep disturbance is perpetuating; passive suicidal ideation is just a feature of her depression." The key is therefore the emotionally unavailable parents / the resulting insecure attachment — the only option that is both psychological and predisposing. Watch for a fourth option that is a symptom of the disorder rather than a factor at all.

12 · Discriminators and exam traps

  • Mood vs affect: mood is what the patient reports; affect is what you observe. Quality (euthymic/elevated/depressed/flat) vs range (broad/restricted) vs stability (fixed/labile) are three different axes.
  • Circumstantial vs tangential: circumstantial gets there eventually after excessive detail; tangential never gets there. Flight of ideas retains discernible connections; loose associations do not.
  • Hallucination vs illusion: a hallucination has no stimulus; an illusion is a distortion of a real one. Depersonalization = self unreal; derealisation = world unreal, both forms of dissociation.
  • Hallucination modality: auditory → schizophrenia; visual → delirium/medical; olfactory → temporal lobe epilepsy; tactile → alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.
  • Insight vs judgement are scored separately and can dissociate — poor insight with intact judgement is possible.
  • Fast speech vs pressured speech: "hard to interrupt" is the upgrade, and pressured speech is a cardinal manic sign. In depression, expect slowed speech / speech latency, not poor grooming, as the best single MSE finding.
  • Transference vs countertransference: whose past relationship is being imported — the patient's (transference) or the clinician's (countertransference)? Resistance vs acting out: blocking the material vs discharging it into behaviour.
  • Withdrawal lethality: CNS depressants (alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates) can kill — seizures, delirium tremens, death. Opioid withdrawal is miserable but not lethal.
  • Diagnosis vs formulation: a label names what; the 4 P's grid answers why now and generates the plan. Placement questions turn entirely on which cell of the 4 P's × bio/psycho/social grid a fact belongs in.
L2 key messages, verbatim (s58): the psychiatric interview is the cornerstone of assessment → safety, rapport, empathy; the MSE (ASEPTIC) is the mental "physical exam"; diagnosis describes what; formulation (4 P's — Predisposing, Precipitating, Perpetuating, Protective) explains why now; and the clinical goal is a person-centred, biopsychosocial understanding and plan of treatment.

guides.title: Week 40 · 11 Treatment of Psychiatric Disorders (Byrne, Lecture 3)
guides.html:
Lecture 3 · Byrne

Treatment of Psychiatric Disorders (Byrne, Lecture 3)

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Biological, psychological and social treatments in psychiatry, mirroring the formulation grid: the seven psychotropic classes and the monoamine systems, drugs by disorder, ECT and neurostimulation, CAM and psychedelics, psychodynamic therapy and defence mechanisms, CBT and cognitive distortions, the DBT skills, and social, cultural and spiritual interventions.

The third of Dr. Byrne's three Friday lectures is the treatment half of the week. It is built to mirror the formulation grid from Lecture 2 exactly: biological risk factors get biological treatments, psychological risk factors get psychological treatments, social risk factors get social, cultural and spiritual treatments. Her words: "It's the same structure." Everything below comes from the L3 slide deck and the lecture transcript; where the two disagree, both are carried.

Treatment categories mirror formulation categories one-for-one — hand a question a factor in one column and it can ask for the matching intervention in the same column.

1. The biopsychosocial treatment frame

Objectives [Byrne L3 s4]: describe the main classes of biological treatment (medications, neurostimulation, CAM, emerging psychedelic therapies); compare the major psychotherapy modalities (CBT, psychodynamic, third-wave); learn and practise selected psychotherapy skills — relaxation training, validation and cognitive restructuring; recognize the importance of social, spiritual and cultural factors.

Outline [Byrne L3 s5]: biological treatments → psychological treatments → social/spiritual/cultural components, drawn beside the same three-circle Venn used in L1 (Biological top, Social bottom-left, Psychological bottom-right), here with no central label.

What a psychiatrist's toolkit actually contains
"Psychiatry residency is a five-year program, and a year's worth of it is actually learning to be a psychotherapist." She prescribes medications and ECT, and also does trauma therapy, group therapy and runs weekly meditation groups on an inpatient unit. The framing she asked the class to take away: "your job as a doctor is largely to instil hope for people, and in psychiatry there's lots of things we can do that help people suffer less."

2. Biological treatments — the seven psychotropic classes

Definition [Byrne L3 s6]: "Psychotropic drugs: medications used to treat psychiatric disorders", "commonly described by their primary clinical application". The seven classes: antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, anxiolytics, hypnotics, cognitive enhancers, stimulants.

The crucial addition she made aloud is that the class names do not map one-to-one onto disorders — "commonly described by" is not "only used for".

ClassWhat it is actually used for (said aloud)
AntidepressantsDepression, "which are also used in anxiety"
AntipsychoticsPsychosis, "and also used in mood disorders"; also to boost antidepressants in depression (augmentation)
Mood stabilizersBipolar disorder
AnxiolyticsTo reduce anxiety
Hypnotics"An old-school term, but basically sedating medicines, which often will be used in [the] case of agitation"
Cognitive enhancersDementia
StimulantsADHD

Her context for the hypnotic/agitation use: the CAMH emergency room "gets half the police drop-offs in the city per night" — agitated people in the community, "someone posing a risk to the public because of their psychosis, or often crystal meth intoxication". On inpatient care: "Almost nobody on my unit [is] not on a psychotropic medication."

3. Monoamine systems — the anatomy slide of L3

The framing claim [Byrne L3 s7, citing Azizi, The Neuroscientist 2020]: "Monoamines are key neurotransmitters (serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine) involved in mood, cognition, and behavior, and many psychiatric medications work by modulating these systems."

The s7 figure. Panel A is a sagittal brain with three labelled functional regions, each arrowed down to a central oval marked "DA / 5HT / NE" sitting above "SC" (spinal cord): Executive Brain = frontal lobes, striatum; Limbic Brain = cingulate gyrus, hippocampus; Sensory Brain = parieto-temporo-occipital cortex. Panel B shows diffuse colour-gradient regions with curved arrows radiating from a central cluster — NE red, DA blue, 5-HT pink — the diffuse projection pattern.

The numbers and the two metaphors (transcript only)
Monoamine cell bodies sit in brainstem nuclei and receive input both from below (spinal cord) and from upper brain centres, then project everywhere. "You have about 100 billion neurons in your brain, but probably only a few million of them are monoamine neurons." Metaphor 1, switches: "they almost act like switches for neural networks." Metaphor 2, highways: "even though they don't occupy a lot of real estate, they spread everywhere — kind of like main highways." Exam-ready: a few million cells out of ~100 billion, arising in brainstem nuclei, projecting diffusely — which is why modulating them changes mood, cognition and behaviour at once, and why side-effect profiles are broad. She hedged twice: "this is over-generalized — these are so complex."
MonoamineFunctionsNucleus of originTargeted by
Serotonin (5-HT) [s8]Mood, anxiety, sleep, appetite, painRaphe nucleiSSRIs (e.g. fluoxetine), SNRIs (e.g. venlafaxine), TCAs
Norepinephrine (NE) [s9]Attention, arousal, mood, stressLocus coeruleusSNRIs, TCAs, bupropion, stimulants
Dopamine (DA) [s10]Reward, motivation, movement, psychosis(not stated on the slide)Antipsychotics, stimulants, bupropion

Dopamine — direction of dysfunction [Byrne L3 s10]: high DA = psychosis; low DA = amotivation, anhedonia. The four pathways ("meso" = midbrain):

  1. Mesolimbic — emotion/reward (midbrain to limbic system)
  2. Mesocortical — cognition/motivation (midbrain to cortex)
  3. Nigrostriatal — movement
  4. Tuberoinfundibular — prolactin regulation

Worked aloud: "someone who uses crystal meth, which is an amphetamine, rapidly increases their dopamine levels. If that gets high enough, they'll start to be paranoid, possibly hallucinate." In schizophrenia "it's not as simple as 'all your dopamine is high' — but there's too much dopamine in certain pathways", and antipsychotics generally drop dopamine. Conversely, depression and substance use disorders with low motivation and anhedonia "you could think about as a low dopamine state" — which is why bupropion sits under dopamine on s10. Psychosis and the dopamine pathways in detail are deferred to Dr. Albert Wong's schizophrenia lecture.

Two misspeaks on s8–s9, both corrected. (1) She expanded SNRI as "selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor"; the correct expansion is serotonin–norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (standard knowledge, not in the module) — the class hits both transporters, which is why it appears under both 5-HT and NE. (2) The caption has her saying NE is targeted by SSRIs; the slide says SNRIs, TCAs, bupropion and stimulants, and SSRIs are selective for serotonin (standard knowledge, not in the module). Follow the slide.

Chemical structures (image only, s8–s10): serotonin is an indole ring with a hydroxyl and an ethylamine side chain; norepinephrine is a catechol ring with a chiral carbon bearing an OH; dopamine is a catechol ring with a plain side chain and no side-chain OH — dopamine and norepinephrine differ only by that one beta-hydroxyl. Scope statement: "You don't need to memorize that chemical structure."

4. Medications by disorder (s11–s14)

IndicationClassNamed agents
DepressionSSRIsfluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram
SNRIsvenlafaxine, duloxetine
Othersbupropion, mirtazapine, TCAs, MAOIs
Bipolar disorderMood stabilizerslithium (mania, depression and suicide prevention); valproic acid (acute mania); carbamazepine / lamotrigine (lamotrigine more effective for bipolar depression)
Atypical antipsychoticsoften for acute episodes or maintenance
Anxiety disordersAntidepressantsSSRIs / SNRIs
Benzodiazepineslorazepam, clonazepam — short-term use only, dependence
Beta-blockerspropranolol — performance anxiety (physical symptoms)
Psychotic disordersFirst-generation (typical)haloperidol
Second-generation (atypical)risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine
Treatment-resistantclozapine
ADHDStimulantsmethylphenidate, amphetamine salts
Non-stimulantsatomoxetine, guanfacine, clonidine
Dementia / cognitiveCholinesterase inhibitorsdonepezil
NMDA receptor antagonistmemantine
Antipsychotics (cautiously)for agitation
Alcohol use disorderAnticravingnaltrexone, acamprosate
Opioid use disorderAgonist therapymethadone (full agonist), buprenorphine (partial agonist)

Names she attached aloud (none are on the slides): benzodiazepines "like Ativan, Xanax"; haloperidol "Haldol is the classic example"; second-generation = "atypical antipsychotics"; clozapine "a really powerful antipsychotic used with treatment-resistant schizophrenia"; methylphenidate = Ritalin; amphetamine salts = "Vyvanse, Adderall"; buprenorphine = Suboxone; fluoxetine = Prozac.

The one management item the slides omit entirely
Diazepam (Valium) cover for alcohol withdrawal, alongside thiamine — "you use Valium, diazepam, to help them withdraw safely". The s14 slide lists only the anticraving agents (naltrexone, acamprosate). Withdrawal management and craving management are two different problems, and only the second is printed.
Pairings most likely to be tested
lithium = the only agent listed for suicide prevention · lamotrigine = bipolar depression · valproic acid = acute mania · clozapine = treatment-resistant schizophrenia · propranolol = performance anxiety, physical symptoms · benzodiazepines = short-term only (dependence) · memantine = NMDA antagonist, donepezil = cholinesterase inhibitor · methadone full agonist vs buprenorphine partial agonist.

Scope statement on drug names: "You don't need to know them all, but if it's on there, I would say it's good to remember that fluoxetine is an antidepressant… in the questions there will be clues, like that this person has depression, they're on a medication." Read that as "you will be given clues, not asked to regurgitate" — not as "skip it".

5. Neurostimulation

Definition [Byrne L3 s15, Kaplan & Sadock 12e 2022]: "Brain stimulation → electrical currents or magnetic fields to alter neuronal firing."

  • Applied transcranially (outside the skull): ECT, transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), rTMS, magnetic seizure therapy.
  • Surgical techniques: cortical brain stimulation (CBS), deep brain stimulation (DBS), vagus nerve stimulation (VNS).
ECT, taught in detail — the largest lecturer-only block in L3
ECT = electroconvulsive therapy, an expansion given aloud and nowhere on the deck: "that's exactly as it sounds: you induce a seizure in a person." Positioning claim, and it is the testable one: "It's still our most effective antidepressant treatment… an incredible antidepressant treatment, life-saving." The procedure: an anaesthetist puts the patient to sleep; the psychiatrist applies electrodes to the outside of the head; the patient has a full grand mal seizure but is given muscle relaxants to reduce its impact; they are woken after a few minutes. The dosing schedule, a hard number on no slide: "you typically need somewhere between 8 to 12 seizures, spread three times a week, usually for a few weeks." Her worked case: a lawyer on her inpatient unit with nihilistic delusions — i.e. a psychotic depression — who failed multiple medications and is now responding to ECT.
Most effective is not first line. "ECT is still our most effective antidepressant treatment" sits alongside Key Message 2: "neurostimulation is reserved for resistant cases" [s34]. Both her worked case and the poll stem reach ECT only after multiple failed medications and therapies. In the WFQ, "recommend neurostimulation due to therapy failure" is the wrong answer because it is premature escalation.

DBS, described: "Sunnybrook is one of the big centres for DBS in the world." A neurosurgical procedure — an electrode is placed in the brain and connected to "a little pacemaker, the same as if you have a pacemaker for your heart, a little thing under the skin", for very treatment-resistant depression. The s15 video (a woman's DBS story, with the neurosurgeon interviewed) was not played, for time: "it's really not testable".

Source caution — the DBS target. She said the electrode goes "in the corpus callosum usually". The established target for DBS in treatment-resistant depression is the subcallosal cingulate (Brodmann area 25), the white matter below the genu of the corpus callosum, not the corpus callosum itself (standard knowledge, not in the module). Do not carry "corpus callosum" forward.
In-lecture poll — identifying ECT from the anaesthesia clue
Stem: a 63-year-old man with severe major depression who has not responded to multiple medications, psychotherapies or psychedelic therapy is preparing for a treatment that involves general anaesthesia. Keyed answer: ECT. Her reasoning, which is also the discriminator: "you can't imagine you would give a seizure to an awake person… [it could] not [be] deep brain stimulation — [DBS patients are] not quite asleep, because you don't have pain receptors on the surface of your brain." Exam-ready contrast: ECT requires general anaesthesia; DBS electrode placement can be done awake, because the brain has no pain receptors.

6. Complementary and alternative medicine (CAM)

  • Definition [s16]: "CAM encompasses non-conventional approaches used alongside (complementary) or instead of (alternative) standard psychiatric care."
  • 30–50% of psychiatric patients use CAM, often without informing clinicians.
  • "CAM aligns with holistic care principles, mind-body-spirit integration." She also placed it inside mainstream practice: CAM agents are "also in all of our guidelines".
CONFLICT — the CAM agents named aloud are not the ones printed. Slide (Key Message 4): omega-3s and chamomile [s34]. Transcript: "Omega-3 has pretty decent evidence for mild depression. Vitamin D for mild depression. Lavender has some evidence as well." Overlap is omega-3 only; chamomile is printed and was never said, vitamin D and lavender were said and are on no slide. If one agent must be chosen, omega-3 for mild depression is the one both sources support. Scope: "You don't need to know those, but you need to be aware that people take those and will ask you about them."

7. Psychedelics in psychiatry

Definition and mechanism [s17]: "Psychedelics → compounds that alter perception, cognition, and affect." Mechanism: 5-HT2A receptor agonism → disrupts default mode network (DMN) activity + increased neuroplasticity and BDNF expression. Compounds listed: psilocybin (magic mushrooms), LSD, DMT (e.g. in ayahuasca), mescaline (peyote), and MDMA and ketamine — "sometimes included, though pharmacologically distinct" (ketamine is an NMDA receptor antagonist, named aloud but not on the slide). She added ibogaine aloud. Indications under study, as she listed them: depression, PTSD, substance use disorders.

The default mode network, explained at length
"Your brain runs on different networks… you have about 8 to 12 different circuits." The DMN is "a loop of frontal structures all the way to lower structures"; its job is monitoring the internal state and "it is [supposed] to turn off in order to do a task". In depression the DMN becomes overactive — it doesn't shut off — and that is experienced as ruminations. What treatments do to it, ranked: SSRIs reduce DMN hyperactivity, ketamine also does, and psychedelics probably do it most intensively — "almost like a reboot… bringing in tons of neuroplasticity factors — brain-derived neurotrophic factor, for example, gets more expressed." Chain: 5-HT2A agonism → DMN hyperactivity (= rumination) disrupted → increased neuroplasticity and BDNF.
ConditionCompoundFinding
Major Depressive DisorderPsilocybin2 doses → rapid, sustained reduction in depression (NEJM 2021)
PTSDMDMA-assisted therapyPhase 3 RCT: 67% no longer meeting criteria at 2 months vs 32% placebo (Nature Med 2021)
End-of-life anxietyPsilocybinOne session → reduced existential distress for months (J Psychopharm 2016)
Alcohol use disorderPsilocybinPilot RCT: significant reduction in heavy drinking days (JAMA Psych 2022)

The slide closes with Carhart-Harris et al. 2017: "Psychedelics may act as a catalyst for psychotherapeutic processes rather than a standalone cure." Her gloss is the set and setting argument, and it is her stated segue into the psychotherapy half: "If you do mushrooms in a dark room with a bunch of scared people around you, it's unlikely to be therapeutic. You do mushrooms with a shaman in the rainforest — likely to be therapeutic. So it's the exact same substrate: how is that having a different effect?" Scope: "You don't need to know these studies."

Second in-lecture poll — which transmitters an antidepressant targets
Stem: a 29-year-old woman prescribed a medication for newly diagnosed major depressive disorder. Keyed answer: norepinephrine and serotonin. The lecture teaches three monoamines, but the antidepressant answer is the 5-HT/NE pair — dopamine is the antipsychotic/stimulant axis. The same item is WFQ Q19, where the losing option fails on glutamate, not on dopamine.

8. Psychotherapy — definition and validation

Norcross (1990), quoted in full on s19: "Informed and intentional application of clinical methods and interpersonal stances derived from established psychological principles for the purpose of assisting people to modify their behaviors, cognitions, emotions, and/or other personal characteristics in directions that the participants deem desirable." Two load-bearing phrases: "derived from established psychological principles" (it is not just talking) and "in directions that the participants deem desirable" (the patient defines the goal). Scope: "You don't need to memorize this definition" — the point was only that there are many types of psychotherapy, based on the model you use to understand psychological problems.

"If you don't know anything else about psychotherapy — if you don't know how to gain rapport with someone — just validate, validate, validate, validate, validate. You can do it until you can't. You can't overdo it." Validation is a central feature of psychotherapy [s20], and one of the three skills named in objective 3.

"It's Not About The Nail", the clip played in the room: a woman describes a relentless pressure she can "literally feel in my head" while a nail is visibly sticking out of her forehead. Her partner points out the nail; she answers "it is not about the nail… stop trying to fix it… what I really need is for you to just listen." He finally says "that sounds really hard", and she replies "It is. Thank you." Her commentary is the examinable principle: "what you think someone should do doesn't really matter. It has to come from within them… A very fundamental thing, before you can even move there, is to validate: to show someone that you understand they're suffering." This pairs with L2's empathy teaching — "at least…" is the anti-validation move; "that sounds really hard" is the validating one.

9. Psychodynamic psychotherapy and defence mechanisms

  • "Unconscious conflicts and early relationships shape current patterns."
  • Focus on self-awareness, emotional insight and the therapeutic relationship, with exploration of defences, transference, and repetition of past relational patterns.
  • "Less structured than CBT; short-term or long-term."
  • Useful for chronic mood disorders, personality disorders, and relational/interpersonal difficulties.
  • Slide example: "A patient who feels abandoned in relationships explores how early parental neglect contributes to intense fear of rejection in therapy."
  • Aloud: "kind of like the old-school Freudian type of psychotherapy — lie on the couch." The named lineage is Freud, Anna Freud and Carl Jung. Scope: "just that it's less structured, short term or long term."

Defence mechanisms in psychiatry [s22, image only]: "unconscious psychological strategies used to protect against anxiety, conflict, or distress."

DefenceDefinitionSlide exampleHer spoken example
DenialRefusing to accept realityPatient insists they don't have cancer despite clear medical evidence"nope, that's not true, I don't believe it"
ProjectionAttributing one's own thoughts/feelings to othersAccusing others of hostility when feeling hostile oneselfYou are angry, but say to your partner "why are you so angry at me?"
SublimationChanneling impulses into socially acceptable outletsAggression expressed through competitive sportsAngry about a breakup, so you go for a 10-mile run
DisplacementRedirecting emotions to a safer targetYelling at family after being criticized by bossMean staff on a rotation; you don't yell at them, you go home and ignore your dog
RegressionReverting to earlier developmental behaviourAdult throwing a tantrum under stress"Why am I acting like 12-year-old me?" at a family dinner
Four typographical errors on s22, reproduced because they could confuse. The heading for Displacement is printed "Displacemont"; Denial's example has "dont" (no apostrophe) and "ovidence" for evidence; Projection's definition reads "one's own own thoughts/feelings"; Sublimation's and Regression's examples each have an unclosed parenthesis. None change the meaning — know the correct spelling Displacement.
Source caution — humour. The caption has her introduce defences with "like humour being [an] immature defence mechanism". In the standard Vaillant hierarchy humour is a mature defence, alongside sublimation, altruism, anticipation and suppression (standard knowledge, not in the module). Do not carry "humour = immature" forward. Note also that the slide's five are a mix of levels (denial and projection primitive/immature; regression and displacement neurotic; sublimation mature), and the slide makes no attempt to rank them. Provenance, stated aloud: defences come from psychodynamic psychotherapy and Freud — "actually his daughter [Anna Freud] was the one who [founded] ego psychology" — and "there are dozens of defence mechanisms"; the slide's five are a selection.
Poll — recognizing psychodynamic therapy
Stem: a 37-year-old man starts therapy for persistent insecurity and conflict in relationships; the sessions focus on his childhood. Keyed answer: psychodynamic psychotherapy. The discriminator she stated: "CBT wouldn't be going back into childhood. That happens in psychodynamic." A therapy vignette is identified by what the sessions do, not by the diagnosis.

10. Cognitive Behaviour Therapy

  • Identify and challenge negative thought patterns ("automatic thoughts"), plus behavioural and relaxation training.
  • Homework, goal setting, and behavioural experiments.
  • Practical and time-limited.
  • Slide example: "A patient with panic attacks learns to recognize catastrophic thoughts ('I'm dying'), and tests them through interoceptive exposure" — the same plan as the L1 panic case.
  • The CBT triangle (s23 figure): Thoughts, Feelings and Behaviors joined by bidirectional arrows between each pair — changing behaviour changes thoughts, not only the reverse.
  • The one disorder–therapy pairing she stated flatly: "Panic disorder would be treated with CBT."

CBT leads to brain changes [s24, Arch Gen Psychiatry 2004;61(1):34–41]:

TreatmentIncreasesDecreases
CBTHippocampus and dorsal cingulate (BA 24)Dorsal (BA 9/46), ventral (BA 47/11) and medial (BA 9/10/11) frontal cortex
Paroxetine-facilitated recoveryPrefrontalHippocampal and subgenual cingulate

The two effective treatments produce opposite directional changes in the same regions. Scope statement: "You don't need to know these brain areas… psychotherapy is not fluffy. It really does actually change the brain." The examinable claim is psychotherapy produces measurable brain change, and the pattern differs from medication — not the Brodmann areas.

Cognitive distortions [s25, image only]. Cognitive restructuring — objective 3's third named skill — is identifying these in an automatic thought and testing them.

DistortionDefinitionExample
All or nothing thinking"Black and white thinking""If I'm not perfect I have failed" · "Either I do it right or not at all"
Over-generalizingA pattern from a single event, or overly broad conclusions"Everything is always rubbish" · "nothing good ever happens"
Mental filterOnly paying attention to certain types of evidenceNoticing our failures but not seeing our successes
Disqualifying the positiveDiscounting the good things that happened or that you did"That doesn't count"
Jumping to conclusionsTwo key types: Mind reading (imagining we know what others think) and Fortune telling (predicting the future)Mind reading: "none of these students like my lecture, because nobody talked to me after". Fortune telling: "I for sure failed my exam"
Magnification (catastrophising) & minimizationBlowing things out of proportion, or inappropriately shrinking something"If I fail my exam and get kicked out of medical school, then I'm not going to pay rent; if I don't pay rent, then I'm probably going to be homeless" — the chain is the giveaway

Why distortions form, a mechanism on no slide: "these are thinking tricks or patterns that happen often because you had some stress and you're trying to simplify reality to reduce anxiety — but in the long run it makes things worse." The intervention is noticing: "oh my, I do a lot of all-or-nothing thinking. This is not reality."

Poll — recognizing CBT
Stem: a 30-year-old woman in therapy for depression with thoughts like "I can't do anything right, I always mess things up"; her therapist tracks her thoughts and evaluates their accuracy using worksheets. Keyed answer: cognitive (CBT / cognitive restructuring). Pair with the psychodynamic poll: childhood focus → psychodynamic; worksheets and thought-testing → CBT.

11. The skills: physiological sigh, TIPP, body scan

The physiological sigh [s26]: "Two inhales through the nose followed by an extended exhale through the mouth." The slide's clip is Dr. Andrew Huberman, 00:43–4:40.

Why a slow exhale calms you — the chain, in order
1. Anxiety is "fight or flight mode — your sympathetic nervous system on overdrive." 2. You can come at it cognitively. 3. Or physically: "when you breathe out slowly, you reduce your intrathoracic pressure; you change the amount of blood flowing back into your heart. So a very slow exhale can reduce your heart rate and lower your blood pressure." 4. "Heart rate lower and blood pressure lower — it communicates up through your brainstem to your limbic system, your midbrain structures of emotion: everything's actually OK." 5. "And then your prefrontal cortex comes back online, so your cognitive techniques kick in." The order matters: the body settles first, then the thinking works.

The technique as taught live: it is called physiological because "when a little kid is upset… they do that double inhale" — something the body does naturally when calming down. Instruction, verbatim: "a really big inhale, followed by another inhale at the top, and then a really long slow exhale, [pursing] your lips to reduce the amount of air leaving your body." The two quantities: the biggest inhale you have taken all day with another sip of air in, and at least 10 seconds on the exhale — the only duration given anywhere for this technique. Who to teach it to: the young man with panic disorder from L1, or "a patient you meet in [the] emergency room who's nervous about going for [an] X-ray". She named box breathing as the alternative she was not teaching.

Safety warning, and it is the kind of detail exams like. "I teach this exercise in my meditation group pretty regularly, and I had a lady faint… when I do the physiological sigh three times, I drop my heart rate by like 15 or 20 beats per minute. And someone fainted because her blood pressure went so low. So it's actually very serious — buyer beware." Two numbers: ~15–20 bpm after three repetitions, and syncope is a real adverse effect. Practise it before an exam or a talk, not where fainting would matter.

Third-wave therapies (ACT, DBT)

Common features [s27]: focus on acceptance, mindfulness, and values-driven behaviour, and "emphasizes changing the relationship with thoughts" rather than changing the thoughts themselves — the contrast with classical CBT.

TherapyWhat it teachesNamed indication
DBT (Dialectical Behavior Therapy)Four skill modules: emotion regulation, distress tolerance, interpersonal effectiveness, mindfulness. Built from "dialectical philosophies, Buddhism, and behaviour therapy""Especially effective in borderline personality disorder"; also emotion-regulation problems generally
ACT (Acceptance & Commitment Therapy)Accept painful experiences while committing to actions aligned with personal values; "a lot of meditation and mindfulness in it"(none named)

The three waves placed in time, which the slide never does: "psychodynamic, which is old-school therapy; CBT, which is more traditional but sort of 80s, nineties type of therapy; then third-wave therapies are newer." Her cross-specialty instruction: "Whether you're on ortho or psychiatry, you might come across patients who are panicking or really dysregulated. You can teach them the physiological sigh… teaching someone a breathing technique right away will help them feel better."

TIPP — DBT crisis survival skills

Purpose [s28]: "reduce physical arousal" — "'tip' the body chemistry from sympathetic to parasympathetic state."

LetterSkillAs she taught it
TTemperatureIce pack on the back of the neck, splashing the face with cold water. Mechanism, transcript only: "we have a bradycardic diving reflex. When our temperature drops, our heart rate lowers" — and a low heart rate tells the limbic system you are OK
IIntense Exercise"You could get someone to do 10 jumping jacks"
PProgressive Muscle RelaxationTaught live as a 5-second countdown per muscle group
PPaced BreathingAnnotated on the slide "exhale > inhale" — the physiological sigh is the paced-breathing limb of TIPP

The unifying mechanism for the whole acronym: every letter drives heart rate down, and the low heart rate is the signal to the limbic system that the danger is over — the same chain as the physiological sigh. The diving reflex is the named physiological basis for the cold-water instruction and appears nowhere on the slide. Her PMR script: squeeze the fists tight (5, 4, 3, 2, 1, release) → shrug the shoulders (5, 4, 3, 2, 1, release) → straighten the legs or push the feet into the ground (5, 4, 3, 2, 1, release) → all three together (3, 2, 1, release). Set-up: eyes closed, a few deep breaths first.

Mindfulness — the body scan (s29)

The seven steps exist only in the slide's infographic, "HOW TO DO A BODY SCAN MEDITATION", a circular 7-step diagram:

  1. Find a quiet place and get comfortable
  2. Warm up with some deep breaths
  3. Slow down your thoughts
  4. Start at one end of your body
  5. Move to the next part of your body
  6. Be mindful in all parts of your body
  7. Begin to come back into the room

This is the relaxation training of objective 3, alongside the physiological sigh and PMR. She ran a live three-minute version whose rationale the slide does not give: "when we're distressed… we often live up here. We forget that we have bodies… if you ground yourself in your body, it's often very helpful for your brain and your mind to feel more relaxed." Her sequence was settle → set aside time → a feet-to-head sweep ending on sound → close, with two repeated instructions that are the actual technique: non-judgement/non-striving ("you're not trying to change it or shift it — just being here with what's here") and returning ("you will definitely get distracted… when that happens, just bring your attention back to your body").

The live script and the slide's infographic are not the same thing. The slide's zencare 7 steps run quiet place → deep breaths → slow thoughts → one end of the body → next part → all parts → back into the room; her spoken version is a feet-to-head sweep ending on sound. The slide's 7 steps are the examinable version, the transcript's is the usable one.

12. Social interventions

Framing [s30]: "Social determinants of health are strongly linked to psychiatric outcomes", with the verbatim quotation "Social interventions are not adjuncts but essential components of effective psychiatric care." (Compton & Shim, 2015). The figure is the social determinants of health wheel — five segments whose names appear nowhere in the slide text: Education Access and Quality · Health Care Access and Quality · Neighborhood and Built Environment · Social and Community Context · Economic Stability.

InterventionExamplesPurpose
Case ManagementAssertive Community Treatment (ACT), Intensive Case Management (ICM)Link treatment with practical support
Supportive HousingHousing First, rent subsidies, shelterSupport stable housing and recovery
Income SupportDisability benefits (e.g. ODSP), medical leaveAddress financial strain and basic needs
Peer SupportPeer mentors, lived experience programsBuild connection, hope, self-confidence
Two things about s31. The Supportive Housing row is printed "support stable housing nad recovery" — a typo for "and". And "ACT" here means Assertive Community Treatment, not the Acceptance & Commitment Therapy of s27 — the same abbreviation for two different things two slides apart. Scope statement: "You don't need to memorize those. I'd say just [know] the bolded section" — i.e. the four intervention categories, not the named programmes.
Poll — choosing a social intervention
Stem: a 62-year-old man with schizophrenia lives alone, is inconsistent with follow-ups, has missed his last two prescriptions and recently ran out of food and electricity. Keyed answer: assertive community treatment and housing support. The stem is built from three failure modes at once — inconsistent follow-up (case management/ACT), missed prescriptions (outreach, not clinic-based care), and lost food and utilities (income and housing support). The correct option brings the service to the patient, rather than asking the patient to come to the service.

13. Cultural and spiritual considerations

Cultural — three items [s32]:

  1. Explanatory models → ask "What do you think is happening?" Her compressed version: "not just assuming your mental model applies."
  2. Language barriers → use trained interpreters, not family.
  3. Social context → racism, migration stress and poverty can worsen illness.

This is WFQ Q17: the keyed answer is "explore his explanatory model of illness and book a follow up", because "understanding a patient's explanatory model builds trust and informs culturally sensitive care."

Spiritual [s33]. The screening question, verbatim: "Do you have spiritual or religious beliefs? Do they help you cope?" Positive effects → community support, meaning, lower suicide risk; negative effects → guilt, feeling punished, conflict with medical advice. Two worked treatment issues: fasting (Ramadan) → adjust medication timing, and diet (Halal/Kosher/vegetarian) → check pill ingredients. "First Nations, Inuit, and Métis patients may want traditional healing (Elders, ceremony, land-based practices) with or without Western care." The closing instruction, printed in bold blue italic: "Approach with cultural humility: be respectful, ask, and collaborate." Added aloud, a stronger claim than the slide makes: "having [a] religious affiliation is very protective for suicide", and the reason to ask at all — "a lot of people are religious [but] they don't think they should talk about it with their doctor."

14. Key messages (s34, verbatim) and the treatment recap

  1. Integrated Care: effective treatment requires biological, psychological, and social/cultural/spiritual approaches.
  2. Biological Treatments: most psychiatric medications target serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine systems; neurostimulation is reserved for resistant cases.
  3. Psychotherapy: approaches vary (psychodynamic, CBT, DBT/ACT) but all emphasize insight, skill-building, and validation.
  4. Emerging Therapies: CAM (e.g. omega-3s, chamomile) and psychedelic-assisted treatments show growing evidence.
  5. Social & Cultural Context: housing, income support, peer programs, cultural beliefs and spirituality strongly shape recovery outcomes.

Non-pharmacological biological treatments in one line: neurostimulation, transcranial (ECT, tDCS, rTMS, magnetic seizure therapy) and surgical (CBS, DBS, VNS), reserved for resistant cases · CAM used alongside or instead of standard care, 30–50% uptake · psychedelics acting via 5-HT2A agonism with DMN disruption and increased neuroplasticity/BDNF.

Psychological modalities in one table [cross-lecture recap, §7.4.4]:

ModalityCore ideaTechniquesNamed indications
PsychodynamicUnconscious conflicts and early relationships shape current patternsDefences, transference, repetition of past relational patterns; less structured than CBT, short- or long-termChronic mood disorders, personality disorders, relational difficulties
CBTAutomatic thoughts; thoughts, feelings and behaviours all influence each otherCognitive restructuring, behavioural experiments, homework and goal setting, relaxation training, in vivo and interoceptive exposure, the physiological sighPanic disorder (the L1 case: fluoxetine 20 mg po QAM plus CBT with exposures)
DBTAcceptance, mindfulness, changing the relationship with thoughtsFour modules plus TIPP crisis survival skillsBorderline personality disorder
ACTAccept painful experiences, commit to value-aligned action(none itemized)(none named)

Discriminators & exam traps

  • ECT vs DBS: ECT needs general anaesthesia (you cannot seize an awake patient); DBS placement can be done awake, because the brain has no pain receptors. An anaesthesia clue in a stem points to ECT.
  • Most effective vs first line: ECT is "still our most effective antidepressant treatment" and neurostimulation is reserved for resistant cases. Recommending it before adequate trials is premature escalation and is keyed wrong.
  • Antidepressant transmitters: the keyed pair is norepinephrine and serotonin, even though the lecture teaches three monoamines; dopamine is the antipsychotic/stimulant axis.
  • Therapy vignettes are identified by what the sessions do: childhood and early relationships → psychodynamic; thought records, worksheets and testing accuracy → CBT.
  • Two meanings of ACT two slides apart: Acceptance & Commitment Therapy (s27) vs Assertive Community Treatment (s31).
  • Anticraving is not withdrawal: naltrexone and acamprosate are on the slide for alcohol use disorder; diazepam (with thiamine) for withdrawal was added aloud only.
  • Bipolar pairings: lithium for mania, depression and suicide prevention; valproic acid for acute mania; lamotrigine for bipolar depression.
  • Dopamine pathway names: prolactin is tuberoinfundibular; movement is nigrostriatal; reward/emotion is mesolimbic; cognition/motivation is mesocortical.
  • Do not carry forward three misstatements: SNRI is serotonin–norepinephrine (not "selective norepinephrine"); the DBS depression target is the subcallosal cingulate, not the corpus callosum; humour is a mature defence.
  • Social interventions: the right answer brings the service to the patient (ACT, outreach, housing) rather than asking the patient to come to the service.
  • Interpreters, not family, for language barriers — the prohibition is explicit on the slide.
Biological, psychological and social treatments are the same three columns as the 4 P's formulation grid. Know the monoamine map (raphe/5-HT, locus coeruleus/NE, four dopamine pathways), the pairings that are unique (lithium–suicide, lamotrigine–bipolar depression, clozapine–treatment resistance, propranolol–performance anxiety), that ECT is the most effective antidepressant treatment but is reserved for resistant cases and requires anaesthesia, that psychodynamic looks backward and CBT tests thoughts, and that the skills — physiological sigh, TIPP, body scan — all work by dropping heart rate so the prefrontal cortex can come back online.

guides.title: Week 40 · 12 Week 40 Integrated Review: CBL 40 and WFQ Walkthrough
guides.html:
Integration · CBL · WFQ

Week 40 Integrated Review: CBL 40 and WFQ Walkthrough

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

CBL 40 (Stanley) question by question with Group 8's unvalidated draft and the cultural formulation grid, all 17 WFQ questions walked through against the official key, and Dr. Byrne's own statements about what is and isn't testable.

This guide pulls Week 40's three integrative pieces together: the CBL 40 case of Stanley (Part A), a question-by-question walkthrough of the Weekly Formative Quiz with the official key (Part B), and Dr. Byrne's own scope statements about what is and isn't testable (Part C). Nothing here is new content — every item points back to where the fact is taught, so use it as the last pass before the assessment rather than as a first read.

The WFQ is the only marked-style question set the week gives you, and the lecturer's scope statements tell you how those questions will be framed: you will be given clues, not asked to regurgitate lists.

Part A · CBL 40 — "Stanley", a refugee claimant with trauma

What exists and what doesn't. The folder holds two Word files only: the blank group-assignment template and Group 8's partially completed copy. The virtual-patient case narrative, the tutor guide, the Wednesday faculty-led session and any tutor feedback are not available. Everything below is (a) the official question set, verbatim, and (b) student draft answers that are not an answer key — a study group's first pass, to be checked against the faculty session. Every "case fact" about Stanley comes from Group 8's formulation and is unverified against the case itself.

A.1 The case, as far as the questions reveal it

Stanley is a refugee claimant with an upcoming refugee hearing. He has an "extremely traumatic past", seems closed off early in the encounter, discloses suicidal ideation at some point, and the supervisor is unsure whether he meets full criteria for PTSD or adjustment disorder — a psychiatry referral is suggested and medical causes are to be ruled out in the meantime. Question 5 (the DSM's historical treatment of homosexuality) and Group 8's formulation add that his persecution is related to his sexual orientation. The group's narrative supplies the remaining detail: severe interpersonal violence, the death of his mother during the attack, forced migration, loss of home and occupation, a shoulder injury from the attack, poor sleep, guilt and self-blame, fear of return, housing and financial insecurity, and a supportive cousin, employment and education on the protective side.

Submission rules: the group representative submits the group assignment to the Wednesday faculty tutor; every student submits the independent questions — Q1, Q5, Q9 and Q12 — by 8 am on the morning of the faculty-led session.

Stale numbering. The template heads the case "Virtual Patient Case 43 (Week 43)" although it is filed and assigned as the Week 40 CBL — and the pre-week reading's header says "Week 46". Read it as CBL 40 unless the tutor says otherwise.

A.2 The fifteen questions, one line each

#TypeQuestion (condensed)Group 8's draft — unvalidated
1IndependentWhat facts do you want about his refugee status?Support networks/resources; health coverage/OHIP
2GroupSpecial considerations for effective communication before meeting him?Language barrier; trauma-informed care; cultural differences — make no assumptions
3GroupWhat can you do when a patient seems closed off?Reassurance; confidentiality; a safe environment; body language; tone of voice; attitude
4GroupHow do you respond empathically once he opens up about trauma?Thank him for trusting you; acknowledge and validate; scripted responses (below)
5IndividualWhat has the DSM historically said about homosexuality, and how has that changed?"Used to be considered a disorder in the earlier DSM"
6GroupMost important next step when a patient reveals suicidal ideation, and the components of that assessment?Drivers; timing and what makes it better/worse; plan; certainty; level of hope
7GroupWhat is similar or different about history-taking with a refugee patient? What else would you ask?Still asking about symptoms the same way (full HPI)
8GroupHow are biological, psychological, social and cultural factors influencing his presentation? Fill the formulation chart.See the grid below
9IndividualPTSD or adjustment disorder — what investigations rule out other medical causes?Basic labs: CBC, TSH, etc.
10GroupWhat community and interdisciplinary supports exist for refugees and newcomers, including finances and housing? What goes in the hearing letter?Settlement agencies; refugee lawyer/legal aid; social work, Ontario Works, housing services; primary care and refugee clinics; LGBTQ+-affirming organizations; culturally appropriate mental health services. Letter part unanswered
11GroupWhat supports could help him, including within this session?Social community supports; the advocacy ladder and named organizations (typed here, but answering Q12)
12IndividualWhich GTA advocacy organizations work on equitable healthcare, housing and financial supports?Blank — see the list under Q11
13GroupHow do you make sense of his symptoms, and what are your next steps?Blank
14GroupDoes trauma go hand-in-hand with a DSM diagnosis — pros and cons of labelling?Blank
15GroupRegardless of diagnosis, how can trauma affect identity and relationships?Blank

The group's scripted empathic responses for Q4, worth having as models: "I'm very sorry. You went through something terrifying, and you lost your mother in the middle of it. Thank you for trusting me enough to tell me. How are you feeling talking about this now?" and "Is there anything you need from me right now before we continue?"

A.3 The formulation grid — four P's × four columns

The CBL's chart is the same 4-P grid taught in Byrne L2 (predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating, protective × biological, psychological, social) with a Cultural column added; the template marks the Psychological column "advanced and not expected of medical students". Group 8's entries, as drafted:

BiologicalPsychologicalSocialCultural
PredisposingNo clear biological vulnerability identifiedLongstanding fear associated with concealing his sexualityLongstanding threat of discovery or persecution related to same-sex relationshipsSevere stigma and criminalization related to sexual orientation in his environment
PrecipitatingShoulder injury and pain following the attackGrief after his mother's death; guilt and self-blame; fear of returnViolent attack; forced migration; loss of home and occupation; upcoming refugee hearingPersecution related to sexual orientation; displacement from familiar community and culture
PerpetuatingPoor sleep; persistent shoulder painTrauma reminders; guilt and self-blame; anticipatory fear about returnHousing instability; financial insecurity; occupational disruption; limited supports; ongoing legal uncertaintyPossible isolation from community because of sexuality; navigating unfamiliar systems; discrimination and stigma
ProtectiveNo significant medical comorbidity or substance-use concerns identifiedFuture orientation; help-seeking; perseverance; capacity to work and planSupportive cousin; employment; education and occupational skills; connection with healthcareOpportunity to access LGBTQ+-affirming communities and greater legal protection in Canada
Column assignment is ambiguous in the source. Group 8 typed their answers as a run-on list under the four headings; the table above follows the order in which they listed them. Confirm against the group's submitted chart before relying on any single cell.

The group's formulation narrative models the "because" that a formulation must contain: Stanley experienced severe interpersonal violence, the death of his mother and forced migration in the context of persecution related to his sexual orientation; his distress is occurring while he faces uncertainty about whether he can remain in Canada, which makes the threat of return feel immediate; poor sleep, pain, trauma reminders, guilt, unstable housing, financial insecurity and limited supports may be perpetuating his symptoms; and he has substantial strengths — education, employment, help-seeking, future orientation and his cousin.

A.4 Where each answer is taught

CBL questionTaught in
Q2–Q4, Q7 — interview technique, empathy, the closed-off patientThe ICE CS2 guide (road map, the "how" of the interview, the process checklist); Byrne L2 on rapport and the MSE
Q5 — DSM historyPW03 History of Psychiatry (the DSM paradigm shift; Evelyn Hooker); Byrne L1 on DSM categories
Q6 — suicidal ideationPD Module 5 (self-harm vs suicide, assessment); the CS2 guide's risk block and suicide ladder
Q8 — formulationByrne L2's 4 P's × bio/psycho/social worked example
Q9, Q13 — PTSD vs adjustment disorder; medical causesWeek 41's trauma- and stressor-related material, and mental disorders due to another medical condition
Q14–Q15 — diagnosis vs labelling; trauma and identityByrne L1 on stigma and what a diagnosis is for; Week 41 ethics
What the draft is missing — expect the tutor to add it
On Q6 the group's answer omits intent, means and access, past attempts, protective factors and safety planning — the CS2 suicide ladder covers all of them. On Q5 the fuller answer is that homosexuality was a disorder in DSM-I and DSM-II, removed by APA vote in 1973, replaced by "sexual orientation disturbance" and then "ego-dystonic homosexuality" in DSM-III, which was dropped in DSM-III-R; Hooker's 1950s projective-test study of 30 gay men against matched controls found no difference. Q10's hearing-letter component and Q12–Q15 are unanswered.

Part B · The Psych I WFQ, question by question

Counting caution. Both the quiz and the key are headed "# of Questions: 22", but only 17 are printed: numbering starts at Question 4 and skips 7 and 8. Questions 1, 2, 3, 7 and 8 appear in neither PDF — verified page by page — so their topics are unknown. The numbers below are reproduced exactly as printed.

Q4 · Military psychiatry in the world wars — keyed C

Which statement is true about the work of military psychiatrists during the two world wars? Keyed: they used hypnosis as one of their interventions. The key: military psychiatrists employed treatments such as hypnosis for "shell shock"; their primary role was rapid return-to-duty, not improving long-term quality of life, and they did not fully connect hysteria and shell shock. Source: the pre-week history-of-psychiatry self-study, slide 13 — shell shock first described by Dr. Charles Myers, the repressed-sexual-fantasy explanation "quickly thrown out", Menninger and colleagues developing talk therapy and hypnosis, and psychiatrists becoming crucial to military systems in order to return soldiers to the battlefield as soon as possible.

Source typo: option D reads "were able ot make a connection", and the answer key mislabels the fourth option "A." while its rationale calls it "(D)".

Q5 · The DSM paradigm shift — keyed C

Which edition of the DSM is widely considered a paradigm shift in the history of psychiatric nosology? Keyed: DSM-III. The key: DSM-III (1980) introduced operationalized criteria and an atheoretical, descriptive approach; DSM-I and II were narrative, and DSM-IV was an update rather than a paradigm shift. Source: pre-week history-of-psychiatry self-study.

Q6 · Degeneration — keyed C

Degeneration is based on which one of the following assumptions? Keyed: some humans have traits that make them less suitable for modern society. The key: degeneration theory posited inherited defects making individuals "unfit" for contemporary society; options A and B describe evolution more accurately, and "mental illness is a treatable condition" contradicts degenerationist thinking — which ended in therapeutic nihilism. Source: the self-study module's "Degeneration and the Lunatic Asylum", with eugenics flagged as a background force.

Q9 · BPD, overdose and the request to admit — keyed C

A 24-year-old woman with BPD presents after acetaminophen overdose; after medical stabilization the ER physician asks you to admit her. Keyed: assess the patient's current mental state in terms of suicidality. The key: after medical stabilization, psychiatric assessment must determine current risk and mental state — automatically admitting, discharging, or dismissing admission needs are all inappropriate without assessment. Source: PD Module 5 (self-harm and risk assessment) plus the CS2 guide's risk block.

Option A is a half-truth trap. The teaching point that many patients with chronic fluctuating suicidal ideation do not benefit from admission is real — stating it before assessing is the error. The key's exact phrase is "inappropriate without assessment".

Q10 · Idealization and devaluation — keyed C

A 28-year-old woman with BPD calls her boyfriend the "best person in the world" at times and "the worst person ever" at others. Which diagnostic criterion is she struggling with? Keyed: unstable relationship. The key: extreme fluctuations in the perception of others characterize the unstable and intense relationships criterion; anger outbursts, unstable self-image and mood instability are other genuine criteria that do not match this vignette. The discriminator is whose stability is fluctuating — another person's, not her own self-image or mood. Source: PD Module 3, interpersonal domain.

Q11 · Which symptom list is BPD? — keyed A

Keyed list, the nine features as printed: affective instability · suicidal behaviour · inappropriate anger · relationship instability · unstable sense of self · fears of abandonment · impulsivity · dissociation/paranoia · feelings of emptiness, threshold ≥ 5 of 9. The key: options B–D mix in traits from other disorders (histrionic, narcissistic, antisocial). The intruders, by the key's own generic attribution: shallow expression of emotions and considers relationships more intimate than they are → histrionic; often envious of others and interpersonal exploitation → narcissistic; reckless disregard for safety and irritability and aggressiveness → antisocial. Source: PD Module 3 (nine criteria across four domains — affect 3, behaviour 2, cognition 2, interpersonal 2) with Module 1 supplying the other cluster-B disorders.

Q12 · What makes symptoms a disorder? — keyed B

A 30-year-old woman with six weeks of sadness, insomnia and poor concentration after a layoff, hopeless even before it, struggling at work and in relationships, with intermittent suicidal thoughts. Keyed: her low mood affects her interpersonal functioning. The key: mental disorders involve clinically significant disturbance with functional impairment, and this is the key distinguishing feature from a normal emotional response. Implied discriminator: a precipitating stressor, a comorbid history and duration do not by themselves establish disorder. Source: Byrne L1's definition of mental disorder; the CS2 guide's severity/impact items.

Q13 · Four of nine criteria — keyed C

A 28-year-old man with low mood, poor appetite and amotivation, significantly impaired at work and socially, meets only 4 of 9 DSM criteria, so MDE is not diagnosed. Keyed: arbitrary cutoffs can exclude clinically significant cases. The key: the categorical approach can miss meaningful distress and impairment when the symptom count falls just below threshold. The distractors invert reality — it is categorical, not dimensional, systems that are rigid; categorical systems do define symptom clusters; and comorbidity is common. Source: Byrne L1 slide 29, "Limitations of Categorical Systems", whose first bullet is literally "4/9 sx ≠ MDE, but 5/9 does"; the four limitations are arbitrary thresholds, comorbidity, heterogeneity, subthreshold illness.

Q14 · Evolutionary psychology and anxiety — keyed C

A 22-year-old student with persistent anxiety and worry about deadlines asks why he feels this way when nothing bad is happening. Keyed: they were once adaptive in ancestral environments. The key: traits like anxiety were once beneficial for survival by helping individuals avoid danger; modern stressors activate the same systems even when physical threats are absent, and anxiety disorders result when the response becomes dysregulated. Source: Byrne L1 slide 32, whose framing question is "Why would the brain evolve to be vulnerable to mental illness?"

Q15 · MSE findings in depression — keyed C

A 36-year-old man, "really sad" for two months, cannot get out of bed, has stopped working and playing guitar, has no appetite, and thinks his family would be better off without him. Keyed: slowed speech. The key: depressive symptoms are often reflected in the MSE as poor eye contact, psychomotor slowing and reduced speech quantity.
