Distractors: broad affect is the opposite of the expected restricted or blunted affect; grandiose delusions belong to mania or psychosis (and delusions in depression would be expected to be mood congruent — nihilistic, somatic, guilty); intact concentration contradicts the concentration impairment typical of depression. Source: Byrne L2 on the MSE, and the CS2 guide's own mania-vs-depression contrast (pressured speech, distractibility, affect lability vs dysphoric, delayed thought processing, poverty of speech).

Q16 · Transference — keyed C

A clerk's patient with a severe depressive episode becomes unusually deferential and repeatedly seeks reassurance, later revealing past abandonment by paternal figures. Keyed: transference. The four-term set, worth memorizing together: transference = the patient unconsciously redirects feelings from past relationships onto the clinician · countertransference = the clinician's own reaction · identification = loss of objectivity · therapeutic alliance = a collaborative clinical relationship. Source: Byrne L2 slide 46, whose worked example this vignette reproduces; countertransference is slides 47–48.

The lecture's example patient is a middle-aged male who repeatedly calls the student "doctor"; the WFQ vignette is a 58-year-old female. Same construct, changed demographics — do not treat the patient's sex as diagnostic.

Q17 · Cultural engagement and the explanatory model — keyed A

A 23-year-old refugee with hypervigilance, nightmares and avoidance, hesitant about Western psychiatric care, believes his distress is due to ancestral spirits. Keyed: explore his explanatory model of illness and book a follow-up. The key's entire rationale is one sentence: understanding a patient's explanatory model builds trust and informs culturally sensitive care. It gives no explanation at all for B, C or D — though B, "challenge his cultural beliefs", is the direct opposite of exploring the explanatory model. Source: Byrne L3's "Cultural Considerations" — explanatory models ("What do you think is happening?"), trained interpreters rather than family, and social context (racism, migration stress, poverty) worsening illness. The CS2 equivalent is history item 3, "elicit the patient's opinion about the nature and the cause of the problem(s)".

Q18 · Medication hesitancy — keyed D

A 36-year-old woman with low mood, anhedonia and early morning awakening, three months of psychotherapy with minimal improvement, hesitant about medication because of side effects. Keyed: explore concerns about pharmacologic options. The key: when patients express medication hesitancy, explore their concerns and provide information — this supports shared decision-making rather than coercion or premature escalation to neurostimulation or inpatient care. Source: Byrne L3's treatment objectives; the CS2 parallel is "elicit the hopes for or expectations of treatment" and the requirement that a plan be feasible.

Q19 · Antidepressant neurotransmitters — keyed C

A 35-year-old man started on medication for moderate MDD; which neurotransmitters are most likely affected? Keyed: norepinephrine and serotonin. The key: most first-line antidepressants target serotonin and/or norepinephrine, monoamines associated with mood regulation; the other options name transmitters not typically involved in standard antidepressant mechanisms. Source: Byrne L3 slide 7 on monoamine systems; slide 6 lists the psychotropic classes.

Read the distractor carefully. The lecture names three monoamines — serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine — while the key marks "dopamine and glutamate" wrong. The discriminator in that option is glutamate, not dopamine.

Q20 · Prevalence in adolescence — keyed D

A parent asks how common mental health disorders are in a 13-year-old. Keyed: 20%. The key: population data suggest 1 in 5 youth meet criteria for a mental health disorder, including anxiety, ADHD and depression, and knowing this guides screening and destigmatization. No Week 40 source states this figure — it appears only in the answer key, and child psychiatry is a Week 42 topic. The adult figures actually taught this week are: about 50% of the population by age 40, and suicide accounting for 24% of deaths at ages 15–24 and 16% at ages 25–44.

Q21 · Commonest child/adolescent diagnosis — keyed C

Keyed: anxiety disorder. The key: anxiety disorders are the most prevalent among children and teens, often go unrecognized, can worsen without treatment, and early intervention improves outcomes. Like Q20, this is key-only content — no Week 40 source ranks childhood diagnoses by prevalence.

Q22 · Temperament — keyed B

Which best describes temperament? Keyed: innate traits influencing early interaction with the world. The key: temperament is present from infancy and biologically based, influences behaviour, is foundational to personality, and is distinct from learned behaviour and from attachment. The distractors decoded: "a stable pattern of behaviour developed through experience" = learned behaviour / character; "enduring traits that deviate from social norms" = a personality disorder; "emotional bond formed with a caregiver" = attachment. Source: Byrne L1 on inherited temperamental traits alongside attachment theory; Byrne L2 lists temperament as a predisposing factor; the CS2 template asks about temperament in the early-childhood block.

B.1 The topic map and answer string

Answer string for self-testing: 4 C · 5 C · 6 C · 9 C · 10 C · 11 A · 12 B · 13 C · 14 C · 15 C · 16 C · 17 A · 18 D · 19 C · 20 D · 21 C · 22 B.

Eleven of the seventeen keys are C. Do not read anything into that — it is a quirk of this quiz, not a strategy, and the exam will not share it.

Part C · What is and isn't testable — the lecturer's scope statements

Everything Dr. Byrne said about testability in the three transcripts, which is the highest-value triage material in the week.

MaterialWhat she said
Intro to nosology module"You do not need to open that… There's no MCQ questions from it." She had asked for it to be removed and the site was not updated in time
History of psychiatry module"Should look at. There might be a question from it. It's kind of interesting. It's not super heavy."
PW01 Introduction to Psychiatry"It's like 2 pages. It's very general. There's nothing to memorize there."
Dermatomes/myotomes; brain and imagingNot hers — "obviously dermatomes is not my realm"; "brain and imaging, that's neuro, so I won't comment". Extending this to the brain-development module is an inference, not a quote
PD modules 07–11"Please do look at those" — they are the pre-reads for the personality-disorders workshop, and "if you haven't looked at these things, it's going to be a total waste of time"
The CBL"You don't need to prepare for that… just show up and just do your best"
Resources for additional learning slideOptional enrichment; the slide is labelled not examinable
DSM-5 category table (L1 s21)"These are the main categories. So this would be good to be familiar with"
Panic disorder criteria (L1 s23)"You don't need to memorize this" — shown to convey what the DSM looks like
The whole L2 interview deck"The slides are heavy and you don't need to memorize all of this right now" — reviewed in the interviewing seminar
The 15-heading interview outline (L2 s12)"You don't need to memorize this… this can be for your reference"
MSIGECAPS / GST PAID and the ROS screens"You're going to have all these memorized by the time you finish clerkship"
Monoamine chemical structures"You don't need to memorize that chemical structure"
Drug names"You don't need to know them all, but… it's good to remember that fluoxetine is an antidepressant… in the questions there will be clues"
Neurostimulation detail; the DBS video"You don't need all of these details"; the video is "really not testable"
CAM agents"You don't need to know those, but you need to be aware that people take those and will ask you about them"
The psychedelics evidence table"You don't need to know these studies. I just wanted to show you what they are helping with"
The Norcross psychotherapy definition; psychodynamic detailNot to be memorized — for psychodynamic, "just that it's less structured, short term or long term"
The CBT neuroimaging slide"You don't need to know these brain areas… just to demonstrate that psychotherapy also changes the brain"
Social interventions table"You don't need to memorize those. I'd say just [know] the bolded section"
Read the "don't memorize" lines carefully. Every one of them is about rote recall of the slide as printed; none says the concept is off the exam. The WFQ keys for this very week test the panic threshold, the MSE vocabulary, the monoamine targets and the 4 P's despite the disclaimers. Treat "you don't need to memorize" as "you will be given clues, not asked to regurgitate" — not as "skip it".

Explicitly deferred elsewhere: depression and mood disorders in detail → next week's mood lecture; schizophrenia, psychosis and the dopamine pathways → Dr. Albert Wong's lecture; brain anatomy underlying monoamine projections → the concurrent neuroanatomy teaching; interviewing technique, the full interview and MSE → the interviewing seminar (which is exactly what ICE CS2 is); DBT and borderline personality disorder → the self-learning modules and the workshop; validation as a skill → its own workshop; specific treatments by disorder → the individual disorder lectures.

Block structure, as stated aloud: four weeks of psychiatry in second year, with Weeks 1 and 2 compressed; the remaining order is mood and anxiety disorders → psychosis, child psych, personality disorders → addiction and substance use. And her framing: "You're not going to learn all of psychiatry in the next three weeks."

Discriminators and exam traps across the week

  • Suicidal ideation disclosed → direct risk assessment first, not a referral, not an admission decision, and never a statement about what patients with BPD do or don't benefit from.
  • Functional impairment is what converts symptoms into a disorder — not the stressor, not the duration, not a comorbid history.
  • 4 of 9 is not an MDE and 5 of 9 is — the textbook illustration of an arbitrary categorical threshold, and the first of four listed limitations.
  • Idealization and devaluation are about others, so they score the unstable-relationships criterion, not unstable self-image.
  • Explore the explanatory model; never challenge the belief. And use trained interpreters, not family.
  • Medication hesitancy is an invitation to explore, not to escalate.
  • Q20 and Q21 have no Week 40 source — know the two numbers (1 in 5; anxiety commonest) as key-only facts.
  • The CBL's Group 8 answers are unvalidated student work. Use them as a scaffold, and expect the tutor to add intent, means, past attempts, protective factors and safety to Q6.
Two integrative habits carry the whole week: assess before you decide (risk before disposition, medical causes before a psychiatric label), and explain before you diagnose — the formulation's "because", not just the DSM's "what".

guides.html:
Night-Before High-Yield

Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite
★ Do-not-miss · first-step reflexes
Suicidal ideation disclosed → direct risk assessment now — ideation, method, means, intent, past attempts, protective factors. Never refer or dispose first.
Overdose or self-harm, medically cleared → assess current mental state and suicidality before admitting, discharging, or declaring that admission won't help.
Self-harm ≠ suicide → deliberate self-harm is tissue damage without suicidal intent, but 1-year suicide risk after self-harm is 37× — believe the stated intent and assess.
Delusions plus confusion → move UP the diagnostic hierarchy: physical or drug-induced cause, not primary psychosis. Always ask about substances and symptoms when abstinent.
MDE needs 5 of 9 in one 2-week period, gated on depressed mood or anhedonia — 4 of 9 is not an MDE, and that gap is the arbitrary-threshold trap, not a reason to withhold care.
Open NTD → 1:1000 pregnancies; risk factors family history, diabetes, obesity, anticonvulsants; most idiopathic; folic acid supplementation reduces risk [as stated in DevBrain].
Imaging safety → iodinated contrast: allergy, contrast-induced nephropathy (renal insufficiency the key risk factor), fluid overload. Gadolinium: nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in renal failure. MR images vessels with no contrast at all.
Nosology module is not testable — the lecturer removed it and stated there are no MCQ questions from it. Do not spend time there.

History of psychiatry & the DSM PW03 · WFQ

DSM-III (1980) Paradigm shift: operationalized criteria, atheoretical and descriptive
DSM-I and DSM-II Narrative, not criterion-based
DSM-IV An update, not a paradigm shift
DSM-III's three rules Distress/impairment; validated checklist; reliably identifiable only
Degeneration theory Inherited defects make people "unfit" for modern society
Degeneration's endpoint Therapeutic nihilism — no role for treatment
Shell shock, first described by Dr. Charles Myers, WW1
Military psychiatry's aim Rapid return to duty, not quality of life
Shell shock treatments Talk therapy and hypnosis (Menninger and colleagues)
Why the hysteria explanation collapsed Male soldiers presented with a "feminine" disease
Evelyn Hooker, early 1950s 30 gay men vs 30 matched controls — no difference
Inter-rater reliability before DSM-III As low as 30%
Only 1930s somatic therapy that survived ECT — built for psychosis, best for mood

Localization — dermatomes and myotomes PW02 · NeuroPrimer

Which list wins on assessments The PW02 handout, over any textbook
The localization method Intersection of the weak muscles' root lists
Biceps (C5,C6) + pronator teres (C6,C7) weak C6
Triceps Predominantly C7
C5 · C6 · C7 sensory points Lateral upper arm · thumb · middle finger
C8 · T1 sensory points Little finger · medial arm
L3 · L4 · L5 · S1 sensory points Medial knee · medial malleolus · dorsum of foot · lateral foot
Ankle inversion and eversion Both labelled L5 in this course's figure
Reflex roots Biceps C5–C6, triceps C7, knee L3–L4, ankle S1
Cauda equina syndrome Back pain + saddle anaesthesia + bladder/bowel dysfunction — surgical emergency

Imaging — CT and MR basics SLM02

Attenuation rule High density → high attenuation → white
Density order Lead > bone > muscle > water > fat > air
Hounsfield anchors Air −1000, fat −60 to −100, water 0, bone +400 to +1000
Grey vs white matter on CT Grey (80 HU) brighter than white (50 HU)
Grey vs white matter on T1 White brighter than grey — the relationship flips
Dark CSF · bright CSF T1 · T2
FLAIR T2 with CSF suppressed — periventricular lesions, oedema, demyelination
Most pathology on T1 and T2 Dark on T1, bright on T2
Restricted diffusion Low ADC, bright DWI — usually acute ischaemia
GRE/SWI finds Haemorrhage and calcification — both dark
Multiple black dots on GRE Cerebral amyloid angiopathy
Enhancement means Blood–brain barrier broken — tumour, infection, inflammation
Sequences you must request by name MRA and MRV
CT vs MR CT urgent, bone, acute blood, trauma; MR parenchyma and subtle lesions

Development of the brain SLM06

CNS vs PNS origin CNS neural tube only; PNS neural tube plus neural crest
Primary neurulation Ectoderm, by folding
Secondary neurulation Mesoderm of the primitive streak remnant, by cavitation
Inducer and product Notochord induces ectoderm → neural plate
Neuropore closure Rostral ~25 days, caudal ~28 days — the 4th week
Rostral failure · caudal failure Anencephaly · myeloschisis
Open NTDs 1:1000; family history, diabetes, obesity, anticonvulsants; folic acid reduces risk
Three zones, inside out Ventricular → ependyma; intermediate → grey; marginal → white
Alar vs basal Alar dorsal sensory; basal ventral motor; sulcus limitans divides
Pontine flexure consequence Everts alar plates — sensory lateral, motor medial
Only vesicle with two derivatives Metencephalon → pons and cerebellum
Chiari II chain Open NTD → foramen magnum herniation → hydrocephalus → shunt
Radial glia Guide neurons outward to build cortex — grey outside
Migration disorders Band heterotopia = DCX; periventricular nodular = FLNA

Personality disorders & clusters SLM07–11

Trait becomes disorder when It causes distress or functional impairment
General criterion A ≥ 2 of 4: cognition, affectivity, interpersonal, impulse control
Antisocial PD's unique requirement Age ≥ 18 plus conduct disorder before age 15
Psychopathy Not a DSM diagnosis — identified by the Hare PCL-R
Cluster A mapping Schizotypal ≈ positive, schizoid ≈ negative, paranoid ≈ paranoia
Schizoid vs avoidant Schizoid doesn't want relationships; avoidant wants but fears rejection
Schizotypal vs avoidant anxiety Schizotypal anxiety is paranoid and doesn't fade with familiarity
OCPD vs OCD OCPD ego-syntonic, no true obsessions or compulsions
Lowest threshold Antisocial, 3 of 7
5-of-9 disorders Schizotypal, narcissistic, borderline
Temperament Innate, biologically based, foundational to personality

Borderline personality disorder SLM08–10 · WFQ

Threshold 5 of 9 → 256 possible combinations
The nine, in short Affective instability, suicidality, anger, relationships, self-image, abandonment, impulsivity, dissociation/paranoia, emptiness
Idealization and devaluation The unstable-relationships criterion — about others, not self
Criterion 4 trap Impulsivity needs ≥ 2 areas and excludes self-harm
Criterion 7 Transient stress-related paranoia or dissociation — not a psychotic disorder
Epidemiology string 2–6% / 6% / 10% / 20% — population, primary care, outpatient, inpatient
Lifetime completed suicide 8–10%; about three quarters self-harm
Biosocial theory Emotionally sensitive temperament × invalidating environment
The temperament's three features Low threshold, high intensity, slow return to baseline
Childhood sexual abuse 10–20% general population vs 40–70% inpatient BPD
Medication for BPD None treats it; psychotherapy first line, polypharmacy the classic error
DBT in numbers 6–12 months, 1 h individual + 2 h group, ~75% response
DBT's fourth mode Phone coaching — not family therapy

Self-harm and risk SLM11 · CS2

Deliberate self-harm defined Tissue damage without suicidal intent
Suicide rate after self-harm 439.1 vs 11.8 per 100,000 person-years — 37×
Self-harm alone Never establishes BPD
First step on disclosure Direct risk assessment, before any disposition decision
Screen order Ideation → method → means → intent → past attempts
Then classify Acute vs chronic; active vs passive; then protective factors
Six risk headings (history) Suicide, other self-harm, violence, inability to self-care, self-neglect, dependents
Four risk items (case-report form) Self-harm or suicide, self-neglect, neglect of dependents, aggression
Template's forgotten risks Safe driving and cooking; dependents
Means restriction 1–2 week prescriptions; firearms locked, ammunition separate
Avoid reinforcing self-harm Neutral acutely, warm when not self-harming; say "for emergencies"

The interview and the MSE CS2 guide

Psychiatry's four domains Behaviour, thought, emotion, motivation
History vs mental state Reported vs observed, in the same domains
Three components of sickness Illness (signs), predicament (context), disease (pathophysiology)
The plan's three requirements Biopsychosocial, feasible, mitigates safety concerns
Course of the sickness Discovered entirely from the history
Checklist rule Never during the interview — at the end or after
Presentation order Not the same as the sequence of information-gathering
Empathy, operationalized Paying attention, then showing that you are paying attention
Language rule "Die by suicide" not "commit"; "drug use" not "abuse"
Sensitive topics Raise them early — never save them for the end
Mood vs affect Subjective 0–10 vs observed quality, range, stability, congruence
Insight vs judgment Recognizing illness vs recent safety and treatment behaviours
Case write-up History, MSE, diagnostic impression, management plan
OSCE scope Interview technique assessed in every station, not just psychiatry

Byrne L1 — introduction Lecture 1

What makes a disorder Clinically significant impairment — not stressor, not duration
Panic criterion A Abrupt surge peaking within minutes, ≥ 4 of 13 symptoms
Panic criterion B ≥ 1 month of worry or maladaptive behaviour change
Four limitations of categorical systems Arbitrary thresholds, comorbidity, heterogeneity, subthreshold illness
Diathesis–stress Illness = predisposition + stressor, both continuous
ACEs 10 items before age 18; ~64% have ≥ 1, ~12% have ≥ 4
At ≥ 4 ACEs Depression ~4.4×, drug use > 10×, suicide attempt up to 12×
Each positive childhood experience Lowers adult depression risk 26%
Attachment to phenotype Anxious → GAD/panic; avoidant → substance, restricting; disorganized → BPD
Papageno vs Werther Recovery coverage lowers suicide; sensationalized coverage raises it
Canada suicide ~12 deaths/day, ~3× higher in men, second leading cause ages 15–34
Bias to know Black patients more likely labelled schizophrenia than mood disorder

Byrne L2 — assessment and formulation Lecture 2

MSE mnemonic ASEPTIC — the psychiatric physical exam
MDE mnemonic MSIGECAPS — nine letters for nine criteria
Mania mnemonic GST PAID — decreased need for sleep, not insomnia
Circumstantial vs tangential Circumstantial gets there eventually; tangential never does
Flight of ideas vs loose associations Connections discernible vs not
Hallucination vs illusion No stimulus vs distorted real stimulus
Depersonalization vs derealization Self unreal vs world unreal
Hallucination modality clues Auditory psychiatric; visual delirium; olfactory TLE; tactile withdrawal
Pressured speech Fast and hard to interrupt; its opposite is speech latency
Diagnosis vs formulation What vs why now — a formulation must contain a "because"
The grid 4 P's × bio/psycho/social; the CBL adds a cultural column
The four P's Vulnerability, trigger, maintainer, strengths
Transference set Patient → clinician; countertransference = clinician's reaction; identification = lost objectivity
PTSD proportion ~90% of post-traumatic symptoms resolve by one year

Byrne L3 — treatment Lecture 3

Antidepressant targets Serotonin and/or norepinephrine — monoamines
Serotonin · noradrenaline sources Raphe nuclei · locus coeruleus
Dopamine, both directions ↑ psychosis; ↓ amotivation and anhedonia
Lithium's unique listing The only agent named for suicide prevention
Valproate · lamotrigine Acute mania · bipolar depression
Clozapine Treatment-resistant schizophrenia
Propranolol · benzodiazepines Performance anxiety · short-term only, dependence
Memantine · donepezil NMDA antagonist · cholinesterase inhibitor
Methadone · buprenorphine Full agonist · partial agonist
ECT Most effective antidepressant treatment; 8–12 seizures, 3 per week
Psychedelics 5-HT2A agonism → default mode network disruption, ↑ plasticity
DBT's four skill modules Emotion regulation, distress tolerance, interpersonal effectiveness, mindfulness
TIPP Temperature, intense exercise, progressive muscle relaxation, paced breathing
Cultural rules Trained interpreters not family; explore the explanatory model
Medication hesitancy Explore the concerns — not escalation to neurostimulation or admission

WFQ traps and scope WFQ key · transcripts

Q9 trap "BPD patients don't benefit from admission" — true-ish, but assess first
Q10 discriminator Fluctuating view of another person = unstable relationships
Q11 intruders Histrionic, narcissistic and antisocial traits salted into B–D
Q13 inversion Categorical systems are the rigid ones, not dimensional
Q15 distractor Broad affect is the opposite of the expected restricted affect
Q16 demographics Lecture example is male, WFQ vignette female — same construct
Q19 discriminator Glutamate is what makes that option wrong, not dopamine
Q17 key One sentence only — no explanation given for B, C or D
Q20 and Q21 Key-only facts: 1 in 5 youth; anxiety commonest — no Week 40 source
Q22 distractors decoded Learned behaviour, personality disorder, attachment
Missing questions 1, 2, 3, 7 and 8 are absent — 17 of a stated 22
Answer distribution C keys 11 of 17 — a quirk, not a strategy
"You don't need to memorize" Means clues will be given, not that it's off the exam
CBL draft answers Unvalidated student work — Q12–Q15 blank
